en.heading: Monday and Tuesday: the two closing-day groups
paragraphs: The Korea Heritage Service runs four of Seoul's five Joseon palaces and the royal ancestral shrine, and it staggers their weekly closures so that something is always open. Changdeokgung, Changgyeonggung and Deoksugung close on Mondays. Gyeongbokgung and Jongmyo close on Tuesdays. The fifth palace, Gyeonghuigung (경희궁), belongs to the Seoul Museum of History rather than the heritage service and follows the museum's calendar: closed on Mondays and on January 1, free on every other day.

The practical consequence is simple once you see it. On a Monday, Gyeongbokgung and Jongmyo are your palace choices, and they sit a short subway ride apart. On a Tuesday, head east to Changdeokgung and Changgyeonggung, which are joined by a gate, or downtown to Deoksugung by City Hall. No ordinary day of the week shuts all of them at once, which is why it pays to plan the order of your palace days around the weekday rather than the map.
Search the Korean names in Naver Map or Kakao Map: 경복궁, 창덕궁, 창경궁, 덕수궁, 종묘 and 경희궁. The English names are shown inconsistently in map apps, while the Korean names always find the main gate.

en.heading: The holiday rule that moves a closing day
paragraphs: Public holidays do not close the heritage-service palaces. When a palace's regular closing day falls on a public holiday or a substitute holiday, the palace opens as normal, and its closure moves to the first following day that is not a holiday. This is the rule printed on the Royal Palaces and Tombs visiting-hours page, and it produces a few days a year when the closures stack up.

The 2027 calendar shows how it works. Seollal runs from Saturday, February 6 to the substitute holiday on Tuesday, February 9, so every palace opens on Monday and Tuesday of that week and they all close together on Wednesday, February 10. Independence Movement Day falls on Monday, March 1: the Monday palaces open that day and close on Tuesday, March 2, the same day Gyeongbokgung and Jongmyo take their regular closure, so all five heritage-service sites are shut on March 2. The same stacking happens on Tuesday, May 4, after the Labor Day substitute holiday on Monday, May 3.

Chuseok 2027 runs from Tuesday, September 14 to Thursday, September 16. Gyeongbokgung and Jongmyo therefore stay open through the holiday and take their closure on Friday, September 17, a day many visitors would not expect a palace to be shut. Gyeonghuigung does not follow this rule: the museum lists only Mondays and January 1 as closed, so treat a holiday Monday there as a closed day.

en.heading: Opening hours by season, and the last-entry hour
paragraphs: Gyeongbokgung, Changdeokgung and Jongmyo change their hours with the season, while Changgyeonggung and Deoksugung keep the same 09:00 to 21:00 day all year. Gyeongbokgung uses a long winter, November to February, when it closes at 17:00; Changdeokgung and Jongmyo use November to January and close at 17:30. In every case entry ends an hour before closing, and staff begin guiding visitors toward the exits about 30 minutes before the gates shut.
Gyeonghuigung opens from 09:00 to 18:00. Because it is a small, free site next to the Seoul Museum of History, it fits around a museum visit rather than anchoring a day.

en.heading: When entry is free
paragraphs: Every Wednesday is Culture Day (문화가 있는 날), and admission is free at Changdeokgung's palace halls, Changgyeonggung, Deoksugung and Jongmyo. Gyeongbokgung and the Changdeokgung Secret Garden are excluded, so a Wednesday is the day to spend at the palaces that charge least anyway and save Gyeongbokgung for another day.

Some visitors never pay at all. Foreign visitors aged 18 and under or 65 and over enter the four palaces and Jongmyo free with a passport, and anyone wearing hanbok that meets the heritage service's guideline enters free, whatever their nationality. The Secret Garden has its own, narrower list: only children aged six and under go in free there. Gyeonghuigung charges nobody.

Otherwise, adults pay 3,000 won at Gyeongbokgung and Changdeokgung and 1,000 won at Changgyeonggung, Deoksugung and Jongmyo. The 6,000-won integrated pass covers one entry to each of the four palaces and Jongmyo within six months, but not the Secret Garden. The heritage service also announces occasional free-for-all periods around holidays and festivals on its notice board; when one is coming up, it appears in the dated notice at the top of this guide.

en.heading: Jongmyo and the Secret Garden keep their own timetables
paragraphs: Jongmyo is open six days a week but not in the same way every day. On Mondays, Thursdays and Fridays you can enter only with a timed guided tour of about 50 minutes; English tours start at 10:00, 12:00, 14:00 and 16:00, and each session takes up to 200 people, half booked online and half sold on site. On Wednesdays, weekends and public holidays the shrine is open for self-guided visits, which is the better choice if you want time with the long main hall.

The Secret Garden (후원, Huwon) behind Changdeokgung is seen only on timed tours of about 100 people. Half the places go online from 10:00 six days ahead and half are sold at the palace from 09:00 on the day. English sessions run at 10:30, 11:30 and 14:30, with an extra 15:30 session from March to November. The garden ticket costs 5,000 won for adults and seniors alike, and you also need a palace-hall ticket. Spring and autumn sessions sell out quickly.

en.heading: Planning a week around the closures
paragraphs: A visitor arriving on a Sunday can see all five palaces in three days without meeting a closed gate. On Monday, take Gyeongbokgung in the morning, with the guard ceremony at 10:00, and join a Jongmyo timed tour at 14:00 or 16:00. On Tuesday, book the Secret Garden for 10:30 or 11:30, walk Changdeokgung's halls, then cross through the connecting gate into Changgyeonggung. On Wednesday, enter Deoksugung free for Culture Day, stay into the evening, since it is open until 21:00, and stop at Gyeonghuigung on the way if you are near Gwanghwamun.

Shift the pattern by a day if a public holiday falls inside your trip, and check the day after a long holiday with particular care: that is when a moved closure catches people out. The checker above applies these rules to any date through 2027, along with the dated notices the palaces have published.

en.heading: What the checker covers
paragraphs: The checker combines the weekly closing days, the holiday rule, seasonal hours, Culture Day and age-free rules with the 2027 public-holiday calendar announced by the Korea AeroSpace Administration, and with dated changes the palaces have posted, such as a free-entry period or an early closing. Occasional changes to hours and one-off closures are posted on each palace's notice board at royal.khs.go.kr, which is the page to check on the morning you go.

faq.q: Are Seoul's palaces open on Seollal and Chuseok?
faq.a: Yes. The heritage-service palaces and Jongmyo stay open on public holidays. If a palace's regular closing day falls during the holiday, its closure moves to the first following day that is not a holiday. In 2027 that means every palace closes together on Wednesday, February 10, after Seollal, and Gyeongbokgung and Jongmyo close on Friday, September 17, after Chuseok.

faq.q: Which palace can I visit on a Monday?
faq.a: Gyeongbokgung and Jongmyo Shrine. Changdeokgung, Changgyeonggung, Deoksugung and Gyeonghuigung are closed on Mondays. At Jongmyo a Monday visit is by timed guided tour only, with English tours at 10:00, 12:00, 14:00 and 16:00.

faq.q: Which palaces are open in the evening?
faq.a: Changgyeonggung and Deoksugung are open until 21:00 every day they are open, with last entry at 20:00. Gyeongbokgung opens at night only during announced seasonal runs.

faq.q: Is any palace free every day?
faq.a: Gyeonghuigung, run by the Seoul Museum of History, is always free. At the other palaces and Jongmyo, foreign visitors 18 and under or 65 and over and visitors in hanbok enter free, and every Wednesday is free except at Gyeongbokgung and the Secret Garden.

title.en: Jongmyo Shrine Guide: Royal Ancestral Rites, Tour Days and Etiquette

summary.en: Why Jongmyo is Seoul's most austere royal site, how its guided-tour and free-viewing days work, the restored main hall, the May and November rites, and etiquette.

audience: Visitors who have seen or plan to see a palace and want to understand the Confucian rites behind the Joseon monarchy, and to visit Jongmyo on the right day.
method: Researched from the official sources listed below, checked on October 20, 2026. Hours, fees and booking rules can change; the linked official pages are the final word.
quickAnswer: Jongmyo (종묘) is the Joseon royal ancestral shrine, and its rules depend on the day: closed Tuesdays, guided-tour-only on Mondays, Thursdays and Fridays, and free to wander on Wednesdays, weekends and holidays. Adult admission is 1,000 won (free on Wednesdays), English tours start at 10:00, 12:00, 14:00 and 16:00, and the royal ancestral rite is performed on the first Sunday of May and the first Saturday of November.

en.heading: A house for spirit tablets, not a palace
paragraphs: Jongmyo (종묘) is the royal ancestral shrine of the Joseon dynasty. It has no throne and no bedrooms. It holds spirit tablets (신주, sinju), the wooden markers in which, in Confucian belief, the souls of deceased kings and queens can reside during rites. The shrine was established on this site in 1395, within three years of the dynasty's founding, following a classical rule for capitals: the palace in the center, the ancestral shrine to its left, and the altar to the gods of land and grain, Sajikdan (사직단), to its right, as seen by a king facing south.

For a Confucian dynasty this was arguably the most important ground in the capital. A king's legitimacy rested on continuity with his ancestors, and the grandest state ceremony, the royal ancestral rite, was performed by the king himself, attended by the crown prince, the royal family and officials. Today the shrine holds the tablets of Joseon's kings and queens and of the emperors and empresses of the short-lived Korean Empire. Every rite performed here restated a political idea: the state was a family line, and the living ruler answered to the dead.

That makes Jongmyo a different kind of visit from the palaces. There is nothing to go inside, no garden to stroll and very little ornament, and visitors who expect another palace can leave puzzled after twenty minutes. Come instead for the scale of the space, the silence and the belief behind it. If you have already seen Gyeongbokgung and want to understand the system it served, Jongmyo is the logical next step. If you have one afternoon and want color, interiors and photographs, a palace will suit you better.

en.heading: Why Jongmyo is deliberately plain
paragraphs: The main hall, Jeongjeon (정전), is a single wooden building roughly 100 meters long: a low roof, a long row of identical red-painted bays with very little carving or decorative color, set on a broad stone platform above a court of rough stone slabs. The austerity is the message. Confucian ritual architecture was meant to express reverence, restraint and permanence rather than wealth, and the repetition of identical chambers presents generation after generation as one unbroken line, each ancestor given the same measure of space.

The building's length is a record of the dynasty itself. Jeongjeon began with seven bays in 1395; as kings died and tablets accumulated, bays were added, reaching 11, then 15 in 1726 and 19 in 1836. Each bay is a chamber, so looking along the facade you are reading a family tree laid on its side. UNESCO inscribed Jongmyo on the World Heritage List in 1995 under its criterion for an outstanding type of building, citing both the distinctive architecture of the ritual space and the survival of the rite and its music in their original forms.

To see what the builders intended, stand at the southern edge of Jeongjeon's stone court and stay still for a minute. The roofline runs out past the edge of your vision in both directions, and there is no tower or central gate to anchor the eye. On a quiet weekday it is one of the most affecting architectural experiences in Seoul. On a busy weekend afternoon the effect is harder to find, which is a good reason to consider a guided weekday visit.

en.heading: Jeongjeon and Yeongnyeongjeon: two halls, two ranks of memory
paragraphs: Jeongjeon's 19 chambers hold 49 tablets, those of 19 kings and 30 queens. Its side corridors house two smaller shrines: Gongsindang (공신당), honoring 83 meritorious officials of successive reigns, and Chilsadang (칠사당), dedicated to seven deities of everyday life, a sign of how state Confucianism absorbed older folk belief. The present core of the hall dates from a rebuilding completed in 1608 after the Japanese invasion of 1592, with the later extensions added at either end as the dynasty went on.

West of it stands Yeongnyeongjeon (영녕전), whose name means eternal peace, built in 1421 under King Sejong when the main hall ran short of room. It now has 16 chambers holding 34 tablets, largely of kings and queens whose reigns were short or whose standing was lower, and its central section rises above the wings on either side. Smaller and more intimate than Jeongjeon, it is easy to skip in the rush toward the exit. Do not: the contrast between the two halls, one for the main line and one for the rest, is the point of the site.

Jeongjeon has just emerged from its largest repair in generations. Work began in 2020, and during it the tablets were kept at the old Seonwonjeon hall in Changdeokgung. On April 20, 2025, they returned in a hwanan rite (환안제), a solemn procession carrying the tablets home that had last been performed in 1870, 155 years earlier. Some summaries date the reopening to 2024, but the tablets came back in April 2025. If you saw the hall wrapped in scaffolding on an earlier trip, it is worth a second look now.

en.heading: Walking the grounds in the right order
paragraphs: From the main entrance on Jongno, a stone path runs into the grounds with a slightly raised central strip. This is the sindo (신도), the road for the ancestral spirits, with lower paths alongside for the living king and crown prince. Out of courtesy, walk beside the raised strip rather than on it; Korean visitors and guides will notice. The route mapped by the shrine office runs from that path past the ritual-preparation buildings to the two great halls and back, and takes about an hour at an unhurried pace on a free-viewing day.

The order below follows that official route. On a guided weekday you cover the same ground in about 50 minutes with a docent and cannot wander off on your own, and the guide decides where the group pauses, so use the list mainly on free-viewing days, when you set the pace yourself.
checklist: Sindo, the spirit road, starting just inside the main gate.
Jaegung (재궁), where the king and crown prince prepared and purified themselves before a rite.
Jeonsacheong (전사청), the kitchen court where ritual food was prepared.
Jeongjeon, with Gongsindang and Chilsadang in its side corridors.
Yeongnyeongjeon, west of the main hall.
Akgongcheong (악공청), where the ritual musicians waited.
Hyangdaecheong (향대청), which stored incense and the written prayers.
Mangmyoru (망묘루), where the shrine's officials worked, and the square pond beside it, near the exit.

en.heading: Jongmyo Jerye: the rite that still happens twice a year
paragraphs: Jongmyo Jerye (종묘제례), the royal ancestral rite, was once performed at Jeongjeon five times a year and at Yeongnyeongjeon twice, with further rites for floods, droughts, epidemics, wars, royal weddings and the naming of a crown prince. Abolished in 1945, it was revived in 1969 and moved in 1971 to the first Sunday of May. Today it is held on the first Sunday of May and the first Saturday of November. It became national intangible heritage in 1975, and in 2001 UNESCO recognized the rite and its music together as intangible heritage of humanity.

The rite follows eight steps: welcoming the spirits with incense, liquor and silk; presenting the sacrificial food; three successive offerings of wine, the first accompanied by a written prayer; the officiants partaking of the sacrificial wine and food; clearing the vessels; and burning the prayer and silk. Offerings include beef, mutton and pork, grains, rice cakes, salted fish and fruit, laid out in prescribed ritual vessels. Nothing is staged for spectators. You are watching descendants and officials honor the dead, slowly and largely in silence.

The music, Jongmyo Jeryeak (종묘제례악), is as old as the rite's present form. King Sejong composed two suites, Botaepyeong and Jeongdaeeop, praising the virtues and achievements of the dynasty's kings; in 1463, under King Sejo, they were adopted for Jongmyo, and each has 11 pieces. Listen for the tuned sets of bronze bells (pyeonjong) and stone chimes (pyeongyeong). Rows of dancers perform ilmu (일무): the munmu, gentle and static, honors learning, and the mumu, strong and forceful, honors military merit.

To attend, watch the shrine's notices from early April for the May rite and from late October for the November one. In May 2026 the rite ran at Yeongnyeongjeon from 10:00 to 12:00 and at Jeongjeon from 14:00 to 16:30, with the chambers open for viewing afterward. Entry to Jongmyo was free that day but regular tours were suspended, and spectator seats were reserved through Ticketlink from about two weeks before. The afternoon Jeongjeon rite is the main event. Bring water and patience, because it lasts more than two hours.

en.heading: Guided-tour days and free-viewing days
paragraphs: Jongmyo has the most complicated visiting rules of any royal site in Seoul, and misreading them is the most common mistake. It is closed on Tuesdays. On Mondays, Thursdays and Fridays it is open only by timed guided tour: you enter at a set time and stay with a docent for about 50 minutes. On Wednesdays, Saturdays, Sundays and public holidays it is a free-viewing day, when you walk in during opening hours and stay as long as you like. Adult admission is 1,000 won, and Wednesday, the government's weekly Culture Day, is free.

Each timed tour admits up to 200 people per language. Individuals and parties of fewer than ten need no reservation and simply buy a ticket on site; online booking, open from 30 to 4 days ahead, is meant for groups. Arrive early, because latecomers are refused. English tours run at 10:00, 12:00, 14:00 and 16:00 on weekdays and Sundays, while Saturdays and holidays have Korean commentary only. As at the palaces, Korean nationals may join a foreign-language tour only with a foreign companion.

The rules flex with the season and the festival calendar. In July and August 2026 the timed system was suspended for the heat and every open day became a free-viewing day, and during palace festival periods the shrine has also switched to general viewing. Hours run 09:00 to 18:00 from February to May and in September and October, to 18:30 in summer and to 17:30 from November to January, with last entry an hour before closing. Check the Jongmyo notice board in the week of your visit.

rows: Timed guided tour only, about 50 minutes

en.heading: How to behave at a place of ancestral rites
paragraphs: Jongmyo is still a working ritual site, so behave as you would at a cemetery or a memorial service. Keep your voice low, especially in the courts of the two halls, and keep children from running across the stone platforms. Save snacks for outside the gates, and do not sit or lean on the halls' doorsteps or railings. Treat the chamber doors as closed: they are opened for rites and special viewings, not for curiosity, and the dim interiors are the dwelling places of the tablets.

Two customs are worth following. Walk beside the raised spirit road rather than on it, and when a guide stops at the edge of a court, stay behind the line the group forms instead of stepping forward for a clearer photograph. There is no dress code beyond ordinary modesty, and hanbok wearers enter free under the same guideline as the palaces. During a rite, switch off flash, stay silent while the music plays, and arrive early for a viewing spot rather than pushing forward once the ceremony has started.

en.heading: Pairing Jongmyo with Changgyeonggung or Insadong
paragraphs: On free-viewing days the shrine's north gate, Buksinmun (북신문), opens onto the path over Yulgok-ro that links Jongmyo with Changgyeonggung, two sites cut apart by a colonial-era road and reconnected in recent years. Each site needs its own ticket, and Changgyeonggung's gate on that side stops admitting visitors at 17:00 in winter and 17:30 in spring and autumn. On a Wednesday, weekend or holiday, the natural sequence is Changdeokgung and its garden in the morning, Changgyeonggung after lunch, and Jongmyo through Buksinmun in the late afternoon.

Insadong (인사동) is the easy pairing on any open day. Leave by the main gate onto Jongno, walk west past Tapgol Park, and you reach the start of Insadong-gil in roughly ten to fifteen minutes, with teahouses and craft shops for a slow end to the day. Search 종묘 for the shrine and 인사동길 for the street in Naver Map or Kakao Map. Jongno 3-ga Station on Lines 1, 3 and 5 is about five minutes from the shrine's main gate by Exit 11 or Exit 8.

A Monday plan works when most palaces are closed: Gyeongbokgung, which opens on Mondays, in the morning; lunch around Anguk; the 14:00 English guided tour at Jongmyo; then tea in Insadong. It is also the best way to see Jongmyo as it deserves to be seen, slowly and with a docent explaining what each building was for, without weekend crowds on the stone court.

faq.q: Can I walk around Jongmyo on my own any day?
faq.a: Only on Wednesdays, Saturdays, Sundays and public holidays, which are free-viewing days. On Mondays, Thursdays and Fridays you can enter only with a timed guided tour of about 50 minutes, and on Tuesdays the shrine is closed. Summer and festival periods sometimes switch every open day to free viewing, so check the notice board.

faq.q: Do I need to reserve the English guided tour?
faq.a: Not as an individual or a party of fewer than ten. Buy a ticket on site and be at the start before 10:00, 12:00, 14:00 or 16:00, because latecomers are not admitted. Groups of ten or more book online between 30 and 4 days ahead. Each session takes up to 200 people.

faq.q: Is the main hall open again after its restoration?
faq.a: Yes. Repairs on Jeongjeon began in 2020, and the 49 spirit tablets kept at Changdeokgung during the work were returned in a formal rite on April 20, 2025. Some sources give 2024 for the completion, but the official return took place in April 2025. The chamber doors stay closed except during rites and announced special viewings.

faq.q: How can I see the Jongmyo Jerye ceremony?
faq.a: It is held on the first Sunday of May and the first Saturday of November. Watch the Jongmyo notice board on royal.khs.go.kr in the weeks before; in 2026 the May rite had free entry to the grounds and spectator seats reserved through Ticketlink about two weeks ahead. The main Jeongjeon rite takes place in the afternoon.

faq.q: How long does a visit take?
faq.a: A guided weekday tour lasts about 50 minutes. On a free-viewing day, allow an hour to walk the full route at a relaxed pace, or 90 minutes if you want to sit for a while in Jeongjeon's court. On a rite day, expect to spend most of an afternoon.

title.en: Hanbok Rental in Seoul: Palace Free-Entry Rules, Fit and Etiquette

summary.en: What counts as hanbok for free palace entry, how Seoul rental shops work, how to time a rental around Gyeongbokgung hours and Bukchon's 10-to-5 rule.

audience: First-time visitors to Seoul deciding whether to rent hanbok for a palace visit, and how to do it without wasting time or breaking the rules.
method: Researched from the official sources listed below, checked on October 20, 2026. Hours, fees and booking rules can change; the linked official pages are the final word.
quickAnswer: Rent hanbok if you want photographs and a slower, more deliberate palace visit, not for the free ticket, which saves an adult foreign visitor 3,000 won at Gyeongbokgung. To qualify, wear a wrap-collar jeogori with a separate skirt or trousers. Book a block of two to four hours near Gyeongbokgung Station, avoid Tuesdays when Gyeongbokgung is closed, and be out of Bukchon's red zone by 5 p.m.

en.heading: A jacket, a skirt or trousers, and a coat for going out
paragraphs: Hanbok (한복) is the umbrella word for Korean dress, and it is built on a simple two-piece logic: an upper garment and a separate lower one. The jacket, jeogori (저고리), is worn by men and women alike. Learn its parts and you can read any hanbok at a glance: the collar band (git), the strip of white trim laid along it (dongjeong, a symbol of cleanliness), the overlapping front panel (seop), roomy sleeves (somae) and the long ties (goreum) knotted at the chest. Women's jeogori are short and fitted; men's are longer and looser.

Below the jacket, women wear the chima (치마), a pleated skirt tied high on the body that falls to the ankles, while men wear baji (바지), wide trousers. Over everything goes the durumagi (두루마기), a full-length coat that both sexes put on for formal occasions or simply to go outdoors. During the Joseon dynasty (1392–1910), fabric, color and ornament signaled rank: commoners wore hemp and cotton in plain colors, while fine silk and embroidered motifs belonged to the court and the aristocracy.

This is not a museum costume. In July 2022 the Cultural Heritage Administration designated hanbok saenghwal, the whole practice of making, wearing and enjoying hanbok, as a National Intangible Cultural Heritage, noting that Koreans still wear it to show respect at Seollal and Chuseok, at weddings and at ancestral rites. That context is worth carrying with you. When you walk a palace path in hanbok, you are borrowing a living dress code, and the people around you will read it that way.

en.heading: Why the rental rack looks nothing like a wedding hanbok
paragraphs: Walk into a rental shop near Gyeongbokgung and most of what hangs on the rails is what Koreans call fusion hanbok: polyester satin in saturated colors, gold-foil prints, lace sleeves, tulle overlays and skirts lifted by a hooped petticoat. Some racks also carry imitations of royal robes or military uniforms. These outfits are designed to photograph brightly and to go on and off quickly, which is exactly what a two-hour rental needs.

A traditional hanbok works differently. It is usually silk or ramie, cut in quieter colors, and its beauty lies in the curve of the collar and the way the skirt moves rather than in surface decoration. Everyday saenghwal hanbok sits at the other end of the scale: simplified cotton or linen pieces meant for daily wear. None of these is wrong to rent. The distinction that matters on the day is that palace staff judge the structure of an outfit, not its taste, and the free-entry rule excludes some of the most theatrical options.

Our advice is to choose restraint. If you want photographs that still look good in ten years, ask for the plainest well-cut set the shop has, in one or two colors, and skip the costume crown. A muted jeogori over a contrasting skirt reads as hanbok in every frame; a glittering one-piece gown reads as a party dress and may not count at the gate. Let accessories carry the tradition instead: a norigae pendant hung from the jacket ties, or a binyeo hairpin, are the details Koreans notice.

en.heading: The free-entry rule, clause by clause
paragraphs: Visitors wearing hanbok enter the major royal heritage sites free: the four palaces (Gyeongbokgung, Changdeokgung, Changgyeonggung and Deoksugung), Jongmyo Shrine and the Joseon royal tombs. The Royal Palaces and Tombs Center's own Q&A states that the benefit applies to Korean and foreign visitors alike, because its purpose is to spread hanbok at home and abroad. One exception matters for planners: the Changdeokgung rear garden (Huwon) tour is a separately ticketed visit whose free list does not include hanbok, so you still pay for it.

The guideline, which is more detailed in Korean than in English, comes down to structure. Both traditional and modernized hanbok qualify. You need an upper garment and a separate lower one, so a durumagi thrown over jeans does not count. The jeogori must keep its overlapping wrap collar; the Korean text says the style of tie or knot does not matter, while the English page asks that ties and buttons stay fastened. Trousers must follow the traditional wide-panel cut, even if they zip at the waist. Any style of skirt is accepted, including a waist-tied one, provided the jacket reaches the waistline.

Refusals follow the same logic. A jeogori over jeans fails, as does a hanbok skirt with a T-shirt, a T-shirt-style top printed or cut to look like a jeogori, and a one-piece hanbok-style dress with no separate jacket. Staff may also turn away outfits they consider too revealing for the setting. Notice what the rules leave out: there is nothing about gender, so men in skirts and women in trousers qualify as long as the structure holds. The table below summarizes the cases that come up most often at the gate.

Keep the money in perspective. At Gyeongbokgung the adult ticket for foreign visitors aged 19 to 64 is 3,000 won, and foreign visitors aged 18 and under or 65 and over enter free regardless of what they wear. Any rental costs many times that. Rent hanbok because you want to wear it, and treat the free ticket as a courtesy rather than a saving.

en.heading: How a rental shop visit runs, from payment to return
paragraphs: Rental shops cluster around Gyeongbokgung Station on Line 3, whose Exit 5 is about two minutes from the palace on foot. Search 한복대여 (hanbok daeyeo) on Naver Map or Kakao Map and dozens appear. The useful filters are opening time, whether the shop takes online reservations, and whether recent customer photos show the plainer styles you want. Weekend mornings in spring and autumn are the busiest slots, so reserve ahead if your dates are fixed.

The sequence is broadly the same everywhere. You choose a time block, commonly a few hours or a full day, and pay up front; returning late usually triggers an extra charge, so read the shop's rule before you leave. Some shops ask for a deposit or an ID. You then pick a skirt or trousers and a jacket, and staff help you dress, often over a thin layer of your own clothes, setting the skirt height and tying the ribbon. Your bag and coat stay in a locker or behind the counter.

Extras are where the bill grows: hair styling (braids finished with a daenggi ribbon, or a low bun with a binyeo pin), accessories such as norigae, a small handbag, and premium garments. Ask exactly what the base price includes before you start choosing, and decide in advance whether hair styling is worth the extra time, since it can mean a second queue at busy hours. Ask whether shoes are included; if you wear your own, flat, closed shoes in a dark color disappear under a long skirt and save your feet on palace gravel.

Before you walk out, check three things. The skirt hem should clear the ground by about a finger's width; the jacket ties should sit centered rather than slipping to one side; and your phone and cash should be somewhere you can reach. Rental hanbok rarely has pockets, so take the small drawstring bag if the shop offers one.

en.heading: Fitting the rental clock to palace hours and weather
paragraphs: Your rental block and the palace's opening hours need to overlap. Gyeongbokgung is closed every Tuesday; when a Tuesday is a public holiday it opens and closes on the next non-holiday instead. It opens at 09:00 and closes at 17:00 from November to February, 18:00 in March to May and September to October, and 18:30 from June to August, with last entry an hour before closing. Changdeokgung, Changgyeonggung and Deoksugung close on Mondays instead, so a Tuesday in hanbok belongs at one of those.

A three-hour block suits a first visit. A sample weekday in October: 09:15 arrive at the shop, choose and dress; 10:00 enter Gyeongbokgung through Gwanghwamun and Heungnyemun and walk up to the throne hall, Geunjeongjeon; 10:45 Gyeonghoeru pavilion and its pond for photographs; 11:20 the quieter northern courtyards toward Hyangwonjeong; 11:50 walk back toward the shop; 12:15 return the hanbok. Add half an hour if you book hair styling, and push everything earlier on weekends.

Weather changes the calculation more than visitors expect. Rental hanbok is layered synthetic fabric, and in July and August the paved courtyards hold heat, so go at opening time or skip it. In December and January the problem reverses: thermal layers underneath are fine, and a coat on top is fine too, but remember that a durumagi only counts as part of hanbok when the jeogori and skirt or trousers are underneath. On wet days long hems soak up water from the stone, so choose a shorter block and carry an umbrella.

Deoksugung and Changgyeonggung, both open until 21:00 with last entry at 20:00, are the palaces where an evening rental works, and Deoksugung's compact grounds suit a short block. Wherever you go, return on time. A late fee on an inexpensive rental is a frustrating way to end a good day.

en.heading: Taking photos without turning the palace into a studio
paragraphs: The palace visitor rules treat ordinary souvenir photography as already permitted, so you can photograph yourself and your companions freely. The same rules draw a line at commercial shoots such as films, dramas and advertising, and at souvenir photos using character costumes, mascot suits or similar non-everyday outfits and props, which require a permit because they can disrupt other visitors or the dignity of the site. Drone filming is limited to approved public-interest projects. A rented hanbok counts as dress, not costume; a cosplay outfit with props may not.

The unwritten rules matter as much. Keep gateways, thresholds and narrow bridges clear, since posing in a gate passage for five minutes blocks everyone behind you. Stay off stone platforms, railings and roped-off steps even when the angle is tempting. If you hire a photographer, keep the session discreet and mobile. Palace grounds are entirely no-smoking, and staff can refuse entry to visitors carrying alcohol, tents or picnic mats.

Other people in hanbok are not part of the scenery. Ask before photographing strangers up close, especially children, and avoid filming staff or guards at close range for social media. A simple test works well: if your shot needs someone else to move, wait or move yourself.

en.heading: Bukchon in hanbok: walk the lanes between 10 and 5
paragraphs: Bukchon, the hanok neighborhood east of Gyeongbokgung, is where many renters head next, and it is where care matters most, because people live in these houses. Jongno District has designated the most crowded lanes around Bukchon-ro 11-gil, about 34,000 square meters, as a red zone where tourist visits are allowed only from 10:00 to 17:00. After a guidance period from November 2024, enforcement began on March 1, 2025, and entering for sightseeing outside those hours can bring a fine of 100,000 won. The surrounding orange and yellow zones have no hour limits but are under closer management.

This shapes your plan. If your rental starts at 09:00, do the palace first and Bukchon after 10:00; if you rent in the afternoon, finish Bukchon well before 17:00 and return the hanbok afterward. In the lanes, speak quietly, do not sit on doorsteps or lean on gates, stay out of courtyards that happen to be open, and never photograph residents or through windows. Search 북촌로11길 on Naver Map before you go to see where the restricted stretch begins.

Our judgment: the palace courtyards are the better backdrop for hanbok, with space, context and no one's front door in the frame. Treat Bukchon as a short walk of fifteen or twenty minutes for one or two street views on the way back, not as a location for a photo shoot.

en.heading: Who should rent, who should skip, and the avoidable mistakes
paragraphs: Rent if you want photographs to remember the trip, if you are with children or a group who will enjoy dressing up together, or if you are curious to see the palace from inside the clothes it was built around. Raised thresholds, steep wooden steps and floor-level rooms make more sense when you move in a long skirt. A first visit to Gyeongbokgung in spring or autumn is the classic case, and it is genuinely worth doing once.

Skip it if you have only half a day for several sights, because dressing, returning and walking back to the shop easily absorb an hour. Skip midsummer afternoons, and think twice if you have mobility concerns, since long skirts and uneven stone are a poor combination. If you want something of the experience without the logistics, buy a single accessory, such as a norigae or a hairpin; it travels home better than a hundred near-identical photographs.

The common mistakes are predictable: renting on a Tuesday for Gyeongbokgung; choosing a one-piece dress and paying at the gate after all; leaving the shop without noting the return time; wandering into Bukchon's red zone after 17:00; and booking hair styling on a crowded weekend morning, which can consume half the rental block. Avoid those five and the hanbok becomes what it should be, the part of the day you remember most clearly.

faq.q: Do foreign tourists get free palace entry in hanbok?
faq.a: Yes. The Royal Palaces and Tombs Center says free admission for hanbok wearers applies to Korean and foreign visitors alike at the four palaces, Jongmyo Shrine and the royal tombs. Your outfit needs a wrap-collar jacket and a separate skirt or trousers. The Changdeokgung rear garden (Huwon) tour still requires its own ticket.

faq.q: Can a man wear a skirt or a woman wear trousers and still enter free?
faq.a: Yes. The official guideline is written around structure, not gender: a wrap-collar jeogori plus a separate skirt or traditional-cut trousers. As long as the outfit keeps that structure and is not overly revealing, who wears which piece does not affect free admission.

faq.q: Is modern or fusion hanbok accepted for free admission?
faq.a: Modernized hanbok is accepted when it keeps the basic form. What fails is anything without a separate wrap-collar jacket, such as a one-piece hanbok-style dress or a T-shirt cut to look like a jeogori, and any mix of hanbok with everyday clothes like jeans.

faq.q: What should I wear under a rental hanbok?
faq.a: A thin, close-fitting layer such as a T-shirt and leggings or shorts works in most seasons, and thermals are fine in winter. Wear flat, closed shoes in a dark color unless the shop supplies footwear, since palace paths are gravel and stone.

faq.q: Can I visit Bukchon in hanbok in the evening?
faq.a: Not the red zone around Bukchon-ro 11-gil, where tourist visits are limited to 10:00–17:00 and sightseeing outside those hours can be fined 100,000 won. Plan Bukchon for late morning or early afternoon, and choose Deoksugung or Changgyeonggung, both open until 21:00, if you want an evening in hanbok.

faq.q: Is it disrespectful for foreigners to wear hanbok?
faq.a: No. The palaces' free-entry program exists precisely to popularize hanbok in Korea and abroad, and it applies to foreign visitors explicitly. What reads as disrespectful is behavior, not nationality: parody costumes, blocking paths for photo shoots, or treating residential Bukchon as a set.

title.en: Seoul Buddhist Temples: Jogyesa, Bongeunsa and How Templestay Works

summary.en: How to visit Jogyesa and Bongeunsa well: temple layout, main-hall etiquette, the Lotus Lantern Festival, Templestay day and overnight formats, and temple food.

audience: Visitors to Seoul who want to see a working Buddhist temple, behave correctly inside it, and decide whether a day program or an overnight Templestay is worth their time.
method: Researched from the official sources listed below, checked on October 20, 2026. Hours, fees and booking rules can change; the linked official pages are the final word.
quickAnswer: Start with Jogyesa, the Jogye Order's head temple in central Seoul, free and open around the clock; add Bongeunsa, across the road from COEX, for an older temple among trees. Enter halls by the side doors with shoes off and socks on, and keep your voice low. If you want more than a walk-through, book a one-day Templestay; save the overnight, with its 4 a.m. start, for travelers who actively want monastic routine.

en.heading: Jogyesa: a head temple squeezed into a city block
paragraphs: 조계사 (Jogyesa) is the chief temple of the Jogye Order, the order that represents mainstream Korean Seon (Zen) Buddhism. By the temple's own account the order has around 3,000 temples nationwide and some 15,000 monks and nuns, including the three great 'jewel temples' of Tongdosa, Haeinsa and Songgwangsa. The order's administrative headquarters, a training center and the Central Buddhist Museum share the compound, so many of the people crossing the courtyard briskly are staff, not visitors.

Its history explains the urban setting. Monks founded it in 1910 as Gakhwangsa, the first temple built inside the boundary of old Seoul's four main gates, as a center for an independent Korean Buddhism. It was renamed Taegosa in 1938 and became Jogyesa in 1954, part of an effort to clear away colonial-era influence on the religion. The main hall is open 24 hours a day, and the temple presents itself as a place anyone can walk into, local or foreign, believer or not.

Jogyesa changes with the calendar, which is the best reason to time a visit. Lotus lanterns hang from roughly March to June ahead of Buddha's Birthday, lotus plants fill the courtyard in July and August, and a chrysanthemum festival runs through September and October. Look for the lacebark pine (baeksong) and the old pagoda tree near the main hall, and note the Information Center for Foreigners on the temple map if you have questions.

en.heading: Bongeunsa: twelve centuries across the road from COEX
paragraphs: 봉은사 (Bongeunsa) is much older, and its setting is the point: a wooded slope of halls and pines directly across the street from the COEX complex and the glass towers of Samseong-dong. Korea's national tourism organization dates its founding to 794, in the reign of King Wonseong of Silla, under the name Gyeonseongsa. In 1498 Queen Jeonghyeon restored it and gave it its present name, and it was moved to its current site during the reign of King Myeongjong in the sixteenth century.

The temple is known for its carved scripture woodblocks, including those of the Avatamsaka (Flower Garland) Sutra; VisitKorea counts 3,479 scripture pieces in 13 types. What most visitors remember, though, is the towering standing Maitreya Buddha on the upper terrace and the sight of office towers framed by temple eaves, which makes Bongeunsa the more photogenic of the two. The grounds are open from 05:00 to 22:00 every day, admission is free, and early morning is the calmest time to walk them.

Choosing between them is straightforward. Pick Jogyesa if you want to see Korean Buddhism as daily institutional life, a short walk from Insadong and the palaces. Pick Bongeunsa if you want architecture, trees and space, or if you are already staying in Gangnam. With time for only one, choose Jogyesa during lantern season and Bongeunsa for the rest of the year.

en.heading: Reading a temple from the first gate to the main hall
paragraphs: Korean temples are laid out as a journey, and knowing the sequence turns a stroll into something you can read. The first gate is usually the iljumun (일주문), the one-pillar gate. Its posts stand in a single line, so from the side it appears to rest on one pillar, an image of the single-minded path to enlightenment. Passing through it marks the step from ordinary ground into the temple precinct, which is why some Koreans pause and bow there.

Larger mountain temples then lead you through a cheonwangmun (천왕문), a gate housing the Four Heavenly Kings, guardians of the four directions whose glaring faces and trampled demons are meant to keep harm out. Some add a final gate of non-duality, the burimun (불이문), before the courtyard opens. City temples compress the sequence: Jogyesa has its one-pillar gate on the street and goes straight into the courtyard, while at Bongeunsa you enter through a gate called Jinyeomun (진여문).

At the head of the main courtyard stands the principal hall. When it enshrines Shakyamuni, the historical Buddha, it is called daeungjeon (대웅전), the Hall of the Great Hero; halls for other Buddhas carry other names, such as geungnakjeon for Amitabha, which Jogyesa also has. In front you will often find a stone pagoda, and nearby a bell pavilion (beomjongnu) whose great bell is struck at the dawn and evening services. The painted eaves in green, red and blue, called dancheong, both protect the wood and mark the building as sacred.

en.heading: Inside the hall: doors, bows and where not to sit
paragraphs: Most visitors only look in from the doorway, which is perfectly fine. If you go inside, the rules are few and they all express one idea: the hall is in use. Enter by a side door, because the large central door faces the main altar and is reserved for monks and nuns. Take your shoes off on the step and leave them neatly with the toes pointing outward, so you can step back into them without turning around. Wear socks; bare feet are not welcome on hall floors.

On entering, a half bow toward the altar with palms pressed together at the chest (hapjang, 합장) is the courteous minimum. Buddhists follow it with three full prostrations, which visitors may join or skip. If you sit, take a cushion to one side rather than the central space directly before the main Buddha, which is kept for the officiating monk. Never walk between someone and the altar while they are bowing; pass behind them. Keep your voice low and your phone silent, and do not touch statues or offerings.

Photography is where visitors most often misstep. Many halls post signs asking you not to photograph the altar, and no hall welcomes close-up photos of people at prayer. Photograph the architecture from the courtyard, and if you want an interior image, ask at the information desk first. Dress modestly, with shoulders and knees covered, and remember that smoking, alcohol and meat have no place on temple grounds.
checklist: Use the side doors; the center door is for monks and nuns
Shoes off on the step, toes pointing out; socks on
Half bow with palms together when entering and leaving
Sit to the side, never center-front of the main Buddha
Pass behind people who are bowing
No photos of worshippers; ask before photographing interiors
Phone silent, voice low, no food or drink in the hall

en.heading: Lanterns, Buddha's Birthday and Yeondeunghoe
paragraphs: Buddha's Birthday (부처님오신날, Bucheonim Osin Nal) falls on the eighth day of the fourth lunar month and is a national holiday; in 2027 it lands on Thursday, May 13. For weeks beforehand, temples hang lotus lanterns by the thousand, and many carry a paper tag naming the family that offered it. That is why the canopy over Jogyesa's courtyard is thick with slips of paper: each lantern is a prayer for someone specific.

The lantern festival itself, Yeondeunghoe (연등회), was inscribed on UNESCO's Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2020. UNESCO's description gives its shape: it opens with a ritual bathing of an image of the infant Buddha, moves into a procession of handmade lanterns, and ends with communal games. Lighting a lantern stands for spreading the Buddha's wisdom to the individual, the community and society, and anyone can take part regardless of faith, which is a large part of why it was recognized.

In Seoul the festival falls on a weekend shortly before the holiday. In 2026 it ran like this: lantern exhibitions from April into May at Gwanghwamun Square, Jogyesa and Bongeunsa; a rally with the infant-Buddha bathing rite at Dongguk University Stadium on Saturday afternoon; the main lantern parade along Jongno from Heunginjimun to Jogyesa from 19:00 to 21:30; a street celebration at Jonggak afterward; and on Sunday a traditional culture fair in front of Jogyesa, ending with an evening procession through Insadong. The 2027 schedule had not been posted as of October 20, 2026, so check llf.or.kr in spring.

For the parade, arrive at least half an hour before the start and stand along Jongno between Jongno 3-ga and Jonggak, where the route ends near the temple. The Sunday fair is the easier choice for families, with lantern making, traditional crafts and temple food to try. In 2026 the organizers also ran a lantern-making session and parade places for international guests, announced in English on the festival site; those notices were closed by the festival weekend, so watch for them early.

en.heading: One-day, experience or rest: choosing a Templestay
paragraphs: Templestay is the program that opens Korean temples to lay visitors for a few hours or a few nights, and its official booking site, eng.templestay.com, sorts everything into three types. One-day programs last about two to three hours and usually combine a temple tour, meditation and tea. Experience-oriented programs are typically weekend overnights built around temple routine: services, 108 prostrations, formal monastic meals and a craft such as lantern making. Rest-oriented programs keep the schedule light and leave you time to sit, walk and sleep.

The booking site has a 'Temples for Foreigners' filter, the quickest way to find programs that work for non-Korean speakers. In Seoul, Jogyesa listed a one-day tea and meditation program called 'Seon of Tea', and Bongeunsa listed BONG-PASS, an open-format temple day every Tuesday from 10:00 to 16:00, alongside its weekend overnight. Program names, days and fees change by season, so treat these as examples of what was listed in October 2026. The site's FAQ also names Geumsunsa, Hwagyesa, Jinkwansa, Myogaksa and the International Seon Center as Seoul temples within easy reach by bus or subway. If you are already near Jogyesa, the Templestay information center is on the same road, at 56 Ujeongguk-ro.

Our judgment: most first-time visitors should book a one-day program. It delivers what is hard to get alone, a monk or trained guide to ask questions, meditation with instruction and a proper tea ceremony, without the dawn alarm. Choose an overnight only if the routine itself appeals to you. If what you actually want is silence and scenery, a rest-oriented stay at a mountain temple outside Seoul will serve you better than any city program.

rows: Short trips and a first encounter
Rest and quiet, often at mountain temples

en.heading: What an overnight at Bongeunsa actually asks of you
paragraphs: Bongeunsa's regular weekend Templestay, as listed for its 2025–2026 season, shows the real shape of an overnight. Check-in and a change into the temple uniform, a vest and loose trousers, start at 13:50 on Saturday, followed by an etiquette lesson and temple tour, a monastic dinner, the evening service, quiet meditation and lights out at 21:00. The wake-up comes at 04:00 for the 04:20 dawn service, then 108 prostrations from 05:00 to 05:50, breakfast, tea with a monk at 09:00 and check-out by 11:00. The listed fee was 120,000 won per person.

The terms are part of the program. Reservations open one month before the date and close the day before. Cancel 14 or more days ahead for a full refund, seven days ahead for 70 percent, and later for nothing; no-shows are discouraged firmly. Bring your own towel, toiletries, socks, a change of clothes and a reusable tumbler; wear modest clothing and skip strong perfume. Rooms are shared and men and women do not room together. You may sit out a session if you feel unwell, but tell the staff.

Whether to do it comes down to attention, not comfort. A thin floor mattress, the 4 a.m. start and 108 full bows are hard on knees and sleep. The reward is the dawn service in near darkness and a meal eaten in complete silence, neither of which a day visit can give you. If both sound like an ordeal rather than a curiosity, take the one-day program and enjoy it without guilt.

en.heading: Temple food, from the four bowls to a city half day
paragraphs: Korean temple food (사찰음식, sachal eumsik) follows the precept against taking life, so it uses no meat or fish, and it also leaves out the five pungent plants known as osinchae. Lists vary slightly, but they usually include garlic, green onion, chives and wild chives. The traditional reasoning is that their strong flavors agitate the mind and disturb meditation. What remains is cooking built on fermented soybean paste and soy sauce, mountain greens, mushrooms, perilla and whatever is in season.

At a Templestay you will likely eat at least one meal as balwoo gongyang (발우공양), the formal monastic meal. Each person uses a nested set of four bowls for rice, soup, side dishes and water. Food is served in a fixed order, you take only what you will finish, and the meal is eaten in silence. At the end you rinse each bowl, traditionally wiping it with a reserved piece of pickled vegetable, and drink the rinse so that nothing is wasted. It is austere by design, and it is the clearest lesson a temple offers about eating with attention.

Without a Templestay, try the temple-food stalls at the lantern festival's Sunday fair, or search 사찰음식 on Naver Map for temple-cuisine restaurants around Jogyesa and Insadong; book lunch ahead. A half day can cover both temples: Jogyesa in the morning via Anguk Station, lunch nearby, then roughly 40 minutes by subway to Bongeunsa Station for a late-afternoon walk as the light drops behind the COEX towers.

faq.q: Do I need to be Buddhist to visit a temple or join a Templestay?
faq.a: No. Both Jogyesa and Bongeunsa welcome visitors of any faith, and Templestay programs are designed for lay people, many of them non-Buddhist. You are asked to follow the etiquette, such as bowing on entering a hall, but joining prostrations or chanting is optional.

faq.q: Is there an entrance fee at Jogyesa or Bongeunsa?
faq.a: No. Admission to both temples is free. Jogyesa's grounds and main hall are open around the clock, and Bongeunsa's grounds are open from 05:00 to 22:00. Donation boxes are common in halls, and giving is entirely voluntary.

faq.q: Can I take photos inside a temple?
faq.a: Photographing courtyards, pagodas and the outside of halls is fine. Inside halls, many temples ask you not to photograph the altar, and close-up photos of people praying are never appropriate. When unsure, ask at the information desk or simply photograph from the doorway.

faq.q: When is the Lotus Lantern Festival in 2027?
faq.a: Buddha's Birthday falls on Thursday, May 13, 2027, and Seoul's lantern parade is normally held on a weekend shortly before it. In 2026 the parade ran eight days before the holiday. The 2027 dates had not been announced as of October 20, 2026; check llf.or.kr from early spring.

faq.q: Can I watch a Buddhist service as a visitor?
faq.a: Yes, quietly and from the back or the side. Jogyesa lists a Sunday Dharma service at 10:00 and services on set days of the lunar month. Stand or sit at the edge, follow the bows if you wish, keep your phone away, and leave by a side door.

title.en: Jjimjilbang Etiquette: How a Korean Bathhouse Visit Works, Step by Step

summary.en: Mogyoktang versus jjimjilbang, the entry routine from shoe locker to hot pool, nudity norms, heat rooms, sikhye and baked eggs, the scrub, tattoos and sleeping over.

audience: Travelers curious about Korea's bathhouses who want to know exactly what happens inside before they walk in, and whether it suits them.
method: Researched from the official sources listed below, checked on October 20, 2026. Hours, fees and booking rules can change; the linked official pages are the final word.
quickAnswer: A mogyoktang is a single-sex bathhouse where everyone bathes nude; a jjimjilbang adds a shared floor where men and women wear the provided T-shirt and shorts and move between heated rooms, a snack bar and sleeping mats. Shower thoroughly before entering any pool, keep your towel out of the water, and check each venue's own rules on tattoos and overnight stays.

en.heading: Bathhouse, sauna, jjimjilbang: three signs, three experiences
paragraphs: Korean has several words for places where you get clean and warm, and they are not interchangeable. A 목욕탕 (mogyoktang) is a neighborhood bathhouse: a men's side and a women's side, each with showers, hot and cold pools and usually a dry sauna, and little else. Many brand themselves 사우나 (sauna) on the sign. A 찜질방 (jjimjilbang) contains a bathhouse too, but adds a shared, clothed floor of heated rooms, a snack bar, TV areas and space to lie down, where families, couples and friends spend hours together.

At the top end are spa complexes with pools, rooftop baths and themed heat rooms, closer to a water park than to a neighborhood bath; VisitKorea's own guide features examples in Goyang and Suwon. One expatriate writer on Korea.net described the ordinary jjimjilbang as part spa, part community center and part budget hotel, which is accurate. People come for a weekly scrub, to sweat out a cold or a hangover, to pass time between trains, or because a night on the heated floor costs a fraction of a hotel room.

Decide which experience you want before you go. If you only want a bath, a mogyoktang is cheaper, quieter and more local. If you want to linger, eat, nap and try the kiln rooms, choose a jjimjilbang. If you are traveling with someone of another sex and want to spend the time together, only the jjimjilbang's shared floor allows that, since the baths are always separate. On Naver Map, search 찜질방 or 사우나 and read recent reviews for hours, overnight policy and whether there is a scrub service.

en.heading: From shoe locker to hot pool: the first fifteen minutes
paragraphs: Entry follows a fixed choreography, and most first-time awkwardness comes from not knowing it. Shoes come off at the door and go into a small shoe locker; keep its key. At the counter you pay and receive towels, a uniform for the shared floor, often in different colors for men and women, and a locker key on a wristband. In many places you hand over the shoe key in exchange. The wristband is your wallet for the rest of the visit: snacks, drinks and extras are charged to it and settled when you return it.

Go into your own sex's locker room, put everything in the locker and undress completely. Take only the small towel and any toiletries you want to use; many bathhouses supply soap and shampoo, but bring a comb, lotion and hair ties if you are particular. Your phone stays in the locker. Before you touch any pool, wash thoroughly with soap at a shower station, hair included, and tie long hair up so it does not trail in the water.

Then the pools, typically a hot one around 40°C, a slightly cooler herbal or mineral pool, and a cold plunge. Ease in slowly, do not swim or splash, and keep the towel out of the water; Koreans fold it on their heads or leave it at the edge. When you leave a shower station, rinse the stool and basin for the next person. To move on to the shared floor, dry off, put on the uniform from your locker and follow the signs out of the changing area.
checklist: Shoes into the entrance shoe locker; keep the key
Pay at the counter; collect towels, uniform and locker wristband
Undress fully in the single-sex locker room; phone stays locked away
Wash with soap before entering any pool; tie up long hair
Keep the towel out of the water
Put the uniform on before entering the co-ed jjimjil area
Return the wristband at the counter and pay for extras

en.heading: Nudity, children and the rules nobody explains
paragraphs: For many visitors the nude bath is the hurdle. It helps to know how ordinary it is: Korean children grow up going with a parent, and in the bath nobody is looking at you, because looking is the one thing you do not do. Bodies of every age and shape share the room. The polite posture is relaxed indifference, with your eyes on your own business and conversation kept low. Holding the small towel in front of you while you walk between stations is normal and goes unremarked.

Some rules are written into law. Under Korea's public hygiene regulations, since June 22, 2022 children aged four (48 months) and over may not enter the opposite sex's bath or changing room, so a father with a five-year-old daughter needs another adult to take her into the women's side. Bathhouses must also refuse entry to visibly drunk customers and to people with infectious diseases. Cameras of any kind are unacceptable in locker rooms and baths, and covert filming is a serious criminal offense in Korea.

The unwritten rules are about sharing space. Sit while you shower where there are low stations, so you do not spray the person next to you. Put basins and stools back where you found them. Do not leave toiletries to claim a shower spot while you soak elsewhere for half an hour. Rinse off sweat before returning to a pool after a heat room. In many bathhouses the showers shut off automatically after a minute or so; just press the button again.

en.heading: Kiln rooms, salt rooms and the ice room: working through the heat
paragraphs: The shared jjimjil floor is what makes a jjimjilbang. Its centerpiece is often a bulgama (불가마), a dome-shaped kiln room lined with clay or stone and run at very high temperatures, sometimes with an hourglass by the door to time your stay. Around it you may find a red clay (hwangto) room, a salt room, a charcoal room, a jade or amethyst room, and an ice room that feels pleasantly mild at first and genuinely cold after a few minutes.

Pace yourself. Korea's tourism organization advises beginners to start in the gentler rooms, around 30 to 40°C, before moving to the hottest ones, and to keep sessions in anything above 60°C to about 20 minutes to avoid burns and dehydration. Lie or sit on a towel rather than bare skin, drink water between rounds, and step out the moment you feel dizzy or your heart is racing. Alternating heat with the ice room, or with a rest on the warm main floor, is the usual rhythm.

You will see towels folded into two rolled 'sheep ears' on people's heads. This is the yangmeori (양머리, sheep head), a style made famous by Korean television; it keeps hair off the face and shields the ears from heat. Any short video shows the fold in a minute, and a photo in one is close to obligatory on a first visit.

en.heading: Roasted eggs, sikhye and how the snack bar works
paragraphs: Eating is half the visit. The classic pairing is a couple of roasted eggs, their shells browned by slow heat, with a cup of sikhye (식혜), a cold, lightly sweet drink made from rice and malt with soft grains floating in it. After a session in the heat the combination is salty, sweet and cooling at once, and VisitKorea singles it out as the pairing that refreshes a dry mouth. Locals sometimes crack the egg on their own forehead, a joke borrowed from television.

Snack bars sell much more: VisitKorea's list includes fish-cake skewers, fried chicken, tteokbokki, cup noodles, ice cream, seaweed soup (miyeokguk) and misutgaru, a drink of roasted grain powder. Larger places run a proper restaurant with rice and stew dishes. You order at the counter and show or scan your wristband, and the cost is added to your locker key and paid when you leave. Keep a mental tally; it is easy to forget how many drinks you have charged by the end of an afternoon.

Eat in the designated areas, never in the heat rooms, and keep noise down near the sleeping zones. Most places do not want outside food brought in, though a water bottle is fine. Massage chairs, coin karaoke and game corners charge to the same key, so agree on a budget in advance if you are with children who have discovered that the wristband buys ice cream.

en.heading: Seshin: what the scrub involves and whether to book it
paragraphs: In the bath area you will notice a corner with vinyl-covered tables and an attendant at work. This is the seshin (세신) station, home of the full-body exfoliating scrub that many Koreans consider the main reason to visit. Attendants work only in their own sex's section. They use a coarse mitt known as an Italy towel (이태리타월), and the gray rolls of dead skin that come away are the whole point, not something to be embarrassed about.

Sign up at the station or the front counter, where prices for a basic scrub and add-ons such as massage, a face mask or a hair wash are usually posted. Soak in the hot pool for 20 to 30 minutes first, because softened skin scrubs more easily and less painfully. When your turn comes, lie on the table; the attendant works over your whole body, turns you onto your back, sides and front with taps or one-word instructions, and finishes with a rinse. Payment is made at the station or added to your key.

Book it if your skin is healthy and you want the full local experience. Skip it if you are sunburned, have eczema, broken skin or a fresh tattoo, and speak up if the pressure is too much: 살살 해 주세요 (salsal hae juseyo) means 'gently, please'. Expect your skin to feel tender and look pink for a few hours, so do not schedule a scrub right before a long hike or a day at the beach.

en.heading: Tattoos, overnight stays and rules that change by venue
paragraphs: Tattoos are handled very differently from Japan. Korea has no national ban on tattooed bathers, and in many neighborhood bathhouses nobody will comment. Individual businesses do set their own rules, however, and Korean newspapers have documented the range: a Gangnam spa refusing guests whose tattoos might bother others, hotel saunas requiring large tattoos to be covered with patches, and gyms asking members to cover up. Hotels and membership venues are the strictest. If your tattoos are large, check the posted rules or ask at the counter before you pay.

Sleeping over is one of the jjimjilbang's oldest functions. At 24-hour places, guests sleep on mats or directly on the heated floor in common halls, with small firm pillows, and some venues set aside darker, quieter sleeping rooms. Expect lights, snoring and late television, and keep valuables in the locker. Overnight stays often cost more than a daytime visit; the price board at the counter will say. Under the public hygiene rules, 24-hour jjimjilbang in Seoul must keep out people under 19 between 22:00 and 05:00 unless a parent or guardian is with them or has signed a consent form, so teenagers traveling without a parent should not plan on staying the night.

Our judgment on the overnight: it is a good fallback after a missed last train or before a very early departure, and an interesting experience once. It is not a substitute for a hotel if you need proper sleep before a demanding day.

en.heading: Who should sit this one out, and a first visit in three hours
paragraphs: Skip the hot rooms and pools, or ask a doctor first, if you are pregnant, have heart or blood-pressure problems, or have been drinking; heat and alcohol are a bad mix, and bathhouses are required to refuse visibly drunk guests in any case. It is customary to stay out of the shared pools during menstruation and use the showers and clothed heat rooms instead. If public nudity is a firm no for you, a spa complex with swimsuit areas suits you better than a classic jjimjilbang.

For a first visit, allow three hours on a weekday afternoon, when it is quieter. A workable plan: 14:00 check in, wash and soak; 14:30 scrub if booked, or more pool time; 15:00 change into the uniform and go up to the shared floor; 15:10 start in a warm clay room, then step up to the kiln, with ice-room breaks; 16:00 roasted eggs and sikhye; 16:30 a nap on the heated floor; 17:00 back to the bath for a final rinse, dress, return the wristband and pay.

A few words make everything easier: 찜질방 (jjimjilbang), 목욕탕 (mogyoktang), 세신 (seshin, scrub), 수건 (sugeon, towel), 열쇠 (yeolsoe, key), 식혜 (sikhye) and 맥반석 계란 (maekbanseok gyeran, roasted eggs). Pack a small pouch with lotion, a hair tie and a card for the counter. Pointing and a smile cover everything else.

faq.q: Do I have to be naked at a jjimjilbang?
faq.a: Only in the single-sex locker rooms and bath areas, where everyone bathes nude. On the shared jjimjil floor with the heat rooms, snack bar and sleeping areas, everyone wears the T-shirt and shorts provided at the counter. You can skip the pools entirely, but you will still change in the locker room.

faq.q: Can couples or mixed groups go together?
faq.a: Yes, on the shared jjimjil floor, which is co-ed and clothed. You will separate at the locker rooms and baths, which are always divided by sex, and meet again upstairs or in the common hall once you have changed into the uniforms.

faq.q: Will I be turned away for having tattoos?
faq.a: Possibly, but far less often than in Japan. There is no national rule; each business decides. Neighborhood bathhouses are usually relaxed, while hotel saunas and membership venues may require large tattoos to be covered or refuse entry. Check the posted rules or ask at the counter before paying.

faq.q: Can I sleep at a jjimjilbang instead of booking a hotel?
faq.a: At 24-hour venues, yes: guests sleep on mats or the heated floor in common halls, sometimes in separate quieter rooms. Expect noise and light, keep valuables locked away, and check the overnight price at the counter. Under-19s are kept out between 22:00 and 05:00 unless a parent or guardian is with them or has given written consent.

faq.q: Can I bring my child into my side of the bath?
faq.a: Only if the child is under four. Since June 2022, children aged 48 months and over may not enter the opposite sex's bath or changing room, so an older child needs an adult of the same sex. On the shared jjimjil floor, families stay together.

faq.q: Does the seshin scrub hurt?
faq.a: It is vigorous rather than painful if you soak first and your skin is healthy. Attendants use a coarse mitt, and your skin will look pink for a few hours. Say 'salsal hae juseyo' to ask for a gentler touch, and skip it with sunburn, eczema or a fresh tattoo.

title.en: Korean Etiquette for Visitors: The Habits That Matter, and Why

summary.en: Practical Korean manners for travelers: why people ask your age, polite speech, bowing, two-handed giving, shoes off, subway seats, tipping, gifts and what to skip.

audience: Independent travelers who want to behave considerately in Korea without memorizing a rulebook, and who want to understand the reasoning behind the customs they notice.
method: Researched from the official sources listed below, checked on October 20, 2026. Hours, fees and booking rules can change; the linked official pages are the final word.
quickAnswer: Korean etiquette rests on a few habits: polite speech with strangers, a small bow, two hands when giving or receiving, shoes off where the floor steps up, and quiet on public transport. Leave priority and pink seats free, do not tip, and treat questions about your age as a way of placing you, not prying. Visitors get generous allowance for nearly everything else.
