en.heading: Why age comes up in the first five minutes
paragraphs: Visitors are often startled by how quickly a new Korean acquaintance asks their age, or the year they were born. The question is practical, not nosy. Korean grammar and social life are organized around relative seniority: it decides which speech level people use with each other, who pours the drinks, who pays, and which kinship word fits. Until two people know where they stand, they cannot settle on how to talk. Asking age is the shortcut.

The arithmetic used to be confusing even for Koreans. The traditional system counted a newborn as one year old and added a year every January 1, so people were often a year or two older than their international age. Since June 28, 2023, revised civil and administrative law has made international age the standard for official and legal purposes. A few matters still go by birth year, including school entry and the minimum age for buying alcohol and tobacco. In conversation, many people simply give their birth year, which sidesteps the problem entirely.

So answer with your birth year or your age, and expect a small reaction. A Korean friend a few years older may jokingly become your unni, oppa, noona or hyung, the words for older sister or brother, chosen according to the speaker's own gender. Colleagues use seonbae for seniors and hubae for juniors. As a visitor you are not expected to slot yourself into any of this; being asked is simply a sign that someone wants to choose the right words for you.

en.heading: One speech rule that covers almost everything
paragraphs: Korean has several speech levels, but a visitor needs only one: the polite ending -yo (-요), plus the more formal -mnida (-ㅂ니다) found in set phrases like 감사합니다. Use polite forms with everyone you do not know well, including people younger than you, shop staff and taxi drivers. Casual speech (banmal) between strangers comes across as rude, however often drama characters use it. Koreans move to banmal only after they become close, and usually after one of them suggests it.

A short phrase set goes a long way, and the table below covers the moments that come up every day. Note how to call restaurant staff: raising a hand and saying 저기요 (jeogiyo, roughly 'excuse me, over here') is normal, not rude, and many restaurants have a call button on the table. Calling out across the room suits a busy barbecue restaurant; in a quiet café, catch someone's eye or walk to the counter instead.

Names follow the same respectful logic. Outside close friendships, Koreans rarely address each other by given name alone; titles and family words do that work. With a guide, host or colleague, use the person's name plus -ssi (씨), or their title, such as seonsaengnim (teacher), unless they invite something more casual. Calling someone older by a bare given name is an easy slip to avoid, and avoiding it signals that you have made an effort.

en.heading: Bows, both hands and the reasoning behind them
paragraphs: The everyday bow is small: a nod with a slight bend from the waist when you greet someone, thank them or apologize. Deep bows belong to ceremonies, such as the formal New Year bow to parents and grandparents. Korean men often combine a handshake with a slight bow and support the right forearm with the left hand. Mirroring that is gracious, but a visitor who simply nods and smiles is doing fine.

The habit you will notice most is the use of two hands. Koreans give and receive objects, from a business card to a credit card to a glass, with both hands, or with the right hand while the left touches the right wrist or forearm. The meaning is easy to read: the exchange has your full attention, and so does the person in front of you. It matters most with older people, teachers, hosts and anyone senior, and it costs nothing to do with everyone.

The same logic shapes drinking, which deserves its own guide. When someone older pours for you, hold your glass with both hands; when you drink in front of a senior, turning slightly away is a traditional courtesy, though friends of the same age relax it. Pouring for others rather than yourself is the norm, and an empty glass is an invitation for someone to fill it. Our table manners guide covers the rest, from chopsticks to who starts eating first.

en.heading: Where the floor is furniture: shoes off
paragraphs: Traditional Korean houses were heated from below by ondol, a system of flues running under the floor, so the floor was where people sat, ate and slept. Shoes stay out because the floor is, in effect, furniture. VisitKorea's own advice to visitors is short: there is no strict dress etiquette in Korea, but you will often need to take your shoes off before entering a house.

Learn to read the threshold. A raised step, a row of shoes or a shelf of slippers means shoes off. That applies in homes, in guesthouses with floor rooms, in temple halls, in some traditional restaurants with floor seating, and occasionally in small clinics and offices. Step from your shoe straight onto the raised floor rather than standing on the lower entry area in your socks. At temples, turn your shoes to face outward so you can slip back into them easily. Socks are expected; bare feet in someone's home or a temple hall feel a little too casual.

In homes you may be handed indoor slippers, and a separate pair for the bathroom, which often has a wet tiled floor. Swap back on the way out rather than wandering into the living room in bathroom slippers. When you sit on the floor, cross-legged is fine for everyone; avoid stretching your legs straight out toward people across a low table, and tuck your feet to the side if you need to shift position.

en.heading: On the subway: seats that are not yours, and a quiet car
paragraphs: Each Seoul subway car has priority seats at its ends, marked for older people, disabled passengers, pregnant women and people with small children. Many Koreans leave them empty even when the train is packed, and a healthy young traveler sitting there will draw looks. Treat them as unavailable. If you do sit in one on an empty train, be ready to stand the moment someone who needs it boards.

The pink seats in the middle of the car are for pregnant passengers. Seoul gave these seats bright pink backs in 2015, two per car, starting on Lines 2 and 5, with a line of text calling the seat a place for 'a future protagonist', because the earlier small emblem disappeared from view whenever someone sat down. Early pregnancy is invisible, so the convention is to leave the pink seat free rather than wait to see who needs it.

Seoul trains are quiet. Calls are brief and low, video and music go through headphones, and loud group conversation earns frowns. In a crowd, wear your backpack on your front or put it on the overhead rack. On the platform, stand at the marked door positions and let people off before you board. Eating on the train is widely regarded as bad manners, and strong-smelling food doubly so; finish your snack before the gates.

en.heading: Paying, tipping and who picks up the bill
paragraphs: Tipping is not part of everyday Korean service. The price on the menu or the taxi meter is what you pay, and leaving coins or notes on the table is more likely to confuse staff than to please them. A smile and 감사합니다 are the thanks expected. In most restaurants you pay at the counter on the way out, carrying the bill with you, rather than handing a card to a server at the table.

Who pays follows the same seniority logic as speech. Traditionally the oldest or most senior person, or whoever issued the invitation, covers the meal, and the others reciprocate later by paying for coffee, the next round or the next dinner. Among younger Koreans and friends of similar age, splitting the bill is common and unremarkable. As a guest, offer to pay; if your host insists, accept graciously and return the favor another time rather than wrestling over the bill at the counter.

Small exchanges follow the two-hands rule: pass cards and cash with both hands or with your left hand supporting your right, and receive change and receipts the same way. Cards are accepted almost everywhere, even for small purchases, so you rarely need to count out coins while a queue waits behind you.

en.heading: Gifts, numbers and the personal questions you will be asked
paragraphs: If you are invited to a Korean home, bring something: a box of fruit, good cookies or pastries, a bottle, or a specialty from your own country. Present it with both hands. Your host may set it aside to open later rather than unwrapping it in front of you, which is courtesy, not indifference. Avoid giving things in sets of four, since the Sino-Korean word for four sounds like the word for death, the same reason some elevators label the fourth floor 'F'. Do not write a living person's name in red ink, a color traditionally associated with the names of the dead.

Expect personal questions that would be unusual at home: are you married, what do you do for work, sometimes a frank comment on your weight or how tired you look. Most of this is the same placing instinct as asking age, and some of it is how care is expressed, through attention to someone's health and appearance. Answer briefly, then redirect with a question of your own. Laughing it off works far better than visible offense, which will puzzle the person who asked.

The topics to handle carefully are the ones that are sensitive anywhere. Politics, North Korea and the country's twentieth-century history carry strong feelings, and strangers may not share your view of them. Let your Korean companion lead those conversations, listen more than you argue, and keep jokes about them out of public places.

en.heading: What you can stop worrying about, and the short list that matters
paragraphs: Visitors tend to overprepare. Koreans do not expect foreigners to master speech levels, the full choreography of drinking with elders or the depth of a ceremonial bow, and most are delighted by any attempt. Eye contact is normal; you do not need to lower your gaze. Asking for a fork is fine, and nobody minds clumsy chopsticks. Wearing hanbok as a foreigner is welcomed rather than resented; the royal palaces even waive admission for visitors who wear it.

The handful of things that genuinely matter are about other people's space and peace. Keep your voice down on public transport and in residential neighborhoods, leave priority seats free, queue, take shoes off where floors are raised, and treat working temples as places of worship. Residential areas popular with tourists now enforce this formally: in Bukchon's most crowded lanes, tourist visits are limited to 10:00–17:00, with fines for sightseeing outside those hours. And never stand chopsticks upright in a bowl of rice, which echoes the offerings made at ancestral rites.

When unsure, watch what the people around you do and copy it; that instinct covers most situations in Korea. If something goes wrong, from a lost item to a dispute with a taxi, the 1330 Korea Travel Helpline offers phone and chat support for tourists in several languages, on 1330 inside Korea or +82-2-1330 from abroad.
checklist: Polite -yo speech with anyone you do not know well
A small bow; two hands when giving or receiving
Shoes off wherever the floor steps up
Priority and pink subway seats left free
Quiet on trains and in residential lanes
No tipping; pay at the counter
Chopsticks never upright in rice

faq.q: Should I bow or shake hands when I meet someone in Korea?
faq.a: Either works, and many Koreans do both: a handshake with a slight bow, the left hand lightly supporting the right forearm. With older people, a small bow first is the safer choice. Visitors are not expected to bow deeply; a nod with a slight bend from the waist is enough.

faq.q: Is it rude to talk on the phone on the Seoul subway?
faq.a: A short, quiet call is tolerated, but long or loud calls are frowned upon, as are videos or music without headphones. If a call will take a while, keep it brief and say you will call back. Most riders stay silent or text.

faq.q: Do I need to tip in Korea?
faq.a: No. Tipping is not customary in restaurants, taxis, cafés or salons, and the listed price is what you pay. Leaving money on the table may simply confuse staff. A sincere 감사합니다 (gamsahamnida, thank you) is the expected way to show appreciation.

faq.q: Can I sit in the pink seat if no one pregnant is on board?
faq.a: The convention is to leave it empty. Early pregnancy is not visible, and Seoul designed the pink seat backs precisely so the seat stays noticeable and free. Standing beside an empty pink seat is completely normal in Seoul.

faq.q: What should I say when someone asks how old I am?
faq.a: Give your birth year or your age and expect a friendly reaction. The question helps the other person choose the right level of politeness and the right word to call you. Since 2023, official documents use international age, but many people still answer with their birth year.

title.en: Korean Table Manners: Spoons, Shared Banchan, Elders and the Bill

summary.en: Eat at a Korean table with confidence: shared banchan and free refills, spoon versus chopsticks, why nothing stands in rice, waiting for elders, paying and tipping.

audience: First-time visitors who want to eat in ordinary Korean restaurants, alone or with Korean hosts, without awkward moments.
method: Researched from the official sources listed below, checked on October 20, 2026. Hours, fees and booking rules can change; the linked official pages are the final word.
quickAnswer: Share the side dishes, eat rice and soup with the spoon, keep your bowl on the table, and never leave chopsticks or a spoon standing upright in rice, which mimics a step in Korean ancestral rites. Let the eldest start, call staff with the table bell or 'jeogiyo', pay at the counter on the way out, and don't tip: menu prices already include tax and service.

keyFacts.label: Calling staff
keyFacts.value: Table bell, or 저기요 (jeogiyo) / 여기요 (yeogiyo)

keyFacts.label: Side dishes
keyFacts.value: Shared; refills are free

keyFacts.label: Chopsticks
keyFacts.value: Never upright in rice (ancestral-rite image)

keyFacts.label: Rice bowl
keyFacts.value: Stays on the table; eat rice with the spoon

keyFacts.label: Who starts
keyFacts.value: The eldest at the table

keyFacts.label: Paying
keyFacts.value: Usually at the counter (계산대) on the way out

keyFacts.label: Tipping
keyFacts.value: Not customary; menu prices include VAT and service

keyFacts.label: Eating alone
keyFacts.value: Some restaurants require 2 portions (2인분 이상)

en.heading: The table is shared, and the side dishes are part of the meal
paragraphs: A Korean meal is built around the bansang (반상): rice and soup in front of each diner, and everything else set down in the middle at once. Korea.net's etiquette series points out that a Korean set meal arrives all together rather than in courses, which is the first adjustment many visitors make. The small shared plates are banchan (반찬): kimchi, seasoned greens, braised potatoes, fish cake, whatever the kitchen made that day. They are not starters to clear before the main dish. They are meant to be eaten with rice from the first spoonful to the last.

Banchan refills are free. VisitKorea notes that asking for more water or side dishes costs nothing, and many restaurants top up the kimchi without being asked. To request more, point at the empty dish and say 이거 좀 더 주세요 (igeo jom deo juseyo, 'a little more of this, please'). What draws looks is waste: asking for a third refill of something you then leave untouched. Take what you will eat, and finish what you asked for again.

You eat from shared dishes with your own chopsticks; there is no serving-spoon ritual for banchan. The courtesy lies in how you do it. Lift a piece cleanly instead of turning the plate over in search of the best bit, take from the side nearest you, and never put a bitten piece back. A bubbling pot of jjigae (찌개, stew) in the center often comes with a ladle (국자, gukja). When one is provided, use it to move broth into your own bowl rather than dipping your spoon straight into the pot.

en.heading: Spoon for rice and soup, chopsticks for the rest
paragraphs: Korea is one of the few chopstick cultures where the spoon does the heavy lifting. Rice, soup and stew travel on a long-handled spoon (숟가락, sutgarak), while the flat metal chopsticks (젓가락, jeotgarak) handle banchan, fish and anything you need to pick up. Together the pair is called sujeo (수저). VisitKorea says plainly that using the spoon alongside chopsticks is fine if chopsticks are a struggle, and no one will think less of you for scooping a slippery bean.

Two habits mark an experienced diner. Use one utensil at a time rather than holding spoon and chopsticks together in one hand, and rest the idle one on the table. And keep the rice bowl on the table. Korea.net lists lifting the rice or soup bowl among the things to avoid; with a spoon doing the scooping, there is no need to bring the bowl to your mouth as diners do in Japan. Restaurant rice often comes in a lidded stainless-steel bowl that is too hot to hold anyway, which makes the rule easy to keep.

Place settings follow a pattern you will see at home tables and in set-meal restaurants: Korea.net describes rice on the diner's left, soup on the right, and the spoon laid beside the chopsticks. When you finish, return both utensils to where they started, as Visit Seoul's etiquette page advises, instead of leaving them in an empty bowl. Blowing your nose is best done away from the table; the same Korea.net episode flags it as something Koreans find unpleasant during a meal.

en.heading: Why nothing stands upright in a bowl of rice
paragraphs: The strongest taboo at the Korean table comes from ancestral rites. In jesa (제사), the memorial service many families still hold on death anniversaries and holidays, there is a step called sapsi jeongjeo (삽시정저). After the last cups of liquor are poured, the spoon is planted in the center of the rice bowl offered to the ancestor, its hollow facing east, and the chopsticks are set straight. The Seoul Facilities Corporation's guide to traditional rites lays out what follows: the participants bow, then leave the room briefly so the ancestors can eat undisturbed.

A spoon or chopsticks left standing in rice therefore looks like a meal set for the dead. Most Koreans will not lecture a visitor about it, but the image is jarring at a dinner table, especially with older people present, and someone may quietly lay your chopsticks down for you. Visit Seoul includes the rule in its short list of dining basics, and Korea.net ties it directly to rituals for the dead. When you need to put utensils down mid-meal, rest them flat on the table, on a napkin or across a side plate.

If you are hosted at a family home during Seollal (설날) or Chuseok (추석), you may see the real thing. The morning holiday rite, charye (차례), follows the same table-setting logic, and afterwards the family shares the food and drink from the ritual table, a custom called eumbok (음복). Wait to be told where to sit and when to begin, accept what you are offered, and treat the ritual dishes with the same care you would any shared plate.

en.heading: Age sets the pace of the meal
paragraphs: Visit Seoul's first dining rule is to start eating only once the eldest at the table has begun, and Korea.net describes younger diners waiting until older people pick up their utensils. This is Confucian courtesy in its most everyday form. In practice the senior person often says 많이 드세요 (mani deuseyo, 'eat plenty') or simply lifts a spoon, and the table follows. Among friends of similar age with no obvious senior, people just start.

Small duties tend to fall to the youngest or most junior person, and you will see them at office lunches all over Seoul. Someone takes spoons and chopsticks from the drawer or box at the table and lays a set on a napkin for everyone; someone fills the water cups. As a guest of Korean colleagues, offering to do this is a graceful gesture, though a visitor will usually be waved off. Matching the eldest's pace matters too: try not to finish far ahead, and don't get up to leave while seniors are still eating.

Visitors get a lot of latitude. Nobody expects a tourist couple to perform seniority rituals, and the family in Korea.net's own example admits that many households are relaxed about formality. The rules matter most in three settings: meals with someone's parents or grandparents, business dinners, and formal occasions. In those, watch the senior person and copy the rhythm. Everywhere else, the shared-dish courtesies and the chopstick taboo are the parts worth getting right.

en.heading: Getting attention: the call bell, 'jeogiyo' and self-service
paragraphs: Korean restaurant staff do not hover, and they are not expected to. Many tables have a call button (호출벨, hochulbel); press it once and someone will come, and VisitKorea warns that it can be louder than you expect. Without a bell, raise a hand and call 저기요 (jeogiyo, roughly 'excuse me') or 여기요 (yeogiyo, 'over here'). Both are normal and not rude, even in a quiet room. Waiting silently to catch someone's eye usually means waiting a long time.

Self-service is common, and signs will tell you. 물은 셀프 (mureun selpeu) means water is self-service: look for a dispenser or a fridge of water bottles and stainless cups near the counter. Some places run a side-dish station, the 셀프바 (selpeu-ba), where you refill kimchi and banchan yourself, and VisitKorea mentions unmanned ordering machines. Tablet and kiosk ordering is now widespread and often has an English option; if not, a translation app's camera mode reads menus well.

These are the phrases that cover almost every exchange in an ordinary restaurant. Said with the 요 or 다 endings shown, they are polite enough for any table, including one with older people. Pronunciation does not need to be perfect; pointing while you speak does most of the work.

en.heading: Eating alone and the two-portion minimum
paragraphs: Eating alone, honbap (혼밥), is ordinary in Korea now. The Korea JoongAng Daily, citing Statistics Korea's 2024 survey, reported that about 27 percent of people eat lunch alone. Restaurant layouts have not fully caught up. Barbecue houses, stew restaurants and places built around a shared pot often require at least two portions per order, written 2인분 이상, and some turn away single diners at busy times. A Fair Trade Commission spokesperson told the paper this is the owner's decision and breaks no law.

The reasons are economic rather than personal: one diner occupies a four-person table and a grill that costs the same to run. Knowing that makes the workarounds obvious. Avoid the noon office rush and the evening peak, choose places with counter seats or one-person menus, and look for 1인분 or 혼밥 on the menu or door. Noodle shops, gimbap chains, food courts and department-store food halls are built for one. If the dish you want only comes as two portions, ordering two is acceptable, and many restaurants will pack cooked leftovers if you ask for 포장 (pojang).

Be direct when you walk in: 한 명이에요 (han myeong-ieyo, 'just one'). If you are waved toward a small table, sit there; if the answer is an apologetic '2인분 이상', you have learned the house rule without any awkwardness. Timing does the rest. A restaurant that hesitates over a single customer at 12:15 is often glad of one at 2:30, when the room is empty and the kitchen is quiet.

en.heading: Paying at the counter, splitting the bill and why there is no tip
paragraphs: In most Korean restaurants you pay at the counter (계산대, gyesandae) on your way out, not at the table. The bill is often left on the table when the food arrives, or staff simply remember your table number; take it to the register when you are done. In kiosk restaurants and cafes you pay before you eat. Cards are widely accepted in Seoul's restaurants, though small market stalls are a different story.

Korean groups have traditionally not split the check. A Korea.net column on the 'sneak pay' describes the usual pattern: one person covers the whole bill, often the oldest for a first meal, and friends race to pay or slip away to settle it quietly, so it evens out over time. Splitting, known as deochi pei (더치페이, 'Dutch pay'), is also common now among friends and colleagues of similar age, often with one person paying and the others sending their share by bank transfer. To pay separately, say 따로 계산할게요; most counters will run several cards, though a long split at the lunch peak is not popular.

Tipping is not customary. Visit Seoul says tipping is not customary in Korea, and VisitKorea says there is no need to tip at Korean restaurants. There is a structural reason as well. Seoul's food safety guidance requires restaurants to show prices as the final amount the customer pays, with VAT and service charges included rather than added separately. The price on the menu is the price, and cash left on the table is more likely to cause confusion than gratitude.

en.heading: A worked example: a weekday lunch for two
paragraphs: Here is how an ordinary lunch runs at a neighborhood restaurant serving kimchi-jjigae and doenjang-jjigae sets. Staff call out a greeting as you enter; hold up two fingers or say 두 명이요 (du myeong-iyo). Sit where you are pointed, or at any free table if no one points. Open the drawer at the table edge for spoons and chopsticks and lay out a set for each of you on a napkin. If a sign says 물은 셀프, fill two cups at the water station rather than waiting.

Order by pointing at the menu or wall pictures, or press the bell. The banchan land first, then the bubbling stews and two bowls of rice. Let the older person start if you are with one. Eat rice and broth with the spoon and pick at the banchan with chopsticks; ask for more kimchi with 이거 좀 더 주세요 if you finish it. When you are done, lay the spoon and chopsticks side by side on the table. Take the bill to the counter, pay by card, and say 잘 먹었습니다 (jal meogeotseumnida, 'I ate well') on the way out. No tip.

Run through this short list before you sit down. None of it is complicated, and these six points cover nearly everything Korean diners notice about a visitor's manners, from the chopstick taboo to the moment you pay at the counter.
checklist: If you are alone, look for 2인분 이상 on the door or menu before sitting.
Check whether water is 셀프 before waiting for someone to bring it.
Find the call bell on the table or the wall.
Keep the rice bowl on the table and rest utensils flat, never upright in rice.
Let the eldest start, and roughly match their pace.
Pay at the counter on the way out; do not leave a tip.

faq.q: Is it rude to ask for a fork?
faq.a: Not rude, but rarely necessary. Most restaurants set out only spoons and metal chopsticks, and the spoon handles rice, soup and soft side dishes. VisitKorea says using the spoon alongside chopsticks is perfectly acceptable. Some places keep forks for children; ask 포크 있어요? (pokeu isseoyo?) if you really need one.

faq.q: Do I have to finish every side dish?
faq.a: No. Banchan are shared and you can leave some. What reads badly is requesting refills and then leaving them untouched. Ask for more only of what you are actually eating, and try to finish your own rice, which is the part of the meal served to you alone.

faq.q: Can I eat with my hands?
faq.a: Only for wraps. Visit Seoul's etiquette guide says to avoid touching food with your fingers except when wrapping food in lettuce or cabbage, which is how grilled meat and some boiled pork dishes are eaten. For everything else, use the spoon or chopsticks; scissors and tongs handle anything large.

faq.q: What should I do if I accidentally stuck my chopsticks in my rice?
faq.a: Just lay them down flat on the table or across a side plate. It is a common slip for visitors, and nobody will make a scene. The reason it matters is the resemblance to the spoon planted in rice during ancestral rites, so simply removing them resolves it.

faq.q: Should I pay for my Korean host's meal?
faq.a: Offer once, sincerely, but expect to be refused if your host is older or invited you. The usual pattern is that one person pays for everyone and the favor is returned another time. A good reply is to say you will pay next time, or to cover coffee or a second round afterward.

title.en: Gwangjang Market Food Guide: History, What to Eat and How to Order

summary.en: One of Seoul's oldest markets explained: its 1905 origins, the food alley layout, bindaetteok and yukhoe, counter-stall ordering, cash, price disputes and timing.

audience: Independent visitors who want to eat well at Gwangjang Market, understand what they are eating, and avoid the usual friction over ordering and paying.
method: Researched from the official sources listed below, checked on October 20, 2026. Hours, fees and booking rules can change; the linked official pages are the final word.
quickAnswer: Head for the central food alley, sit at a counter stall with a posted price board, and say exactly what you want and how many before the food is served. Start with mayak gimbap and bindaetteok with makgeolli, add kalguksu or yukhoe, and carry small notes because some stalls still prefer cash. The food alley runs 09:00–23:00 every day, but the fabric and hanbok shops close on Sundays.

keyFacts.value: 광장시장 (Gwangjang Sijang); map search 광장시장 먹자골목

keyFacts.value: 09:00–23:00, open year-round

keyFacts.value: 1330 Travel Hotline (+82-2-1330), English available

en.heading: Founded in 1905 by Korean merchants pushing back
paragraphs: The market's own history begins in July 1905, when Korean merchants formed the company that would run it, Gwangjang Jusikhoesa (광장주식회사). The timing matters. Japan was tightening its grip on the Korean Empire that year, and a Japanese-led currency overhaul shook Korean traders; the market's official history describes the new venture as a market built on Korean capital at a time when other Seoul markets were under Japanese management. The Encyclopedia of Korean Culture calls the founding company the first privately run market-management company in Korea.

The name hides a story. The founders first planned to cover over the stream between the Gwanggyo (광교, 'wide bridge') and Janggyo (장교, 'long bridge') crossings of what is now Cheonggyecheon, and named the company 廣長, 'wide and long', after them. A flood swept away the building materials. They moved the plan east to the Baeogae (배오개) area, one of the three great market districts of late Joseon Seoul, kept the sound of the name and changed its characters to 廣藏, 'gather widely and keep'. According to the encyclopedia, the market settled on its present site in early March 1909.

For decades it went by another name. The market's history says it applied for its permit from the Hanseong city authorities in 1905 under the name Dongdaemun Market, and the Gwangjang name took hold from the 1960s. The Korean War destroyed part of it; refugees trading daily goods and military surplus revived it, the start of the imported secondhand clothing trade still found here. VisitKorea describes it as Korea's first permanent market, although the Encyclopedia of Korean Culture dates Seoul's first urban permanent market to 1897, on the site of today's Namdaemun Market. Gwangjang remains a working wholesale market for silk, bedding and wedding goods as much as a food destination.

en.heading: How the market is laid out, and where the food is
paragraphs: Think of Gwangjang as a covered grid of arcades with a food crossroads at its heart. The food alley (먹자골목, meokja golmok) is a long central aisle lined with rectangular counter stalls, each a cooking station ringed by benches. VisitKorea says the food street connects to the East Gate, North Gate 2 and South Gate 1, so whichever entrance you use, follow the smell of frying oil toward the middle. Around it, and far quieter, are the trades that built the market: silk and fabric, hanbok makers, bedding, and shops selling pyebaek (폐백) gifts for weddings.

The imported secondhand clothing arcade (구제상가, guje sangga) keeps its own hours and is worth a look if vintage clothing interests you. Two merchants' bodies share the site, which is useful to know if anything goes wrong. The Korea Herald reported that the Gwangjang Market Merchants' Association represents about 200 shops in the main building, while the Gwangjang Traditional Market Merchants' Association oversees roughly 250 stalls, including the food stalls. Most of what you eat in the alley comes from the second group.

In Naver Map or Kakao Map, search 광장시장 for the market as a whole, or 광장시장 먹자골목 to be routed straight to the food alley. The official address is 88 Changgyeonggung-ro, Jongno-gu (서울 종로구 창경궁로 88). The market's own directions give Jongno 5-ga Station, Exit 8, on Line 1, or Euljiro 4-ga Station, Exit 4, on Lines 2 and 5, about 100 meters away.

en.heading: Bindaetteok, and the three other dishes that define the alley
paragraphs: Bindaetteok (빈대떡) is the market's signature. It is a thick pancake of soaked, ground mung beans mixed with bean sprouts, kimchi or pork and fried in a generous layer of oil until the edges crackle. Several stalls grind the beans in full view, which is part of the show. It comes cut into pieces with a dip of soy sauce and sliced onion, and it is made for sharing. The traditional partner is makgeolli, and the Korea JoongAng Daily's report on makgeolli's heritage status names bindaetteok among the foods it is most often drunk with.

Mayak gimbap (마약김밥) is the opposite: finger-length rolls of rice and a few simple fillings, brushed with sesame oil and served with a sharp mustard dip. The name borrows the word for narcotics as a joke about how hard they are to stop eating. Order a plate first while you decide on everything else. Kalguksu (칼국수), knife-cut wheat noodles in a light anchovy broth, is the alley's comfort bowl; a VisitKorea feature on a guided morning walk to the market recommends it, often with dumplings (만두, mandu) from the same counters.

Yukhoe (육회) is the splurge: raw beef cut into strips and dressed with sesame oil and sweet pear, often topped with an egg yolk. It is generally ordered at specialist sit-down restaurants rather than snack counters, and it is the priciest of the common orders. Eat it promptly once served, and skip it if you are pregnant or have a weakened immune system, as with any raw meat. Beyond these four, the counters sell sundae (순대, blood sausage), tteokbokki, assorted jeon (모둠전, modumjeon) and japchae.

en.heading: How ordering at a counter stall works
paragraphs: Counter stalls do not work like restaurants. There is no host and usually no printed menu at your seat: the food on display is the menu, with prices on a board above the cook. Choose a stall with a clear price board, sit on the bench and point. The vendor cuts, reheats or plates your order in front of you, and you normally pay when you finish. You can stay at one stall for everything or graze, eating one dish per stall and moving on, which is the better way to cover the alley.

Friction usually comes from vague orders. Name the dish and the quantity, ask the price before the food arrives if it is not posted, and decline extras clearly. The disputes described below involved portion sizes and dishes charged differently from the board, and the most effective protection is agreeing the amount before you eat. If a vendor suggests adding another dish, 이것만 주세요 (igeonman juseyo, 'just this, please') is polite and final. Sharing benches with strangers is normal; keep bags on your lap rather than on the seat.

These phrases handle almost every exchange at the counters. Vendors in the alley are used to visitors and to pointing, so speed matters more than perfect pronunciation. Hold up fingers for quantities, and repeat the price back if you are unsure you heard it correctly.

en.heading: The overcharging stories, and what has changed since
paragraphs: Gwangjang's fame has brought scrutiny, and it is fair to know the record. In late 2023 a YouTube video showed a 15,000-won plate of assorted pancakes that many viewers found meager. Seoul responded with plans to print serving weights next to menu prices, to display food models of signature dishes such as bindaetteok, and to send mystery shoppers to check prices and portions. In November 2025 another viral video alleged a stall charged 10,000 won for sundae listed at 8,000 won; the vendor said the customer had agreed to extra meat. The Korea Herald reported that the street-stall association suspended that stall for 10 days.

That episode exposed a rift between the two merchants' associations, with the main-building group seeking damages from the stall association over harm to the market's reputation, according to the Herald. In December 2025 the Ministry of SMEs and Startups met both groups with Seoul and Jongno District officials and called for accurate price displays, transparent payment and multilingual signs with QR-code information. The city and district proposed real-name management of stall operators plus mandatory hygiene and service training, according to the ministry's announcement.

In May 2026 Seoul and Jongno District announced a joint May–June inspection of 159 food businesses and 109 food stalls, to be followed by regular checks, along with ongoing visits by mystery shoppers, foreign nationals among them, and a real-name system for stall vendors from June in which violations bring penalty points, suspensions and, at worst, loss of the stall's road-occupancy permit. Keep this in proportion: most visits involve nothing more than good food at posted prices. If something does go wrong, stay calm, note the stall, and call the 1330 Travel Hotline (+82-2-1330), which VisitKorea lists for the market and which offers English.

en.heading: Cash, cards and settling up
paragraphs: VisitKorea's listing says cards are accepted, and most shops and sit-down restaurants do take them. The food counters are less consistent. Seoul's 2023 measures included training vendors not to steer customers toward cash, and the government's December 2025 meeting still named transparent payment as a priority. The practical answer is to carry enough small notes (1,000-, 5,000- and 10,000-won bills) for a few dishes, ask 카드 돼요? before you order if you want to pay by card, and treat a card-friendly stall as a bonus.

A request to pay by bank transfer was part of the 2023 story, and a visitor without a Korean bank account cannot use one anyway. If a vendor asks for a transfer, pay with cash or a card instead. Keep coins and small notes handy as you go; you will want them at the next counter, and exact money speeds things up when the benches are full.

en.heading: When to go, and what Sunday means here
paragraphs: The market runs on two clocks. Its official site lists the shops at 09:00–18:00 with Sunday closing and the secondhand clothing arcade at 10:00–19:00 (closed Sundays, though the market says it opens on public holidays), and VisitKorea lists the food alley at 09:00–23:00 with no closing day. Individual stalls set their own hours within that, so a favorite counter may close early or take a day off.

For food, the best window is a weekday late morning, roughly 10:30 to 11:30, when counters are stocked and the lunch crowd has not arrived; mid-afternoon on a weekday is the next best. Evenings are lively with after-work drinkers and tour groups, which is fun but means waiting for bench space. Sunday is the trade-off: the food alley runs as usual while the fabric, hanbok and vintage sections are shuttered, so the market feels like a food court surrounded by closed stores. Come on a Sunday only if food is the whole point.

en.heading: Pairing it with Cheonggyecheon, Jongmyo and a three-hour plan
paragraphs: Gwangjang sits between two of central Seoul's best walks. Its southern edge faces Cheonggyecheon (청계천), the restored stream whose old bridges gave the market its name, so a stream walk ending at the market is the natural approach. A guided morning walk featured by VisitKorea follows the stream east from the Gwanghwamun end to Jongno 5-ga and finishes at the market for noodles and pancakes. It is a long stretch on foot, and you can join or leave it at any bridge.

North across Jongno lies Jongmyo (종묘), the royal ancestral shrine; the market's own directions send drivers to the Jongmyo public parking lot, which tells you how close the two are. Pair them as a morning and a lunch: shrine first, market second. Jongmyo has its own visiting rules and closing day, so check the shrine's official site before you go. The Dongdaemun fashion district to the east is also within walking distance if you would rather shop than sightsee.

A sample three-hour weekday plan: arrive at Jongno 5-ga Station, Exit 8, at 9:30 and loop the fabric and hanbok arcades as shutters go up. At 10:45 take a bench for mayak gimbap and a shared bowl of kalguksu. Around 11:30 move to a bindaetteok stall for one pancake and a bottle of makgeolli between two. At 12:15 either finish with yukhoe at a specialist restaurant or climb to the vintage arcade. Leave by the south side around 12:30 and walk west along Cheonggyecheon to let lunch settle.

Before you take a seat at any counter, run through these five habits. They prevent nearly every misunderstanding described in the news coverage above, they cost nothing but a few seconds, and vendors who run an honest stall will not mind them at all.
checklist: Find the price board and check the dish you want is on it.
Name the dish and the quantity, and ask the price if it is not posted.
Ask 카드 돼요? first if you need to pay by card; otherwise have small notes ready.
Decline add-ons clearly with 이것만 주세요.
Remember the stall's name or number in case you need the 1330 hotline.

faq.q: Is Gwangjang Market a tourist trap?
faq.a: Not as a whole, but it is a crowded tourist favorite with a documented history of overcharging complaints, especially in 2023 and 2025. Seoul and Jongno District have since stepped up inspections, sent in mystery shoppers and announced a real-name system for stall vendors. Choose stalls with posted prices, confirm the amount before you eat, and you will usually pay what the board says.

faq.q: Is the food alley open on Sundays?
faq.a: Yes. VisitKorea's official listing gives the food alley as open 09:00–23:00 year-round, while the general market shops and the secondhand clothing arcade close on Sundays. On a Sunday you can eat normally, but most of the fabric, hanbok and vintage sections will be shuttered.

faq.q: Do I need to speak Korean to order?
faq.a: No. Food is displayed at every counter and pointing works. A few phrases help: 이거 얼마예요? (how much is this?), 이거 하나 주세요 (one of this, please) and 이것만 주세요 (just this, please). Multilingual signs and QR guides were among the improvements officials called for in December 2025.

faq.q: What should I order if I can only try two things?
faq.a: Bindaetteok and mayak gimbap. The mung bean pancake is the dish the market is known for and pairs naturally with makgeolli, while mayak gimbap is quick, cheap and shows how Korean market snacks are meant to be eaten: on a bench, shared, with a sharp dip.

faq.q: Is there anywhere to sit with a back rest?
faq.a: The counter stalls have backless benches. If you want a proper table, look for the sit-down restaurants around the alley, which include the yukhoe specialists. They take longer than a counter but suit older travelers, families and anyone carrying shopping.

title.en: Korean BBQ Ordering Guide: Pork vs Beef, Portions, Grilling and Ssam

summary.en: How Korean barbecue works: pork vs beef houses, reading 인분 and per-100g prices, the two-portion rule, who grills, building ssam, and what to order to finish.

audience: Visitors who want to order Korean barbecue confidently in an ordinary Korean-language restaurant rather than a tourist set menu.
method: Researched from the official sources listed below, checked on October 20, 2026. Hours, fees and booking rules can change; the linked official pages are the final word.
quickAnswer: Decide on a pork house (samgyeopsal, moksal) or a beef house (galbi, hanu) before you go, then order by the portion, 인분 (inbun), usually at least two to start. Menus must show meat prices per 100 grams, so use that line to compare. Wrap grilled meat in lettuce or perilla with ssamjang and garlic, eat each wrap in one bite, and finish with rice and doenjang jjigae or cold naengmyeon.

keyFacts.label: Portion word
keyFacts.value: 인분 (inbun); 1인분 = one portion

keyFacts.label: Menu price rule
keyFacts.value: Meat priced per 100 g; portion weight shown with any per-portion price

keyFacts.label: Usual minimum
keyFacts.value: 2 portions on the first order (varies by restaurant)

keyFacts.label: Domestic beef labels
keyFacts.value: 한우 hanu / 육우 yugu / 젖소 jeotso

keyFacts.label: Map search
keyFacts.value: 삼겹살 (pork belly) or 한우 (Korean beef) + neighborhood

keyFacts.label: Tipping
keyFacts.value: Not customary

en.heading: Pork house or beef house: the first decision
paragraphs: Korean barbecue restaurants, gogitjip (고깃집, 'meat house'), usually specialize. A pork house builds its menu around samgyeopsal (삼겹살), the three-layered belly, and moksal (목살), the leaner neck and shoulder, with extras such as hangjeongsal (항정살, jowl) and marinated pork ribs, dwaeji galbi (돼지갈비). A beef house offers cuts like deungsim (등심, sirloin), chadolbagi (차돌박이, wafer-thin brisket), galbisal (갈비살, boneless rib meat) and short rib, plain or marinated: saeng-galbi (생갈비) or yangnyeom galbi (양념갈비). The sign often tells you which you are entering: 돼지 means pork, 소 or 한우 means beef.

The choice shapes the evening. Pork houses are loud, relatively inexpensive by barbecue standards and built for friends with soju, and you will usually do the grilling. Beef houses, especially hanu (한우) specialists serving Korean native cattle, cost more, feel calmer and are more likely to have staff manage the grill. Bulgogi (불고기), the sweet soy-marinated beef many visitors know first, sits slightly apart: it is commonly cooked with its juices in a pan or on a domed griddle and appears on lunch menus as often as at barbecue houses. For a first night, a pork house is the classic introduction and the safer bill.

en.heading: Reading the menu: 인분, grams and the 100-gram rule
paragraphs: Meat is ordered by the portion, written 인분 (inbun): 1인분 is one portion, 2인분 two. A portion is not a fixed national size. Under Korea's food sanitation rules, as summarized by the government's Easy Law service and Seoul's food safety office, restaurants must show the price of meat per 100 grams. They may also list a per-portion price, but only together with the weight they define as a portion, in a pattern like '100g ○○원 (1인분 ○○g △△원)'. One restaurant's portion can therefore be noticeably larger than another's at a similar headline price.

Use the per-100-gram figure to compare restaurants and cuts; the per-portion line is what you actually order. Seoul's guidance applies the rule to raw meat you grill and marinated meat you cook at the table, and excludes dishes served ready to eat, such as stews, steamed dishes and yukhoe. Small places do not always follow it to the letter, but when you see two prices beside one cut, that is why.

Look for the origin label too, 원산지 (wonsanji). Restaurants must state where their beef and pork come from, and for domestic beef the type of cattle: 한우 (hanu, Korean native cattle), 육우 (yugu, domestic beef cattle of other breeds) or 젖소 (jeotso, dairy breed), as a Yeongdeungpo District guide to the rules sets out. Hanu is graded. The Korea Institute for Animal Products Quality Evaluation grades beef 1++, 1+, 1, 2 and 3, and since December 2019 the agriculture ministry has required 1++ beef on sale to carry its marbling score of 7, 8 or 9, because the top grade was widened that year to include score 7 and the price gap between the three is real.

Most of the words on a barbecue menu fall into a short list. Learn these and you can read a typical pork or beef house menu without a translation app. Menus in tourist areas often add English, but neighborhood places rarely do, and the Korean names are what staff will recognize when you order.

rows: Pork belly, alternating layers of fat and meat
Pork neck and shoulder, leaner and chewier
Pork jowl, rich and slightly crunchy
Paper-thin beef brisket; cooks in seconds
Country or type of origin of the meat

en.heading: The two-portion minimum, and how to order around it
paragraphs: Most barbecue houses want at least two portions on the first order, often printed as 2인분 이상 or 주문은 2인분부터. The grill, the charcoal and the spread of side dishes cost the restaurant the same whether one person eats or two. The Korea JoongAng Daily found barbecue restaurants among those turning away solo diners at busy times, and the Fair Trade Commission told the paper this is the owner's decision. For a pair, two portions is the natural opening order.

For larger groups, a sensible pattern is to order one portion fewer than the number of people, then add as the grill empties; additional single portions are usually fine once the minimum has been met, and 추가 1인분 돼요? (chuga irinbun dwaeyo?) settles it. Many places let you mix cuts to reach the minimum, so one belly and one neck is a good first order for two at a pork house. Solo travelers have three options: a restaurant advertising 1인분 or 혼밥, a one-person lunch set, or two portions and a slower evening.

en.heading: Who holds the tongs
paragraphs: At a typical pork house the staff bring the meat, may lay the first strips on the grill, and then leave the rest to you. The tools are tongs (집게, jipge) and kitchen scissors (가위, gawi): Koreans grill long strips whole, then snip them into bite-size pieces on the grill. Turn pork belly once the underside is golden, cut it, and let the pieces finish; pale pork needs more time. At many beef and hanu restaurants staff grill for you, both to protect expensive meat and because well-marbled beef needs only moments per side. If a server reaches for your tongs, let them.

Grilling is social as well as practical. In a group, the person nearest the grill or the most junior often takes charge, and placing cooked meat on someone else's plate is a small act of care. When the grill plate chars and starts to stick, ask for a fresh one: 불판 갈아 주세요 (bulpan gara juseyo). Charcoal grills (숯불, sutbul) bring more smoke and flavor; gas and electric grills are cleaner. Most tables have an extractor hood or vent, but clothes still pick up the smell, so many restaurants hand out aprons or bags for coats.

en.heading: Building a ssam, and what else goes on the grill
paragraphs: Ssam (쌈) means a wrap, and it is how most Koreans eat grilled meat. Lay a lettuce leaf (상추, sangchu) across your open palm, add a perilla leaf (깻잎, kkaennip) on top if you like its minty, anise-like edge, then a piece of meat. Dab on ssamjang (쌈장), a thick sauce based on doenjang soybean paste and gochujang chili paste, and add a slice of raw or grilled garlic (마늘, maneul), a coin of green chili or a pinch of dressed scallion salad (파채, pachae). Fold the leaf closed around the filling.

Then eat it in one bite. VisitKorea's advice is to open wide and put the whole wrap in at once, and Visit Seoul's etiquette notes make wrapping the one time it is fine to handle food with your fingers. Biting a wrap in half sprays sauce and falls apart, so keep each one small: one piece of meat, a leaf or two, a little sauce. Between wraps, dip plain pieces in gireumjang (기름장), sesame oil with salt and pepper, which flatters pork belly and beef alike.

The grill takes more than meat. At pork houses, set sliced garlic in a small foil cup or at the grill's edge to soften in the rendered fat, and move kimchi onto the grill once there is fat to fry it in; grilled kimchi turns sweet and smoky, and for many Koreans it is the best part of the meal. Mushrooms and onion slices go the same way. Myeongi namul (명이나물), pickled wild-garlic leaves, often appear at pork houses; use them like lettuce, wrapped around a piece of belly.

en.heading: The second act: rice, stew or cold noodles
paragraphs: A Korean barbecue meal rarely ends with the last piece of meat. Staff will often ask whether you want siksa (식사, 'the meal'), meaning the rice course, and the word says a lot about how Koreans think about food: meat with drinks is one thing, but a meal involves rice. The most common order is doenjang jjigae (된장찌개), soybean-paste stew, with a bowl of rice, 공기밥 (gonggibap). Some pork houses serve a small doenjang stew alongside the meat; others sell it as an add-on.

Naengmyeon (냉면), chewy buckwheat noodles in icy broth (mul-naengmyeon) or tossed in chili sauce (bibim-naengmyeon), is the classic finish at galbi and beef houses, the cold, tangy broth cutting through the fat. Many pork houses offer a smaller bowl, often listed as 후식 냉면 (husik naengmyeon, 'dessert naengmyeon'), for exactly this purpose. Where the restaurant offers it, fried rice, bokkeumbap (볶음밥), made on the grill plate with chopped kimchi and seaweed, is another finish; ask 볶음밥 돼요? (bokkeumbap dwaeyo?).

en.heading: Soju, beer and the rhythm of a barbecue table
paragraphs: Barbecue is drinking food in Korea, and pork belly with soju is the pairing most Koreans would name first. Green-bottle soju is cheap, clean-tasting and noticeably stronger than it seems, and the small glasses empty quickly in a round of toasts. Many tables order beer as well and combine the two into somaek (소맥), a measure of soju in a glass of beer. Nobody needs to drink: soft drinks (음료수, eumnyosu) and the free water are always fine, and a raised glass of saida (사이다, lemon-lime soda) works for any toast.

The pouring rules apply here as anywhere: fill others' glasses rather than your own, use two hands when pouring for or receiving from someone older, and turn slightly away from elders when you drink. Our guide to makgeolli, soju and traditional liquor explains those gestures and Korea's year-based drinking age in detail. At barbecue the practical point is pacing. Meat arrives in waves, and so do toasts, so drink water between rounds and order the rice course before the night runs late.

en.heading: Courtesies at the grill, and how the bill adds up
paragraphs: Use the tongs, not your own chopsticks, to handle raw meat; chopsticks go to your mouth, tongs touch the raw pieces. Offer the last piece around before taking it. Don't flip meat constantly: let it brown, then turn it. If someone else is grilling, don't take over without asking, and thank whoever cooked. When you leave, pay at the counter. Tipping is not customary, and Seoul's price-display rules require menu prices to include VAT and service charges, so the menu price is what you pay.

A barbecue bill is built from three parts: the per-portion meat price multiplied by the number of portions, the drinks, and the rice or noodle course. Banchan and lettuce refills are normally free; ask if unsure. The biggest swing is the meat itself. Hanu at 1++ grade with a high marbling score sits at the top of any menu, imported beef and pork well below it, and the origin label tells you which you are buying. If cost matters, read 원산지 and the per-100-gram line before you order.

en.heading: A worked order for two at a pork house
paragraphs: You walk in and say 두 명이요 (du myeong-iyo, 'two people'). The server switches on or lights the grill and sets out ssamjang, gireumjang, lettuce and banchan. You order: 삼겹살 1인분, 목살 1인분 주세요 (samgyeopsal irinbun, moksal irinbun juseyo), adding 소주 한 병이요 (soju han byeong-iyo) if you are drinking. The meat arrives raw on a tray. Lay the strips flat, put garlic and kimchi at the edge, turn when golden, snip into pieces, and build small wraps. Point at the empty lettuce basket for more.

When the grill is empty, decide between another portion and the rice course. 된장찌개하고 공기밥 하나 주세요 (doenjang-jjigae-hago gonggibap hana juseyo) brings stew and a bowl of rice; 후식 냉면 하나 주세요 brings a small bowl of cold noodles. If the plate is scorched before a second round, say 불판 갈아 주세요. Finally take the bill to the counter, pay by card, collect your coat from its bag, and head out smelling faintly of charcoal, which is how everyone leaves a gogitjip.

faq.q: Do I have to grill the meat myself?
faq.a: At most pork houses, yes, though staff often start the first batch and will help if you look unsure. At many beef and hanu restaurants, staff grill for you because the cuts are expensive and need precise timing. If you would like help anywhere, ask 구워 주실 수 있어요? (guwo jusil su isseoyo?, 'could you grill it for us?').

faq.q: Can one person eat Korean barbecue?
faq.a: Yes, but choose the place carefully. Many barbecue restaurants require two portions to start, and some turn away solo diners at busy times, which the Fair Trade Commission treats as the owner's choice. Look for 1인분 or 혼밥 on the door or menu, go outside peak hours, or simply order two portions.

faq.q: Are side dishes and lettuce refills free?
faq.a: Normally, yes. VisitKorea notes that extra side dishes and water do not cost anything in Korean restaurants, and lettuce, garlic and kimchi refills at barbecue houses are typically part of the meal. You pay for meat, drinks and the finishing course; if a premium place charges for something, it will be on the menu.

faq.q: What is the difference between galbi and bulgogi?
faq.a: Galbi (갈비) means ribs: beef or pork short rib, grilled plain or after marinating, often on charcoal at a barbecue house. Bulgogi (불고기) is thinly sliced beef in a sweet soy marinade, usually cooked with its juices in a pan or on a domed griddle and common on lunch menus.

faq.q: Which cut should a first-timer order?
faq.a: At a pork house, one portion of samgyeopsal and one of moksal shows the contrast between fatty belly and leaner neck. At a beef house, chadolbagi is quick and forgiving, while galbisal or yangnyeom galbi gives the classic rib flavor. Save top-grade hanu for when you know you enjoy rich, marbled beef.

title.en: Makgeolli, Soju and Traditional Korean Liquor: What to Drink and How

summary.en: How Korean alcohol works: nuruk, takju vs yakju vs soju, regional bottles, pouring etiquette, the year-based drinking age, The Sool Gallery and getting home safely.

audience: Adult visitors who want to understand and enjoy Korean alcohol, from convenience-store soju to regional rice wines, and handle a Korean drinking table gracefully.
method: Researched from the official sources listed below, checked on October 20, 2026. Hours, fees and booking rules can change; the linked official pages are the final word.
quickAnswer: Makgeolli is unfiltered rice wine brewed with the starter nuruk; filter the same brew and you get yakju or cheongju, distill it and you get soju, though the cheap green-bottle soju is diluted ethanol. At the table, pour for others, use two hands with elders and turn slightly away when you drink. You can legally drink from January 1 of the year you turn 19, so in 2026 anyone born in 2007 or earlier qualifies.

en.heading: Everything starts with nuruk
paragraphs: The Korean word for alcohol, sul (술), covers everything from beer to whisky, but the traditional drinks share one ingredient: nuruk (누룩). Nuruk is a dried cake, usually of coarsely milled wheat, on which molds and wild yeasts have grown. Korea's Liquor Tax Act defines this family of starters, guk (국, 麴), as starchy material on which molds have been cultivated. The molds release enzymes that turn grain starch into sugar while the yeasts turn that sugar into alcohol, both in the same vessel at the same time.

A basic brew is steamed rice, nuruk and water, left to ferment for days or weeks. Because nuruk carries a mixed, local population of microbes, it gives Korean rice wines their tang and earthy depth, and two brewers using the same rice can produce very different results. Many modern producers add cultured yeast for consistency, which is why labels that make a point of 전통 누룩 (jeontong nuruk, traditional nuruk) are telling you something about the brewer's approach.

From one fermented mash come three families of drink, and their names describe what happens next. Leave the mash unfiltered and cloudy, and you have takju (탁주, 'cloudy liquor'), of which makgeolli is the everyday form. Let the solids settle and draw off or filter the clear liquid, and you have yakju (약주) or cheongju (청주). Distill it, and you have soju (소주). The Liquor Tax Act still sorts Korean drinks along exactly these lines.

en.heading: Takju, yakju, cheongju and soju, side by side
paragraphs: The legal definitions are sharper than most bar menus. In the Liquor Tax Act's annex, takju is made from starchy grain, a mold starter and water and finished without filtering, so it stays cloudy; yakju is the filtered equivalent; cheongju is a filtered rice wine whose grain must be rice, glutinous rice included. Soju is distilled and comes in two legally distinct forms: one distilled by a non-continuous, pot-still method from a fermented starch mash, and one made by diluting high-proof ethanol with water. That second form is the green bottle in every convenience store.

One practical note for makgeolli. A label marked 생 (saeng, 'live') means it is unpasteurized and still contains active yeast, so keep it cold, drink it within the date printed, and open it slowly because it can foam over. Pasteurized makgeolli, 살균 (salgyun), is shelf-stable and flatter. Gently tip the bottle to mix the sediment before pouring; shaking a live bottle hard is the classic first-timer's mistake.

rows: Milky, lightly sour, often fizzy; mix gently before pouring
The same kind of mash, filtered
Clear and golden, smoother; served chilled in small cups
Filtered rice wine made only from rice
Strong and aromatic; sip it, don't shoot it
High-proof ethanol diluted with water and sweetened
Neutral and smooth; the everyday green bottle

en.heading: Why the green bottle tastes the way it does
paragraphs: Most of the soju Koreans drink is the diluted kind, and the reason is twentieth-century policy. The National Archives of Korea explains that after the 1965 Grain Management Act banned making liquor from pure grain, distilled soju with its traditional flavor all but disappeared, and producers switched to ethanol from sweet potato or molasses, diluted with water and sweeteners. Makgeolli suffered as well: brewers turned to imported wheat flour, and some added carbide to hurry fermentation, which did lasting damage to its reputation.

The archives also explain why every region seems to have its own soju. In 1976 the government consolidated 254 soju makers into ten diluted-soju producers, one per province, and protected each in its home market. That rule was abolished in 1996, but regional loyalties outlived it, so ask for the local soju outside Seoul and you will usually be handed a provincial brand. Distilled soju, with Andong soju from North Gyeongsang Province as its best-known example, is the version worth seeking out: sip it neat or over ice to taste the grain.

en.heading: Makgeolli's comeback, and what 'traditional' means on a label
paragraphs: Rice makgeolli returned in the early 1990s, when large harvests produced a rice surplus, according to the National Archives, though it took until the late 2000s for the drink to become fashionable again; the archives note it topped the Samsung Economic Research Institute's list of hit products for 2009. In June 2021 the Cultural Heritage Administration designated makgeolli-making (막걸리 빚기) a National Intangible Cultural Heritage, honoring the shared practice of brewing and drinking it rather than any single master brewer.

The heritage administrator's column on the designation, published in the Korea JoongAng Daily, shows where the drink sits in Korean life. An old saying held that farmhands favored farms that served good makgeolli at their breaks; it is still poured at ceremonies for new buildings, new cars and restaurant openings; and it remains the natural partner for kimchi, bindaetteok and hongeo samhap, fermented skate with pork and kimchi. Households once brewed it at home the way they made kimchi and soybean paste.

'Traditional liquor', jeontongju (전통주), is a legal category and narrower than you might expect. Under the Liquor Tax Act it covers drinks made by holders of a national or provincial intangible heritage title for liquor, by designated Korean Food Masters, or by farm and fishery businesses making regional specialty liquors from local produce with a provincial recommendation. A mass-market makgeolli can be traditional in style without qualifying. When shopping, the brewery's region and the origin of its rice tell you more than the word 'traditional'.

en.heading: Regional bottles worth seeking out
paragraphs: Regional liquors are where Korean drinking culture gets interesting. Andong soju (안동소주), from Andong in North Gyeongsang Province, is the archetype of distilled soju, and the National Archives uses it as the representative example of the pot-still style. Munbaeju (문배주) is a distilled spirit that smells of wild pear although no pear goes into it; KOCIS's English guide to Korean drinks describes a mixed-grain recipe with millet in the starter and sorghum in the main mash.

Hansan sogokju (한산소곡주), from Hansan in South Chungcheong Province, is a glutinous-rice liquor fermented at low temperature for about 100 days, according to Korea.net. Its nickname, anjeunbaengi-sul (앉은뱅이술), roughly 'the drink that keeps you sitting', comes from stories of drinkers who found they could not stand up; Korea.net lists the standard version at 18 percent alcohol and a stronger version, bulsogokju, at 43. Gamhongno (감홍로), an herbal distilled spirit whose name means 'sweet red dew', is described by KOCIS as one of the three famous liquors of the Joseon era.

You don't need to travel to try them. Department-store food halls, specialist bottle shops and many Seoul restaurants stock regional liquors, and a tasting is the fastest way to discover whether you lean toward sweet, sour, dry or smoky. Our suggestion: start with a good live makgeolli and a clear yakju to taste the same kind of mash two ways, then try one distilled soju neat. That trio teaches more than a week of green bottles.

en.heading: The pour: how Koreans share a bottle
paragraphs: Korean drinking etiquette grew out of Confucian manners codified in the Joseon era, and Korea.net's series on alcohol traces it to the Sohak (소학), the 'Lesser Learning' primer. The core rule survives intact: you pour for others, not for yourself, and someone will notice when your glass is empty. Tradition also says a cup should be emptied before it is passed back or refilled, and the person pouring watches the glasses around the table rather than their own. A friend who fills your glass will expect you to return the favor when theirs runs dry.

With elders, the gestures matter. Pour with your right hand on the bottle while your left hand supports it or touches your right forearm, a gesture Korea.net traces to holding back a long sleeve so it would not trail over the food, and receive a pour with your glass held in both hands. When you drink in front of someone older, turn your head slightly aside and shield the glass with a hand. Korea.net's etiquette material lists these moves, and its alcohol series adds that one hand is acceptable between companions within about five years of age.

The first round is usually a group toast, geonbae (건배, 'dry cup'). After that, pace is personal. If you don't drink, accept the first pour, touch glasses, then sip or don't and set the glass down; Korea.net describes much the same for non-drinkers, and a full glass signals that you are fine. Visitors get latitude, but these gestures land well with older Koreans and in business settings. Nobody should pressure you, and 술을 못 마셔요 (sureul mot masyeoyo, 'I can't drink') is a complete answer.

en.heading: Pajeon on rainy days, and other pairings
paragraphs: Koreans rarely drink without food, called anju (안주). The pairing every Korean knows is makgeolli with jeon (전), savory pan-fried pancakes, especially pajeon (파전, scallion pancake) and bindaetteok. On a wet day many Koreans crave exactly that combination. The popular explanations range from the hiss of batter in hot oil sounding like rain to rainy days once being rest days for farmers. Neither can be proven, but the habit is real: ask a Korean friend what to eat on a rainy evening and jeon with makgeolli is the likely answer.

Soju suits strong, salty or fatty food: grilled pork belly, stews, spicy stir-fries and soups. Clear yakju and cheongju suit lighter dishes such as jeon, steamed fish or raw fish, while a distilled soju stands up to grilled beef. The venues follow the drinks. Jeon houses (전집, jeonjip) and folk taverns (민속주점, minsok jujeom) are where makgeolli lives; barbecue restaurants and tent bars (포장마차, pojangmacha) are soju territory. In Naver Map, search 막걸리 or 전집 plus a neighborhood name to find them.

en.heading: Where to learn: The Sool Gallery in Bukchon
paragraphs: The best single stop for an introduction is The Sool Gallery (전통주갤러리, Jeontongju Gallery), a showroom and tasting room set up by the Ministry of Agriculture, Food and Rural Affairs and the Korea Agro-Fisheries & Food Trade Corporation (aT). Its official site places it on the first floor of Ieum, the Korean food culture space (한식문화공간 이음), at 18 Bukchon-ro, Jongno-gu, open 10:00–19:00 and closed on Mondays, New Year's Day, Seollal and Chuseok. Search 전통주갤러리 in Naver Map.

The gallery picks a themed 'liquor of the month' lineup and runs tasting programs, including sessions for foreign visitors in English, Japanese and Chinese, according to its site. A March 2025 government article described free tastings on the hour from noon to 6 p.m., Tuesday to Sunday, with the 3 p.m. and 4 p.m. sessions reserved for foreign visitors in English and about ten places per session, most booked through Naver Reservation. Treat that as a guide and confirm the current schedule when you book through Naver Reservation, by phone (02-555-2283) or by email (soolgallery2@gmail.com).

The gallery is a short walk from Anguk Station, Exit 2, on Line 3, which makes it easy to pair with Bukchon or Insadong. Make the tasting your afternoon anchor, then walk to a jeon house for dinner and order what you liked. If you prefer to read first, KOCIS publishes a free English guide, Hidden Charms of Korea: SOOL, on Korea.net, covering traditional drinks, soju and food pairings.

en.heading: Legal age, strength and getting home
paragraphs: Korea's drinking age is set by calendar year, not by birthday. The Youth Protection Act defines a youth as someone under 19 but excludes anyone who has reached January 1 of the year they turn 19. In 2026 that means anyone born in 2007 or earlier can legally buy and drink alcohol, whatever their birthday. Bars, clubs and convenience stores can ask for identification and refuse a sale without it, so carry your passport if you look young.

Strength sneaks up on visitors. Diluted soju tastes mild but is far stronger than beer, the small glasses empty fast in a rhythm of toasts, and fizzy makgeolli goes down easily too. Eat as you drink, alternate with water, and decide your limit before the second round, 2차 (icha), when groups move on to another bar. The morning after has its own vocabulary: haejang (해장) means easing a hangover, and haejangguk (해장국) is the soup Koreans eat to do it.

Plan the ride home before you order the last bottle. The subway does not run through the night, so check your station's last train in Naver Map or Kakao Map before the second round. After that, Seoul's late-night N buses cover major routes, and taxis add a night surcharge: Seoul's official fare page lists 20 percent from 10 to 11 p.m. and from 2 to 4 a.m., and 40 percent from 11 p.m. to 2 a.m. Never drive after drinking.

A short checklist before a night out keeps the evening easy and the journey home predictable. None of it is specific to visitors; Korean office workers heading out for a team dinner run through much the same list, usually while checking the last train.
checklist: Carry your passport if there is any chance you will be asked your age.
Check the last subway time from the bar to your hotel before the second round.
Order food with every round; Korean drinking is meant to come with anju.
Alternate soju or makgeolli with water.
Keep a taxi app or cash ready for the night-surcharge fare home.

faq.q: Is makgeolli the same as Japanese sake?
faq.a: No. Both are rice-based, but makgeolli is unfiltered and cloudy, usually lower in alcohol and often fizzy, and it is traditionally fermented with nuruk, a wheat-based starter carrying wild yeasts and molds. Korea's clear, filtered rice wines, yakju and cheongju, are the closer comparison to sake.

faq.q: I turn 19 in December 2026. Can I drink in Korea now?
faq.a: Yes. The Youth Protection Act excludes anyone who has reached January 1 of the year they turn 19, so in 2026 anyone born in 2007 or earlier can legally buy and drink alcohol regardless of birthday. Carry your passport, since staff may ask for proof of age.

faq.q: Do I really have to turn away when I drink?
faq.a: Only in front of someone noticeably older, and mainly in formal or family settings. Turning your head slightly and shielding the glass is a sign of respect. Among friends of similar age it is not expected, and visitors who forget will be forgiven, but the gesture is noticed and appreciated.

faq.q: How can I tell if a makgeolli is unpasteurized?
faq.a: Look for 생 (saeng) or 생막걸리 on the label, usually with a short shelf life and a refrigeration note. Unpasteurized makgeolli keeps fermenting in the bottle, so it tastes livelier and can foam when opened. Pasteurized bottles are marked 살균 (salgyun) and last longer at room temperature.

faq.q: Is green-bottle soju a traditional Korean liquor?
faq.a: Not in the historical sense. It is diluted soju, ethanol cut with water and sweeteners, which became dominant after the 1965 grain rules pushed out grain-distilled soju. Traditional soju is pot-distilled from a fermented mash, as in Andong soju. Legally, 'jeontongju' is a narrower category still.

title.en: National Museum of Korea in Three Hours: What's Open and Worth It

summary.en: A three-hour plan for Seoul's free National Museum of Korea: the pensive bodhisattvas, a 1348 marble pagoda, Silla gold, and how to route around gallery closures.

audience: First-time visitors to Seoul who want to see the National Museum of Korea's essential works in one afternoon or evening without walking into closed galleries.
method: Researched from the official sources listed below, checked on October 20, 2026. Hours, fees and booking rules can change; the linked official pages are the final word.
quickAnswer: Give the National Museum of Korea three hours and three anchors: the Gyeongcheonsa pagoda in the first-floor central hall, the Silla gold crown in the ancient history galleries, and the two pensive bodhisattvas in the second-floor Room of Quiet Contemplation, then add the celadon and buncheong rooms (303 and 304) if you have energy left. The permanent galleries are free.

en.heading: Pick three objects, not three floors
paragraphs: The National Museum of Korea (국립중앙박물관, Gungnip Jungang Bangmulgwan) in Yongsan holds far more than a first-time visitor can absorb, and because its permanent galleries are free, it is tempting to walk every corridor. That approach usually ends in fatigue somewhere on the second floor, with the best objects reduced to a blur of glass cases. A better plan chooses a few works that each explain a different chapter of Korean history and gives each one real attention.

This guide uses three anchors. The Gyeongcheonsa pagoda tells a story that runs from fourteenth-century Goryeo through colonial-era removal to its return home. The Silla gold crown shows what royal display meant in a kingdom that buried its elite with extraordinary wealth. The two pensive bodhisattvas show how Buddhism shaped Korean sculpture in the Three Kingdoms period. The third-floor ceramic rooms are the optional fourth stop.

Who should ignore this plan? If you already know Korean art, or you have a whole day, follow your own interests through the Goryeo and Joseon history rooms and a special exhibition instead. If you have only one hour, see the pagoda and then go straight up to the Room of Quiet Contemplation, and leave everything else for another trip.

en.heading: The 2026–27 gallery renovation: what is closed and what is not
paragraphs: Check the renovation notice before you build any route. On July 6, 2026 the museum closed several second- and third-floor galleries, and two more calligraphy and painting rooms followed on August 10. All of them are scheduled to reopen on January 29, 2027. Older blog itineraries that send you to the Buddhist Sculpture Gallery or the Metal Crafts Gallery will lead you to a closed door, so do not copy a highlights route written before mid-2026.

What stays open matters just as much. The Room of Quiet Contemplation is not on the closure list, and the museum's floor listing still shows it on the second floor. Celadon (Room 303) and Buncheong Ware and White Porcelain (Room 304) remain open on the third floor, as do Calligraphy and Painting Rooms 202-1 and 202-2. Short closures for exhibit changes also happen: the Central Asia Gallery, for example, shut from October 12 to 22, 2026 to install a new display. Read the notice board on the museum's English site in the week you go.
