en.heading: Insadong-gil from Naminsa Madang to Buginsa Madang
paragraphs: The main street, Insadong-gil (인사동길), runs roughly north from Jongno to Anguk Station, with a small plaza and tourist information point at each end. Naminsa Madang, the south plaza off Jongno 2-ga, is where you enter if you come from Tapgol Park. Walking north, you pass street stalls selling snacks and trinkets before the shops thicken into dealers in old paintings, frames, brushes and ceramics.

At Insadong Negeori, the main crossroads, a right turn heads toward Nagwon Arcade, Seoul's long-established musical instrument market, and a left turn leads in a few minutes to Jogyesa temple. Along this stretch stand the Tong-in Store, a multistory craft and antique emporium in business since 1924, and Insadong Maru, a 2014 complex with craft shops, cafés and the kimchi museum Museum Kimchikan on its upper floors.

Farther north, past Sudo Pharmacy (open since 1946 and listed as Seoul Future Heritage), is Ssamziegil (쌈지길), opened in 2004. Its four floors are linked by a continuous ramp, so you browse small design and craft shops as if you were still walking up the street. It is busy and youthful, good for contemporary Korean design rather than antiques. The street ends at Buginsa Madang, marked by a giant brush sculpture beside Anguk Station, where you can cross to Bukchon.

en.heading: Hanji, brushes and ceramics: telling craft from souvenir stock
paragraphs: Insadong has always mixed serious craft with tourist filler, and the two often share a shelf. Your best protection is to know what a material should look and feel like. Hanji (한지) is made from the inner bark of the paper mulberry, called dak (닥). Hold a sheet up to the light: handmade hanji shows long, irregular fibers and slight variations in thickness, while machine paper printed with a hanji texture looks uniform. Korea has nominated the knowledge and skills of hanji-making for UNESCO's list of intangible heritage, with a decision due at the UNESCO committee session that opens on November 30, 2026.

Brush shops sell the four treasures of the scholar's study: brush, ink stick, inkstone and paper. Guhasanbang, a Seoul Future Heritage brush shop dating to around 1913 and said to have supplied brushes to the palace, is the kind of specialist that can explain hair types and why one brush costs ten times another. For ceramics, turn a piece over: a maker's seal or signature on the foot, a box signed by the potter, and small differences between cups in a set suggest handwork. Identical items stacked in five neighboring shops suggest a factory.
checklist: Ask 직접 만든 거예요? (jikjeop mandeun geoyeyo, did you make this?) or 어디서 만들었어요? (eodiseo mandeureosseoyo, where was it made?).
Look for a maker's name, stamp or workshop card; real craft shops are proud to tell you who made a piece.
Check the country-of-origin label (원산지, wonsanji) on fans, bags and trinkets.
Compare prices for the same item across two or three shops before buying anything costly.
Be wary of anything sold as an antique without written provenance, and ask the dealer about paperwork for taking it home.
Buy hanji in sheets or simple stationery if luggage is tight; it is light, flat and genuinely useful.

en.heading: Galleries, old books and a poet's teahouse in the side alleys
paragraphs: The slower Insadong lives off the main street. Commercial galleries rotate exhibitions frequently and generally let you walk in without a ticket; climbing one flight of stairs is often the difference between souvenir stalls and contemporary ink painting. Tongin Gallery, a Seoul Future Heritage space, has shown leading Korean artists including Park Seo-bo and has held hundreds of exhibitions alongside its trade in antique art.

Tongmungwan (통문관), founded around 1934 and run by the same family for three generations, is regarded as the oldest bookshop in Korea and deals in rare books, old manuscripts and out-of-print titles; it has also published scholarship in Korean studies. Even if you cannot read the spines, the shop is a window into the bibliophile culture that once filled this street.

For a pause, Cafe Gwichun continues Gwichun, a teahouse long associated with the poet Cheon Sang-byeong, and visitors still come to read his verses over tea. Traditional teahouses throughout the alleys serve infusions such as jujube, ginger or quince, a good way to rest your legs between galleries.

en.heading: Tapgol Park, where the March 1st Movement went public
paragraphs: At the south end of Insadong, on Jongno, Tapgol Park (탑골공원) carries more history per square meter than anywhere else on this walk. In 1465 King Sejo dedicated the temple Wongaksa here; its ten-story stone pagoda, completed in 1467, still stands, now protected inside a glass shelter. The temple fell into ruin under later kings, and in 1897 the site reopened as Pagoda Park, Korea's first Western-style modern park. It took its present name in 1992 from the old local name, Tapdong, the pagoda neighborhood.

On March 1, 1919, the Declaration of Independence was read aloud here, by tradition from the octagonal pavilion, Palgakjeong, and the crowd poured out along Jongno shouting for independence from Japanese rule. The March 1st Movement spread across the country in the following weeks and is commemorated every year as a national holiday. Look for the main gate, Samilmun, named for the date, and the relief panels that depict scenes from the protests.

Today the park is also a gathering place for older Seoul residents, many of whom spend long afternoons here. Walk through quietly, treat it as a memorial first and a sight second, and do not expect a manicured attraction. Fifteen to twenty minutes is enough to see the pagoda, the pavilion and the reliefs.

en.heading: Jogyesa, a working temple a few minutes from the antique shops
paragraphs: Turn west at the Insadong crossroads and within minutes you reach Jogyesa (조계사), head temple of the Jogye Order of Korean Buddhism. It was founded in 1910 as Gakhwangsa, renamed Taegosa in 1938 and given its present name in 1954, a change intended to clear away traces of the colonial era. The large main hall, Daeungjeon, faces a courtyard shaded by old trees, including a lacebark pine whose pale, flaking bark is easy to spot.

Unlike a palace, this is a place of daily worship, with lay believers bowing in the main hall at almost any hour. Enter the hall through the side doors rather than the central one, remove your shoes, keep to the back if a service is under way, and do not photograph people while they pray. In the weeks before Buddha's Birthday the courtyard is roofed with rows of lotus lanterns, the temple's best-known look, but an ordinary weekday visit shows its daily rhythm more clearly.

en.heading: Ikseon-dong: Jeong Se-kwon's small houses, now cafés
paragraphs: Ikseon-dong (익선동) is smaller and plainer than Bukchon, and that is the point. The name dates from 1914, when the colonial administration merged several wards. In the 1920s the developer Jeong Se-kwon (정세권, 1888–1965), whose company Geonyangsa is often called Korea's first modern real estate developer, bought large lots here, including the site of a former royal-relative mansion, subdivided them and built rows of small hanok for ordinary Korean households. Seoul's hanok portal says this created the layout you walk today; most houses are under 30 pyeong, roughly 100 square meters.

Jeong was more than a builder. He used his profits to support Korean nationalist causes, donating a building to the Joseon Language Society, the scholars' group that defended and studied the Korean language under colonial rule. Building Korean-style houses for Koreans in central Seoul was, in that context, a political act as well as a business.

The neighborhood nearly vanished. It was slated for redevelopment in 2004, but the plan collapsed in 2014, and cafés, restaurants and vintage shops moved into renovated hanok instead. In 2018 Seoul designated it a hanok-concentrated area; 118 houses built before the 1930s remain. One loss marks the change: Ojinam, a historic hanok restaurant where talks before the 1972 South-North Joint Statement were held, was demolished in 2010 and its parts moved to Buam-dong.

Expect narrow, crowded lanes on weekends and a café-district atmosphere rather than a heritage site. Go on a weekday before the lunch rush to see the rooflines and lane pattern clearly, and remember that some of these small houses are still homes. From Jongno 3-ga Station, take Exit 6 and walk north into the alleys.

en.heading: A three-and-a-half-hour walk that strings it together
paragraphs: This sequence works on most days and keeps backtracking to a minimum. At 10:00, start at Buginsa Madang beside Anguk Station and walk Ssamziegil while it is still quiet. From 10:30, work south down Insadong-gil, climbing into galleries and visiting a brush shop and Tongmungwan in the side alleys. At 11:15, turn west at the crossroads for twenty minutes at Jogyesa, then return to the main street.

Around 12:00, exit at Naminsa Madang and cross to Tapgol Park for the pagoda and the March 1st memorials. Have lunch in the alleys south and east of the park, then walk east along Jongno to Jongno 3-ga Station Exit 6 and turn north into Ikseon-dong at about 13:30. Finish with tea or coffee in a converted hanok, looking up at the eaves and tile ends on the way.

If you prefer an afternoon start, reverse it: Ikseon-dong first, then Tapgol Park and Insadong northward, ending at Anguk Station with Bukchon a short walk across the road. Shoppers should note that serious buying takes time; if you plan to choose ceramics or hanji carefully, allow an extra hour and skip Jogyesa for another day.

faq.q: Is everything sold in Insadong made in Korea?
faq.a: No. The street mixes genuine craft shops, galleries and antique dealers with stalls selling mass-produced souvenirs, some of them imported. Check origin labels, ask who made a piece, and favor shops that can explain materials and makers. Specialist brush shops, hanji stores and gallery shops are the safest places for Korean-made goods.

faq.q: Does Insadong really ban signs in English?
faq.a: The famous Hangul-only Starbucks sign was described at the time as the company's own choice for the location, and we found no current blanket ban on foreign-language signs. The district's formal rules restrict which kinds of businesses can open on the main street. Many shops still use Korean signs, so learning a few words helps.

faq.q: Can non-Buddhists visit Jogyesa?
faq.a: Yes. The temple welcomes visitors who are not Buddhist, and you may look into the main hall. Remove your shoes before entering, use the side doors, stay quiet, keep to the back during services and avoid photographing people at prayer. If you want to go further, temples in Seoul offer short templestay and temple-life programs.

faq.q: When is Ikseon-dong least crowded?
faq.a: Weekday mornings, before the lunch crowd arrives. Weekends and evenings are busiest, when the narrow lanes can feel packed. If you want photographs of the rooflines rather than the cafés, come early on a weekday and walk the side alleys rather than the main café lane.

faq.q: Is Insadong worth visiting if I am not shopping?
faq.a: Yes, if you use it as a walk through art and history rather than a market. Free galleries, Tongmungwan's old books, a traditional teahouse, Jogyesa and Tapgol Park's 1919 memorials make a satisfying half day without buying anything. Skip the main-street stalls and spend your time upstairs and in the alleys.

title.en: Seochon Walk: Tongin Market Coin Lunch, Poets' Houses and Inwangsan Valley

summary.en: A half-day Seochon walk west of Gyeongbokgung: how Tongin Market's coin lunchbox works, Park No-soo's house, Suseongdong valley, Yun Dong-ju's hill and Inwangsan.

audience: Walkers on a first or second Seoul trip who want an older residential neighborhood with market food, literature and a mountain edge rather than a photo-stop hanok street.
method: Researched from the official sources listed below, checked on October 20, 2026. Hours, fees and booking rules can change; the linked official pages are the final word.
quickAnswer: Seochon is the old neighborhood between Gyeongbokgung's west wall and Inwangsan. Start at Gyeongbokgung Station Exit 2, build a coin lunchbox at Tongin Market, visit the Park No-soo Art Museum, then walk up to Suseongdong valley and either climb Inwangsan or ride a bus to the Yun Dong-ju Literary Museum. Avoid Mondays, when both museums close.

en.heading: Clerks, poets and painters: who lived west of the palace
paragraphs: Seochon (서촌, west village) is the informal name for the slope between Gyeongbokgung's west wall and Inwangsan (인왕산), taking in neighborhoods such as Hyoja-dong, Sajik-dong, Tongin-dong, Nuha-dong and Okin-dong. In late Joseon it was known as Sangchon or Udae, and the Seoul City Wall office notes that its closeness to the palace and government offices made it home to many lower-ranking officials and clerks rather than the grand families of Bukchon.

That social mix produced something distinctive. Toward the end of Joseon, intellectuals from outside the yangban elite organized poetry clubs here, and the area became a center of what Koreans call yeohang or wihang literature, writing by the middle classes. Earlier, the valleys at the foot of Inwangsan had been celebrated scenic spots, and after the dynasty's founding royal relatives and influential families built retreats here.

The twentieth century layered on more. During the colonial period the Governor-General's official residence stood in the area, as did mansions of pro-Japanese aristocrats such as Yun Deok-yeong's Byeoksusanjang. In modern times poets Yi Sang and Yun Dong-ju, and painters including Yi Jung-seop, Cheon Gyeong-ja and Lee Sang-beom, lived or worked here. Today the houses are a jumble of 1930s urban hanok, modern brick villas and small apartment buildings, which is exactly why the neighborhood still feels lived in.

en.heading: Why Seochon feels nothing like Bukchon
paragraphs: Bukchon presents hanok in concentrated rows on a hillside; Seochon scatters them among laundromats, family diners, a market and corner bakeries. There is no single postcard lane, and the district's tourist-hour zones are drawn around Bukchon, not here. What you get instead is the texture of an older Seoul neighborhood: alleys that follow buried streams, tiled roofs glimpsed between villas, and a mountain rising directly behind the last houses.

Choose Seochon if you have already seen a palace and want to understand how Seoul lives, if you like literature and small museums, or if you would rather eat at a market than queue for a café. Skip it if your priority is the classic rows of hanok rooftops, which Bukchon does better, or if steep walking is difficult for you, since the best parts lie uphill toward Inwangsan.

The courtesy rules are the same as anywhere residential. Keep voices down in the lanes, do not photograph into homes, and give way to residents, delivery riders and the small village buses that squeeze through. Seochon has so far avoided the friction that led to Bukchon's rules; visitors who behave like guests help keep it that way.

en.heading: Tongin Market and the coin lunchbox
paragraphs: Tongin Market (통인시장) opened in June 1941 as a public market for Japanese residents during the colonial period; after the Korean War it became a market for Korean street vendors. Today it has more than seventy shops, mostly food stalls and groceries, along a covered lane at 18 Jahamun-ro 15-gil, about 500 meters from Gyeongbokgung Station Exit 2. Individual shops keep their own hours within a broad 7:00 to 21:00 window.

The market's best-known feature is the dosirak café (도시락카페), a coin-operated lunchbox system. You buy old-style coins called yeopjeon (엽전), each worth KRW 500, at the café, collect a tray, then walk the lane and trade coins for small portions at participating stalls before sitting down in the café to eat. A Seoul city report from 2025 describes exchanging KRW 10,000 for 20 coins and notes that unused coins can be refunded.

Check the schedule before you go, because official listings disagree. The café runs from late morning until mid-afternoon, and coin sales stop earlier, around 15:00 on weekdays and 16:00 on weekends according to the 2025 report. Visit Seoul and the 2025 report both close the café on the third Sunday of each month but disagree on the weekly day off: Visit Seoul says Monday, though its own hours line runs Wednesday to Monday, while the report gives Tuesday. The market's listed number is +82-507-1378-0940; aim to arrive by 11:30 to beat the lunch crowd.

Here is a typical first round, in order. Walk the whole lane once before spending anything. Then pick two or three items: the market's signature gireum tteokbokki (기름떡볶이), rice cakes stir-fried in oil with chili rather than simmered in sauce; a couple of jeon, savory pancakes; and a side or two of japchae or seasoned vegetables. Twenty coins, the KRW 10,000 bundle described in the city's 2025 report, is a sensible starting budget for one person; you can always buy more.
checklist: At the café counter: 엽전 주세요 (yeopjeon juseyo), coins, please.
At a stall, pointing: 이거 몇 개예요? (igeo myeot gaeyeyo), how many coins is this?
To order: 이거 주세요 (igeo juseyo), this one, please.
If you have leftover coins, ask at the café: 환불돼요? (hwanbul dwaeyo), can I get a refund?

en.heading: A painter's house, a poet's yard and a bookstore front
paragraphs: The Park No-soo Art Museum (박노수미술관) at 34 Okin 1-gil is the best single building in Seochon. Park No-soo was an ink painter who kept traditional subjects but rendered them with spare brushwork, bold touches and startling color. He bought this house in 1973 and lived here until the end of 2011, when, already ill, he agreed to donate it with his works to Jongno-gu. He died in February 2013, before the museum was ready, and it opened that September.

The house is an exhibit in itself. Built around 1937 for a daughter of Yun Deok-yeong, it is a leading example of the colonial-era culture house, a Korean–Western eclectic design, and it is designated a Seoul heritage building. Galleries keep the names of the rooms Park used, from reception room to studio and attic. Hours are 10:00 to 18:00 with last entry at 17:30; it closes on Mondays, January 1 and the days of Seollal and Chuseok. Adult admission is KRW 3,000, and no more than 15 visitors are allowed inside at once, so expect a short wait.

Nearby, Yi Sang's House (이상의 집) marks where the modernist poet and writer Yi Sang (1910–1937) lived from about age three for some twenty years, in his uncle's house. The large property was later split into small hanok, and in 2009 a heritage trust saved part of it through public donations. It now serves as a small memorial space, so check its hours before planning around it.

In Nuha-dong, look for the faded front of Daeoh Bookstore (대오서점), opened in 1951 by a couple, Jo Dae-sik and Kwon O-nam, who combined syllables of their names for the sign. Seoul city reporting says it stopped selling books in 2016 and has since operated as a café behind the original facade. Treat it as a streetscape to admire in passing rather than a shop to plan around.

en.heading: Suseongdong Valley, painted by Jeong Seon and rescued from apartments
paragraphs: Walk uphill from Tongin Market through Okin-dong and the houses give way to granite. Suseongdong Valley (수성동계곡) is a stream valley that the painter Jeong Seon (정선) painted in his true-view landscape style, with scholars and a boy crossing a stone bridge among mossy rocks. A viewing point at the valley entrance stands where Seoul believes he worked, so you can compare his composition with the real scene.

For decades the valley lay under an apartment complex, the Okin pilot apartments. As the blocks came down, Seoul designated the valley a city monument in 2010, covering the stone bridge and the surrounding ground, and the restored valley opened to the public on July 11, 2012, replanted with more than 18,000 trees and given a small pavilion and wooden footbridges. The single-slab bridge, identified with the one in Jeong's painting, is described as the longest one-stone bridge still in its original place within the old city walls.

The valley is at its best after rain, when water actually runs over the rocks; in dry winter weeks it can be little more than a stony gully. If you do not want the uphill walk, the Seoul City Wall office lists Jongno village bus 09 from Gyeongbokgung Station Exit 3 to the Okin Apartment stop, named for the vanished complex, near the foot of the valley.

en.heading: Two ways out: the Inwangsan ridge or Yun Dong-ju's hill
paragraphs: Inwangsan (339 meters) rises directly behind the valley, a rocky mountain known for formations such as Seonbawi, said to resemble a monk in meditation. Access was banned after a North Korean commando unit infiltrated Seoul on January 21, 1968, and the mountain reopened to the public only in 1993. The official Inwangsan section of the Seoul City Wall trail runs 4.0 kilometers from the site of Donuimun gate to Changuimun gate and takes about two and a half hours; from the Suseongdong side, the city wall office estimates about 30 minutes on foot toward the summit.

Our recommendation for a half day: climb from Suseongdong to the ridge, then follow the wall north and downhill to Changuimun and the Yun Dong-ju Literary Museum. The rock steps are steep and polished in places, and the city warns of extra care in winter, so wear proper shoes, carry water and allow two hours. If you are not a hiker, skip the climb and take the bus instead.

The Yun Dong-ju Literary Museum (윤동주문학관) honors the poet who boarded in nearby Nusang-dong, at the home of novelist Kim Song, while studying at Yonhi College, and who often climbed Inwangsan. It occupies a water pressure station decommissioned in 2008 and opened as a museum in 2012. One disused water tank had its roof opened to make the Open Well, a courtyard inspired by the well in his poem Self-Portrait; the other, left sealed, is the Closed Well, where a short film on his life plays in the dark.

The museum is open 10:00 to 18:00, with last entry at 17:30 and a daily cleaning break from 13:30 to 14:00; it closes on Mondays, January 1 and the days of Seollal and Chuseok, and admission is free. There are no toilets inside; use the Cheongun Park restrooms about 100 meters away. Without climbing, take bus 1020, 7022 or 7212 from Gyeongbokgung Station Exit 3 to the Jahamun Gogae stop. Behind the museum, steps lead to Poet's Hill and a stone carved with his poem Prologue, with views back over the city and Changuimun, the only auxiliary gate of the old wall whose gate tower survives.

en.heading: A half-day sequence, timed around the closures
paragraphs: This plan assumes a Tuesday-to-Sunday visit and avoids both the literary museum's cleaning break and the market's lunch peak. Allow about four and a half hours from start to finish, or two hours more if you take the Inwangsan ridge. Walking times between stops are short, mostly ten minutes or less, except the climb from the market to the valley.

en.heading: Getting the day right: Mondays, weather and pairings
paragraphs: Monday is the one day to avoid. Both the Park No-soo Art Museum and the Yun Dong-ju Literary Museum close, and Visit Seoul lists Monday as a closing day for the Tongin lunchbox café as well. On a Monday, see Seochon's lanes in the morning and spend the rest of the day elsewhere, or simply swap your Seochon and palace days. On a Tuesday, call the market first, since a 2025 city report gives Tuesday as the café's day off, and skip the third Sunday of the month, when both sources list the café as closed.

Weather changes the route more than in most Seoul neighborhoods. Light rain improves Suseongdong and does little harm to the market, but it makes Inwangsan's granite slippery; in that case take the bus to the museum. In summer, do the uphill parts before noon. In autumn, the ridge views over Gyeongbokgung and toward Namsan are at their clearest.

Seochon pairs naturally with Gyeongbokgung, whose west side it borders, so a palace morning followed by a Seochon lunch and afternoon is an easy, low-transit day. Readers drawn to Korean poetry should save energy for the Yun Dong-ju museum, which is small but carefully made. Allow time at the end simply to wander: Seochon rewards the person who turns down an unplanned alley.

faq.q: How does the Tongin Market coin lunchbox work?
faq.a: Buy yeopjeon coins at the dosirak café, each worth KRW 500, and pick up a tray. Walk the market and exchange coins for small portions at participating stalls, then eat in the café. Coin sales stop in mid-afternoon and the café has a weekly closing day, so check Visit Seoul or call before going.

faq.q: Is Seochon better than Bukchon?
faq.a: It is different rather than better. Bukchon has the famous rows of hanok rooftops and visiting-hour rules; Seochon has a market, small museums and an everyday residential feel with hanok scattered among newer houses. If you have time for only one and want the classic view, choose Bukchon. For food, literature and a quieter walk, choose Seochon.

faq.q: Do I need hiking gear for Inwangsan?
faq.a: Not technical gear, but proper walking shoes with grip, water and a layer for the wind on the ridge. The wall trail includes steep stone steps and exposed rock, and the city advises extra care in winter. If your footwear is not up to it, take the bus to the Yun Dong-ju Literary Museum instead.

faq.q: Can I visit the Yun Dong-ju Literary Museum without speaking Korean?
faq.a: Yes. The building itself, especially the Open Well and Closed Well spaces made from old water tanks, communicates without much text, and admission is free. Read one or two of his poems in translation beforehand, such as Prologue or Self-Portrait, and the visit will mean far more.

title.en: Namsangol Hanok Village and Namsan: Old Houses, City Wall, Tower Routes

summary.en: Free Namsangol Hanok Village read house by house, the 1994 time capsule and Gugakdang, plus the best way up to N Seoul Tower: on foot along the wall, by bus or cable car.

audience: Visitors staying around Myeong-dong or Chungmuro who want a hanok village they can actually walk into, a taste of Korean music, and a sensible way up Namsan.
method: Researched from the official sources listed below, checked on October 20, 2026. Hours, fees and booking rules can change; the linked official pages are the final word.
quickAnswer: Namsangol Hanok Village is a free open-air museum of five late-Joseon houses gathered here in 1998, four moved from around Seoul and one rebuilt as a replica, open Tuesday to Sunday from 9:00, about 300 meters from Chungmuro Station Exit 4. Give the houses an hour, then go up Namsan: walk the city wall if you have two hours and steady legs, ride bus 01B for the cheapest trip, or take the cable car from Myeong-dong for the view.

en.heading: Five houses from across Seoul on one hillside
paragraphs: Namsangol (남산골), the valley of Namsan, lies in Pil-dong on the mountain's northern foot. On April 18, 1998, Seoul opened Namsangol Hanok Village here, bringing together four late-Joseon houses designated as Seoul folk heritage, moved from scattered parts of the city and restored, and a faithful replica of a fifth house from Okin-dong. Behind them the city rebuilt a traditional garden on Namsan's original terrain, planted with native trees and laid out around a stream valley, a pond and a pavilion.

The result is the opposite of Bukchon. Nobody lives here, so you can step through the gates, cross the yards and look into rooms, kitchens and wooden halls without worrying about anyone's privacy. The trade-off is context: these houses have been lifted out of their original streets, so you see the buildings but not the neighborhoods that shaped them.

That makes Namsangol the better classroom and Bukchon the better street. If you want to understand how a hanok works, from the heated rooms to the open wooden hall and the separation of family quarters, an hour here will teach you more than a morning photographing Bukchon's lanes. It is also free, which helps.

en.heading: Reading rank in timber: the five houses compared
paragraphs: Each house is named for its original neighborhood and owner, and together they span a revealing range of late-Joseon society, from a master builder to the in-laws of the last emperor. Walk them in order of rank, starting with the carpenter, and the jump in scale, number of buildings and refinement of detail tells the story better than any label.

Start with Yi Seung-eop's house, built in the 1860s by the chief carpenter on the rebuilding of Gyeongbokgung; it rewards a close look, since its roofline is handled differently front and back. Kim Chun-yeong's house shows a household in between, combining commoner and yangban features. The Min family house is a different order of wealth, with separate inner quarters and detached buildings. The two Yun properties, linked to the family of Empress Sunjeonghyo, consort of the last Joseon ruler Sunjong, date from 1906 and the 1910s and show how elite households built as the dynasty came to an end.

Notice the jaesil in particular. It was not a family home but a building used for preparing ancestral rites, and its unusual plan sets it apart from the others. Inside the yards, look for the raised wooden maru, the heated ondol rooms behind sliding paper doors, and the kitchens set lower than the living rooms so their fires could heat the floors.

en.heading: Games, weddings and night tours: using the yards
paragraphs: Namsangol is set up for doing as well as looking. In the yards you will often find traditional games laid out for anyone to try, such as jegichagi, in which you keep a weighted shuttlecock aloft with your foot, and tuho, tossing arrows into a narrow-necked jar. Visit Seoul also lists traditional archery, performances and, on weekends, traditional wedding ceremonies, which you are welcome to watch from a respectful distance.

For depth, join a guided tour. The village runs 40- to 60-minute commentary tours from Tuesday to Sunday, in English at 14:00 and 15:30 on weekdays and at 10:30 and 12:00 on weekends. Individuals need no reservation and simply join at the guide office by the main gate; groups of 25 or more book by phone. Evening is a good choice in summer: the houses stay open until 21:00 from April to November, and the yards are cooler and calmer after dark.

Practical details: the houses are open Tuesday to Sunday, 9:00 to 21:00 from April to November and 9:00 to 20:00 from December to March, and close on Mondays unless the Monday is a public or substitute holiday; entry is free. The traditional garden and time capsule plaza stay open around the clock, so a Monday visit is still worthwhile if you only want the garden and a walk up the mountain. Search 남산골한옥마을 in Naver Map or Kakao Map; Chungmuro Station Exit 4 is about 300 meters away.

en.heading: A letter to 2394: the Seoul Millennium Time Capsule
paragraphs: Climb through the garden to its highest point and you reach a plaza with a bell-shaped marker. Beneath it, about 15 meters underground, lies the Seoul Millennium Time Capsule (서울천년타임캡슐), buried on November 29, 1994, to mark 600 years since Seoul became the capital of Joseon in 1394. Its shape echoes Bosingak, the bell pavilion whose bell once regulated the city's day.

The capsule holds about 600 objects chosen to show how Seoul residents lived in 1994. It is scheduled to be opened on November 29, 2394, the city's 1,000th anniversary as capital. The idea is more poignant than it first appears: a city that demolished so much of its own past in a few decades of rapid growth decided to set aside an ordinary year for people four centuries ahead.

There is nothing to open or enter, so ten minutes is enough. Go for the idea and for the view back down over the hanok roofs, which is one of the best angles in the village: tiled roofs in the foreground, the office towers of central Seoul behind them, and the northern mountains on a clear day, six centuries of the capital in a single frame.

en.heading: Seoul Namsan Gugakdang: Korean music below ground
paragraphs: Just inside the village sits Seoul Namsan Gugakdang (서울남산국악당), a venue for gugak, traditional Korean music, and performing arts that opened in 2007. The roughly 300-seat hall lies underground, so it does not compete with the hanok roofs above, and a sunken garden called Chimsangwon brings daylight down into the building. Even if you do not attend a show, the descent into that courtyard is worth a look.

Programs change through the year, and Seoul's own reporting mentions festivals and building tours alongside concerts. Music needs little translation, which makes a gugak performance one of the easier cultural evenings for visitors who do not speak Korean. The building is open Tuesday to Sunday, 9:00 to 21:00, and closes on Mondays. For the current schedule and tickets, see the venue's official site, sgtt.kr, which has an English option, and see our guide to traditional performances in Seoul for how gugak compares with other stages in the city.

Our suggestion for a first visit is to pair a performance with the village rather than making a separate trip. From April to November the houses stay open until 21:00, so you can walk the yards in the early evening, go down into the hall for the show and still reach Myeong-dong for a late dinner. Book ahead for weekend dates, and arrive early enough to see the sunken garden before the doors close.

en.heading: Up Namsan three ways: on foot, by bus or by cable car
paragraphs: N Seoul Tower sits near the summit of Namsan, and private cars have been barred from the summit road since 2005, so you will arrive on foot, by local bus or by cable car. Each suits a different visitor, and the right choice depends less on money than on the time of day, the state of your knees and whether you want to experience the mountain or simply reach the top.

The Namsan circulation buses are the bargain. Route 01B runs every 14 minutes from 06:30 to 23:00 via Chungmuro Station Exit 2, Dongguk University Station and the National Theater to N Seoul Tower, and also stops at the cable car's lower station. Route 01A loops through the city center, including Gwanghwamun, Anguk and Namdaemun Market. Both cost KRW 1,500 and accept transit cards only, with no cash.

The Namsan Cable Car operates daily from 10:00 to 23:00, with last tickets sold 30 minutes before closing, and it can stop running in bad weather. From Myeong-dong Station Exit 3 it is a 10- to 15-minute uphill walk along the road beside the Pacific Hotel, or ride the free Namsan Oreumi incline elevator from the entrance of Namsan Tunnel No. 3, about two minutes to the boarding area. Adult fares are KRW 15,000 round trip and 12,000 one way. A city-built gondola from near Myeong-dong has been blocked in court, most recently by an appeal ruling on September 17, 2026, so do not plan around it.

Our pick: walk up in daylight, when the wall and the views keep you company, and ride down by cable car or bus after dark. The tower's observatory costs KRW 29,000 for adults and is open 10:00 to 22:30 on weekdays and to 23:00 on weekends and holidays; the summit terraces, beacon mound and wall views are free.
checklist: Walk: free; from Namsangol (Chungmuro Exit 4), Jangchung (Dongguk University Station Exit 5 or 6) or Baekbeom Square (Hoehyeon Station Exit 4); 40 minutes to over an hour, steep in places.
Bus 01B or 01A: KRW 1,500 by transit card; 06:30–23:00; easiest for limited mobility.
Cable car: KRW 15,000 adult round trip; 10:00–23:00; long weekend and sunset queues.

en.heading: The city wall over Mongmyeoksan, and the beacon at the top
paragraphs: Namsan's Joseon name was Mongmyeoksan (목멱산), and the Seoul City Wall, Hanyangdoseong (한양도성), ran along its ridge as part of the loop of walls and gates that enclosed the capital. The official Namsan section runs 6.7 kilometers from Jangchung Gymnasium to Baekbeom Square, takes about three hours and is rated three stars out of five for difficulty. In the 1920s colonial authorities tore down much of the wall here to build the Joseon Shinto Shrine; restoration began in the 1970s, and a mid-1990s recovery project returned most sections to their earlier form. Wall foundations unearthed in good condition at Hoehyeon in 2013 show how much still lay buried.

For the best wall walking, start on the east at Jangchung and climb with the masonry beside you to the summit, then descend west toward Baekbeom Square and Myeong-dong. At the top, look for Palgakjeong, an octagonal pavilion on the site of Guksadang, a state shrine the Japanese moved to Inwangsan in 1925, and a stone marking the geographical center of Seoul.

The summit's most meaningful structure is the smallest. The Mongmyeoksan beacon mound was the end of the line for Joseon's signal network: messages relayed hill to hill from the border regions, as smoke by day and fire by night, all ended here in the capital. Built in 1423 and used until 1895, the beacons were restored in 1993. Stand beside them and look out at the ring of mountains, and the logic of a capital defended by fire signals becomes immediately clear.

en.heading: An afternoon that ends in Myeong-dong
paragraphs: Namsangol, Namsan and Myeong-dong fit into one afternoon with no transit beyond the first subway ride. Arrive at Chungmuro Station Exit 4 around 14:00 and spend an hour in the five houses, trying the yard games if you like. At about 15:15 climb through the garden to the time capsule plaza, then head uphill on Namsan's footpaths (the city wall office lists Namsangol as one of the trail's access points); allow an hour or a little more at an easy pace.

Aim to reach the summit around 16:30 to see the beacon mound and Palgakjeong in daylight, then stay for sunset over the city; decide on the observatory only if the sky is clear. Check the day's sunset time before you set out and plan to be at the top about 45 minutes ahead of it, because the light over the Han River fades quickly once the sun drops behind the western hills. After dark, ride the cable car down, or catch bus 01B, and walk from the lower cable car station toward Myeong-dong Station Exit 3 for dinner and the evening street-food stalls.

On a Monday the houses are closed, but the garden, capsule plaza and mountain are not, so start at the garden instead. If you prefer mornings, reverse the plan: take bus 01B up from Chungmuro Exit 2, walk down past the beacon mound and along the wall, and finish at Namsangol after its 9:00 opening, before Myeong-dong's shops are fully awake.

faq.q: Is Namsangol Hanok Village really free?
faq.a: Yes. Entry to the houses and the traditional garden is free, according to Seoul's culture portal and Visit Seoul. Performances at the neighboring Seoul Namsan Gugakdang and some hands-on programs may be ticketed or need advance booking, so check before you go if you have a specific activity in mind.

faq.q: Is Namsangol open on Mondays?
faq.a: The houses close every Monday. The traditional garden and the time capsule plaza are open 24 hours, and Namsan's trails are always open, so a Monday visit can still include the garden and a walk up the mountain. The village's own site says the houses open as usual when a Monday is a public or substitute holiday.

faq.q: Which is better for seeing hanok, Namsangol or Bukchon?
faq.a: For understanding hanok, Namsangol: you can walk into yards and see rooms, kitchens and halls at five houses of different social ranks. For the experience of a living hanok neighborhood and its famous rooftop views, Bukchon. Many visitors do both on different days, starting with Namsangol so that Bukchon's lanes make more sense.

faq.q: How long does it take to walk up Namsan to N Seoul Tower?
faq.a: From the Myeong-dong or Namsangol side, allow roughly 40 minutes to an hour at a steady pace, mostly on stairs and paved paths. The full official city-wall section from Jangchung Gymnasium to Baekbeom Square is 6.7 kilometers and takes about three hours. The bus is the alternative if stairs are difficult.

faq.q: Can I see the time capsule contents?
faq.a: No. The capsule is sealed about 15 meters underground and scheduled to be opened on November 29, 2394. What you can see is the plaza and bell-shaped marker at the top of the garden, which is open around the clock and offers one of the best views over the village rooftops.

title.en: Seoul Subway and T-money Guide: Fares, Passes, Transfers and Exits

summary.en: How to pay for Seoul's subway and buses: T-money vs Climate Card passes, current fares, free transfers, exit numbers and a worked palace-to-palace trip.

audience: First-time independent visitors who will ride Seoul's subway and city buses to palaces, museums and old neighborhoods.
method: Researched from the official sources listed below, checked on October 20, 2026. Fares, pass rules and payment options can change; the linked official pages are the final word.
quickAnswer: Buy a T-money card (about 3,000 won) at a convenience store or station machine, load it with cash, and tap it at every subway gate and on every bus, both boarding and leaving. The adult card fare is 1,550 won on the subway and 1,500 won on regular city buses, with free transfers inside a 30-minute window. If you will make two or more separate journeys a day for five days or longer, a Climate Card short-term pass usually costs less.

keyFacts.value: 1,650 won plus a 500 won refundable deposit

keyFacts.value: 30 minutes (60 minutes from 9 p.m. to 7 a.m.), up to 4 transfers

en.heading: Why a transit card beats a single-journey ticket
paragraphs: Seoul's subway lines, the Korail commuter lines that run through the city and its city buses share one distance-based fare system. Pay with a transit card and an adult subway ride costs 1,550 won for the first 10 km, plus 100 won for each further 5 km up to 50 km. A single-journey ticket, a contactless card you tap like T-money, costs 100 won more, and the machine also takes a 500 won deposit that you only recover by feeding the ticket into a refund machine at your destination. The bigger difference is that only cards earn transfer discounts, so a bus-plus-subway trip is priced as one journey instead of two.

The card nearly everyone uses is T-money (티머니). It is a plain stored-value card: you load won onto it, tap it on the reader at the gate or beside the bus door, and the fare comes off the balance. Convenience stores such as GS25, CU, 7-Eleven and emart24 sell it, as do the vending machines in subway stations, for around 3,000 won before any balance; designer versions cost more. At a store counter, ask for a T-money card and name the amount you want loaded, and the clerk handles the rest.

Every traveler needs a card of their own, because the subway gate reads one card per passenger and a couple cannot share. Children and teenagers ride for less, but Visit Korea notes that travelers under 18 must have their date of birth registered to the card at a convenience store for the reduced fare to apply. One small bonus for early risers: tapping in before 6:30 a.m. takes 20 percent off the base fare, handy if you want a palace gate or a mountain trailhead before the crowds.

en.heading: Topping up: keep some cash for this one job
paragraphs: Plan on cash for ordinary T-money top-ups. Since March 17, 2026, 440 newer ticket machines in 273 stations on Lines 1 to 8 accept foreign-issued credit and debit cards and several mobile payment apps, but Seoul limits that to buying single-journey tickets and buying or charging Climate Card short-term passes, with an average service fee of 3.7 percent. Topping up a regular T-money card is not on that list, and Tmoney's own visitor guide warns that some machines take cash only. Convenience store counters also charge cards; do not assume a store that takes your foreign card for snacks will accept it for a top-up.

The machine sequence is short. Choose English on the screen, pick the transit card top-up option, set the card on the reader pad, insert notes, and wait for the new balance before lifting the card. Tmoney suggests loading roughly 30,000 to 40,000 won for a three-night, four-day stay, which is a sensible ceiling. Leftover balances can be refunded at convenience stores, minus a small fee, but the card price is not refundable, and Visit Korea says balances above 50,000 won can only be refunded at Tmoney Town near Exit 10 of Seoul Station.

If you would rather not handle cash at all, WOWPASS is the main alternative. It is a prepaid card with a transit function, issued for 5,000 won through its app or at its own kiosks in airports, stations and hotels, and it requires a passport. You recharge it in won or several foreign currencies at those kiosks, and leftover balance comes back as won cash from a kiosk. The trade-off is dependence on finding one of its machines, whereas T-money can be topped up at almost any convenience store in the country.

en.heading: Climate Card short-term passes: when unlimited rides pay off
paragraphs: Seoul's Climate Card (기후동행카드, Gihu Donghaeng Kadeu) is the city's unlimited-ride pass. The versions that suit visitors are short-term passes of one, two, three, five or seven days, priced at 5,000, 8,000, 10,000, 15,000 and 20,000 won and loaded onto a physical card that costs 3,000 won. A pass covers subway rides within Seoul and Seoul-licensed city, village, night and circular buses. It does not cover the Shinbundang Line, GTX, subway sections outside Seoul, red express buses, airport buses or buses licensed by neighboring cities.

Two rules decide whether it suits you. First, validity runs by calendar day: a pass starts on the day you charge it, from the first train, and ends with the last train of its final day, so a one-day pass charged at 1 p.m. is finished that night, and passes cannot be charged in advance. Second, a subway trip must begin and end inside the coverage area; ride out of Seoul and station staff charge the fare for the whole trip. One useful exception: you may board inside the zone and get off at Incheon Airport Terminal 1 or 2, though a trip cannot start there.

Now the arithmetic. On T-money, a transfer inside the time window costs nothing extra, so count journeys rather than rides. A three-day pass works out to about 3,333 won a day and beats card fares once you make three separate journeys daily. The five- and seven-day passes, at 3,000 and about 2,857 won a day, win at two journeys. The one-day pass needs four. Add the 3,000 won card and the verdict is clear: buy a five- or seven-day pass for a week of sightseeing, and stay on T-money for shorter stays. Refunds require a Korean bank account or a trip to Tmoney's headquarters, so treat the pass as spent.

Buy the pass at the newer vending machines in Line 1 to 8 stations, which accept foreign cards, or at the Myeongdong and Seoul Tourism Plaza tourist information centers, Line 1 to 8 customer service offices (cash only) and convenience stores near stations. Tmoney says the tourist pass is not sold at the airport, so your first ride into the city goes on T-money or a single ticket. Like T-money, a Climate Card is one card per person.

en.heading: Your contactless bank card is not a ticket yet
paragraphs: Visitors used to tapping a Visa or Mastercard at a London or Singapore gate often try the same here. As of October 2026 it still does not work in Seoul. The city is moving toward EMV open-loop payments in stages through 2030, and in September 2026 Tmoney signed agreements with Visa, Mastercard, UnionPay, JCB and Hana Card, naming Seoul city buses as the first target for next year. The agreement set no date for the subway. Until a launch is announced, keep your bank card out of the same sleeve as your T-money card so the reader does not get confused.

You will see Seoul residents tapping what look like ordinary bank cards. Those are Korean-issued credit cards with a built-in transit function, billed monthly, which the subway operator accepts alongside prepaid cards. Foreign cards do not have that function yet. The one place a foreign card helps today is the newer station machine, where it buys a single-journey ticket or a Climate Card pass without cash, at the cost of the service fee.

en.heading: Transfers: the 30-minute window and the tap people forget
paragraphs: Changing lines inside the subway is free as long as you stay behind the gates. Between subway and bus, or bus and bus, you get the transfer discount when you board the next vehicle within 30 minutes of tapping off the last one; from 9 p.m. to 7 a.m. the window stretches to 60 minutes. You can transfer up to four times, five rides in all, but reboarding the same bus route does not count. The combined trip is charged at the highest base fare among the modes you used plus distance charges beyond 10 km, and cash payers get no transfer discount at all.

On a bus you board at the front door and tap, then tap again on the reader by the middle or rear door before you step off. Tmoney calls forgetting that second tap the most common mistake foreign riders make: you lose the transfer discount and may be charged extra on your next ride. Bus colors tell you the type of route. Blue trunk buses run long distances on main roads, green branch buses connect neighborhoods to stations, yellow circular buses loop the center, and red express buses run to the suburbs for 3,000 won. Small green village buses (마을버스, maeul beoseu) cost 1,200 won.

For short hops between central sights, a bus that stops near a palace gate can beat a subway trip that involves long corridors, stairs and an exit climb, and you see the city on the way. For anything crossing the Han River or running more than a few kilometers through traffic, the subway's predictability wins, especially at rush hour. Your map app will compare both; when the times are close, take whichever leaves you nearer the entrance you actually want.

en.heading: Exit numbers are the addresses that matter
paragraphs: Koreans give directions as a station plus an exit number, and you should too. Every exit is numbered, signs inside the station point to them, and choosing the right one can spare you a long detour around a wide boulevard. The palace offices publish exits in their own directions: Gyeongbokgung Station (Line 3) Exit 5 for Gyeongbokgung, two minutes on foot; Anguk Station (Line 3) Exit 3 for Changdeokgung, five minutes; City Hall Station (Lines 1 and 2) Exit 2 for Deoksugung, two minutes; Jongno 3-ga Station Exit 11 or 8 for Jongmyo, five minutes; and Hyehwa Station (Line 4) Exit 4 for Changgyeonggung, about 12 minutes.

Decide on your exit before you tap out. Large interchange stations have a dozen or more exits spread across several blocks, and surfacing on the wrong side can mean an underpass or a long wait at a crossing. The neighborhood maps posted near the gates show which landmarks sit above each exit. When you arrange to meet someone, 'Anguk Station, Exit 3' is a complete, unambiguous address in Seoul; 'Anguk Station' on its own is the start of a phone call.

en.heading: Worked example: Changdeokgung to Deoksugung by subway
paragraphs: Suppose you leave Changdeokgung through its main gate, Donhwamun, at 11:40. You have two subway options. The obvious one is Anguk Station Exit 3, five minutes away, but from there you would ride Line 3 one stop and then change to Line 1 at Jongno 3-ga, adding a transfer to a short journey. The better move is to walk about ten minutes to Jongno 3-ga Station Exit 7, which the palace office lists as its second entrance option, and board Line 1 directly.

Inside Jongno 3-ga, tap in and follow the Line 1 signs to the platform for trains toward Seoul Station (서울역, Seoul-yeok). Ride two stops, past Jonggak, to City Hall (시청, Sicheong). The trip is well under 10 km, so the card fare is the 1,550 won base. Tap out, follow the signs for Exit 2, and Daehanmun, Deoksugung's main gate, is a two-minute walk away. Allow roughly 25 minutes door to door, which leaves room for lunch near City Hall before you go in.

Two checks make this pairing work. Both palaces close on Mondays, so plan it for Tuesday to Sunday. And order matters: Changdeokgung closes between 5:30 and 6:30 p.m. depending on the season, with last entry an hour earlier, while Deoksugung's grounds stay open until 9 p.m. with last entry at 8 p.m. Doing Changdeokgung first means a long lunch or a slow afternoon costs you nothing, and Deoksugung's stone buildings look their best once the lights come on.

en.heading: Last trains, Owl buses and small courtesies
paragraphs: The subway does not run all night. Last trains leave around midnight, and the exact time varies by line, direction and day of the week, so check the last departure from your station in your map app before an evening performance. After that, Seoul runs 14 overnight Owl bus routes, numbered with an N, from about 11 p.m. to 6 a.m., at 2,500 won by card. Seoul-licensed night buses are covered by the Climate Card, which makes a late return free if you hold a pass.

Etiquette on Seoul transit is mostly about space and noise. Let passengers off before you board and step clear of the doors. Seats at the ends of each car are set aside for older, disabled and pregnant riders, and many passengers leave them empty even when the car is full. Keep calls brief and quiet, take a large backpack off in a packed car, and hold on as soon as you board a bus, because drivers often pull away before everyone is seated.

faq.q: Can two people share one T-money card on the subway?
faq.a: No. The subway gate reads one card per passenger, so each traveler needs a card. Children and teenagers should have their date of birth registered to their card at a convenience store, otherwise the reduced youth and child fares will not apply.

faq.q: Can I tap my own Visa or Mastercard at the gate instead?
faq.a: Not yet. As of October 2026, foreign contactless cards cannot be used at Seoul subway gates or on buses. Tmoney and the card networks plan to start with Seoul city buses in 2027, with no subway date announced. A foreign card can buy single tickets or Climate Card passes at the newer station machines, with a fee of about 3.7 percent.

faq.q: Is a Climate Card pass worth it for a three-day trip?
faq.a: Only if you make at least three separate journeys every day. The three-day pass costs 10,000 won plus a 3,000 won card, while three days of two daily journeys on T-money cost 9,300 won. Five- and seven-day passes are the better value, paying off at two journeys a day.

faq.q: What happens if I forget to tap off when leaving a bus?
faq.a: You lose the transfer discount for your next ride, and Tmoney warns you may be charged extra on that next trip. Tap the reader by the middle or rear door every time, even if you are not planning to transfer.

faq.q: Can I ride to Incheon Airport on a Climate Card pass?
faq.a: Yes, by rail, if you board at a station inside the pass's Seoul coverage area: getting off at Incheon Airport Terminal 1 or 2 is allowed. You cannot start a trip at the airport on the pass, and airport buses are excluded.

title.en: Naver Map and Kakao Map in Korea: Navigating in English and Hangul

summary.en: Why Google Maps still can't guide you on foot in Korea, how to use Naver Map or Kakao Map in English, and the Hangul search terms that find palaces fast.

audience: Independent visitors who rely on their phone to find palaces, museums, stations and bus stops in Seoul and want to stop getting lost at the last few hundred meters.
method: Researched from the official sources listed below, checked on October 20, 2026. App features and Google's Korea rollout can change; the linked official pages are the final word.
quickAnswer: Install Naver Map (네이버 지도), set it to English, and search in Hangul whenever an English name fails. Google Maps in Korea still offers places and public-transit routes but no turn-by-turn walking or driving directions, even after Korea conditionally approved Google's map-data request in February 2026.

keyFacts.value: Korean, English, Chinese, Japanese

keyFacts.value: The Hangul name, e.g. 경복궁 (Gyeongbokgung)

keyFacts.label: To find the station

keyFacts.label: Seoul bus colors
keyFacts.value: Blue trunk, green branch/village, yellow circular, red express

en.heading: What Google Maps can and cannot do in Korea
paragraphs: Google Maps works in Korea as a directory: it shows places, reviews and public-transit routes. What it has never offered here is turn-by-turn walking or driving navigation, and the walking legs of its transit routes appear only as dotted lines. The reason is legal rather than technical. Korea restricts the export of its government survey map data on security grounds, and Google's requests to move 1:5,000-scale map data to its overseas servers were refused in 2007 and 2016.

That changed on paper on February 27, 2026, when an interagency review body approved Google's request with conditions: military and other sensitive sites blurred in imagery, coordinates for Korean territory restricted, raw data processed on domestic servers run by a local partner, and a dedicated map officer stationed in Korea. In August 2026 Google told The Korea Herald it plans full navigation in Korea, but it gave no launch date. Until walking directions actually appear in the app, plan your trip as if they will not.

Keep Google Maps for what it does well, such as browsing reviews in English and opening the saved lists you built at home. Do the on-the-ground navigation in a Korean app. Naver and Kakao route you along real footpaths, crossings and underpasses, they know the bus network stop by stop, and they tell you which subway exit to use. That last detail matters in a city where the straight line on a map often crosses an eight-lane boulevard with no crossing in sight.

en.heading: Naver Map or Kakao Map: pick a main app
paragraphs: Both apps are free, Koreans split their loyalty between them, and either will get you there. For a first visit, make Naver Map (네이버 지도, Neibeo Jido) your main app. Naver says it supports Korean, English, Chinese and Japanese, following either your phone's language or a setting inside the app. It machine-translates business names, addresses, categories and opening hours, and since October 2024 it also translates written reviews through its Papago translator. The translations are rough in places, but they let you judge a restaurant without copying text into another app.

Setting the language takes one step. If your phone already runs in English, Naver Map follows it; if not, change the language in the app's own settings, which leaves your phone's system language alone. Much of the interface and place information then appears in English, while smaller businesses may still show Korean. Keep that split in mind: the menus speak English, but the data underneath is a Korean database, which is exactly why the Hangul name remains your most reliable search key.

Naver's transit guidance is the other reason to choose it. Since December 2023 it has followed you along a route with boarding and get-off alerts, a count of stops remaining, the train door closest to your transfer and the station exit number you need. On iPhones, where location tracking underground is limited, you select the train you boarded and the alerts follow that train. In practice this means you can ride with the phone in your pocket and still know when to stand up.

Kakao Map (카카오맵, Kakaomaep) is the strong second choice. Its App Store listing names English as a supported language alongside Korean, and its route search covers the same subway and bus network. Expect more untranslated Korean on its place pages than on Naver's. Install both before you fly: when one app's route looks odd, a second opinion takes ten seconds, and a backup app also covers you if one of them misbehaves on your phone.

en.heading: Type the Hangul name and the right place comes up
paragraphs: English searches work for the biggest landmarks and break down quickly for anything smaller. Korean place databases are written in Hangul, while English names come in competing forms: an official translation (Gyeongbok Palace), the Revised Romanization of the Korean name (Gyeongbokgung) and older spellings that survive on signs and in guidebooks (Kyungbok, Kyongbok). Korea's current romanization rules, published by the National Institute of Korean Language, spell words as they are pronounced, which is why 국립 (national) becomes gungnip rather than guklip. A Hangul search sidesteps all of that; 경복궁 can only mean one thing.

Learn a handful of endings and you can read a result even when you cannot read the rest: 궁 (gung) is a palace, 사 (sa) a temple, 역 (yeok) a station, 시장 (sijang) a market, 박물관 (bangmulgwan) a museum and 마을 (maeul) a village. You do not need a Korean keyboard. Copy the Hangul from the table below, or from a venue's official website, and paste it into the search bar. If you plan to use Korean often, adding the Korean keyboard in your phone's settings takes a minute and costs nothing.

Address 율곡로 99; nearest exit Anguk Station Exit 3
Address 세종대로 99; City Hall Station Exit 2
Address 종로 157; Jongno 3-ga Station Exit 11 or 8

en.heading: Stations, gates and look-alike results
paragraphs: Add 역 (yeok) when you want the station rather than the sight: 경복궁역 (Gyeongbokgung-yeok) returns the Line 3 station, while 경복궁 returns the palace. For large sites, think about which gate you will use, because a palace like Gyeongbokgung covers so much ground that the default pin can sit far from your entrance; zoom in and set the destination on the gate itself. Chain restaurants and cafés produce dozens of identical names, so add the neighborhood, such as 인사동 (Insa-dong), after the business name, and read the district shown under each result before you tap Directions.

One more habit saves real time: check the result category before you navigate. A search for a palace can also return a parking lot, a ticket office, a nearby café that borrowed the name, or the station. The category label sits just under the name in both apps, and Naver shows it in English. Ten seconds of reading here prevents the classic mistake of walking confidently to a car park on the wrong side of the walls.

en.heading: Copy the road-name address, not the English
paragraphs: Korean addresses run from large to small: city, district, road name, building number. Gyeongbokgung's official address is 서울 종로구 사직로 161, which reads as Seoul, Jongno-gu, Sajik-ro, number 161. Changdeokgung is 율곡로 99 (Yulgok-ro 99) in the same district, and Deoksugung is 세종대로 99 (Sejong-daero 99) in Jung-gu. Place pages show this road-name address (도로명, doromyeong) and often the older lot-number address (지번, jibeon) as well. Use the road-name version, which is what drivers and delivery riders expect.

Address words carry meaning once you know the suffixes. 구 (gu) is a district, such as Jongno-gu; 동 (dong) is a neighborhood, as in Insa-dong; 로 (ro) is a major road and 길 (gil) a smaller street, often numbered off a main road, as in Toegye-ro 34-gil, the lane that leads to Namsangol Hanok Village. 가 (ga) marks a numbered section of a long street, which is why the station called Jongno 3-ga sits on the third section of Jongno. Reading these lets you sanity-check a result: a palace pin in the wrong district is the wrong pin.

Copying the Hangul address is the most useful thing you can do before a taxi ride. Drivers type the destination into their navigation, and Hangul goes in cleanly where a romanized address invites typos and guesswork. Keep the addresses of your accommodation and of each day's first stop in a notes app, in Hangul, so you can show them even when the map app is slow to load or your battery is low.

en.heading: Reading a transit result: exits, doors and bus colors
paragraphs: A transit result reads top to bottom like a script. It tells you which station and exit to walk to, which line to board and in which direction, how many stops to ride, where to change and which exit to leave by. Directions on the platform are shown by station names rather than compass points, so note the name of the next stop or the end of the line before you go down. Naver adds the door position for the quickest transfer, which is worth following at large interchange stations.

Bus legs show a route number and a color. In Seoul, blue marks trunk routes, green marks branch and small village routes, yellow marks downtown circular routes and red marks express routes to the suburbs, and late-night routes carry an N before the number. Tap the bus leg to see the arrival estimate and the full list of stops. Then check the name of the next stop, because stops for opposite directions usually face each other across the road under the same name.

Walking legs deserve a glance too. Seoul's main roads are wide, and pedestrian crossings on them can be far apart, so a walking leg that looks short on the map may include a detour to a crossing or a dip through an underground passage. If the walking time seems long for the distance, that is usually why. Following the app's line rather than the route your eyes suggest normally gets you there sooner and keeps you off the median.

A quick test before you rely on any result: compare the app's final step with the venue's own directions. Changdeokgung's palace office lists Anguk Station (Line 3) Exit 3 and a five-minute walk. Search 창덕궁, tap Directions, choose public transport and look at the last line of each option. If a route ends at Anguk Station Exit 3, it matches the official guidance, and you can tap Start and let the get-off alert do the rest.

en.heading: Saving places so the day plan travels with you
paragraphs: Searching and getting directions work without signing in, but saving places requires an account with Naver or Kakao. If you build lists, do it at home on Wi-Fi: save your accommodation, each palace or museum, and a couple of fallback restaurants near each, so the map shows the whole day at a glance. A shared list link is also the easiest way to coordinate with companions, and it survives a dead phone if someone else in the group has it open.

Do not let the list replace the official page. Map apps show opening hours, but palace and museum hours shift with the season, and holiday openings and closures are announced as notices on official websites, sometimes only days ahead. Use the app to get there and the venue's own site to confirm that it is open, then save that official page next to the place in your list.

en.heading: When the signal or the battery gives out
paragraphs: Treat both apps as online tools. Route search, live bus times and translation need data, so arrange an eSIM, a local SIM or pocket Wi-Fi before you land, and carry a battery pack on long days. As insurance, screenshot the day's key route cards and the Hangul addresses. That is enough to finish a journey, ask a passer-by for help or show a taxi driver where you are going, even with no connection at all.

If you are truly stuck, the 1330 Korea Travel Hotline runs around the clock; from a foreign phone, dial +82-2-1330. It provides tourist information and interpretation, and Visit Korea also offers it as a free online call over Wi-Fi and through chat on KakaoTalk, LINE and WhatsApp. Reading out the nearest station name and exit number is the fastest way to describe where you are, which is one more reason to notice exit numbers as you walk.

faq.q: Will Google Maps have walking directions in Korea by 2027?
faq.a: Possibly, but nothing is confirmed. Korea approved Google's map-data export with conditions in February 2026, and in August 2026 Google said it plans full navigation in Korea without naming a date. Check the app before you travel, and install Naver Map regardless.

faq.q: Can I search Naver Map in English at all?
faq.a: Yes. Major sights usually appear under their English names, and Naver translates business names, addresses, categories and hours into English. Small restaurants, shops and alleys are where English searches fail, so switch to the Hangul name when the result list looks wrong.

faq.q: How do I type Hangul if I don't have a Korean keyboard?
faq.a: Copy and paste. Take the Hangul from this guide, a venue's official site or a message, and paste it into the search bar. If you expect to search often, add the Korean keyboard in your phone's language settings; it is free and takes about a minute.

faq.q: The app says to board toward a station I've never heard of. Is that wrong?
faq.a: No. Platforms are labeled by station names, usually the next station or the end of the line, not by north or south. Match the name in the app to the sign on the platform, and check the line color before you board.

faq.q: Which app should I use for buses?
faq.a: Either works in Seoul. Both show route numbers, stop lists and arrival estimates. Whichever you use, confirm the name of the next stop so you board on the correct side of the road.

title.en: Seollal and Chuseok in Korea: Holiday Travel Guide With 2027 Dates

summary.en: What Seollal and Chuseok mean, what closes and which palaces open free, the official 2027 holiday dates, and how to spend a Korean holiday well in Seoul.

audience: Visitors whose Seoul trip overlaps Seollal, Chuseok or another Korean public holiday and who want to know what that means for sights, food and transport.
method: Researched from the official sources listed below, checked on October 20, 2026. Holiday openings, fees and events are announced shortly before each holiday; the linked official pages are the final word.
quickAnswer: Seollal (Lunar New Year) falls on Sunday, February 7, 2027, with the public holiday running February 6 to 9; Chuseok falls on Wednesday, September 15, 2027, with the holiday September 14 to 16. Seoul empties rather than fills: intercity transport is packed, the royal palaces opened free over both 2026 holidays, and many family-run restaurants close, so book transport early and plan your meals.

keyFacts.value: Wed Sep 15; holiday Tue Sep 14 to Thu Sep 16

keyFacts.label: Korean names

keyFacts.value: Free in both 2026 holidays; Secret Garden excluded

en.heading: Why the dates move every year
paragraphs: Seollal (설날) and Chuseok (추석, also called 한가위, Hangawi) are fixed to the lunar calendar, so their solar dates shift from year to year. Seollal is the first day of the first lunar month; Chuseok is the fifteenth day of the eighth, the harvest full moon. Each is a three-day public holiday covering the day before, the day itself and the day after. When one of those days lands on a Sunday or on another holiday, the government adds a substitute holiday (대체공휴일, daechegonghyuil) on the next working day, which is why the 2027 Seollal break runs four days.

Both holidays exist to bring families together, and that is what shapes a visitor's experience. Huge numbers of people leave the capital for their parents' or grandparents' hometowns, so Seoul becomes noticeably quieter while highways, trains and terminals strain. For a traveler the result is an unusual mix: calmer palaces and subways, hard-to-find intercity seats, and many family-run kitchens shut for the day. Plan for all three and the holiday becomes one of the more interesting times to be in the city.

en.heading: Inside the family day: charye, sebae and the foods that mark it
paragraphs: The holiday morning traditionally begins with charye (차례), a rite in which the family lays out food for its ancestors and bows before the table. It grows out of Confucian ancestor worship, which treated serving the dead as a central duty of descendants. Many families also make seongmyo (성묘), a visit to the ancestral graves; for Seollal 2026, Seoul added extra trips on the bus routes serving Manguri Cemetery in Jungnang-gu. The National Folk Museum notes that these rites are changing as beliefs diversify, while the core idea of honoring ancestors and wishing descendants well has held.

Seollal adds sebae (세배), the deep New Year's bow that children and younger relatives make to their elders, with the greeting 새해 복 많이 받으세요 (saehae bok mani badeuseyo), 'receive many New Year blessings.' Elders answer with good wishes and sebaetdon (세뱃돈), New Year's money, often in crisp new notes. The dish of the day is tteokguk (떡국), a clear soup of sliced rice cake; eating a bowl is said to add a year to your age. Families then gather for yutnori (윷놀이), a board game decided by throwing four wooden sticks.

Chuseok is the harvest counterpart. Its signature food is songpyeon (송편), small half-moon rice cakes steamed over pine needles, and its traditional entertainments include ssireum (씨름) wrestling and ganggangsullae (강강술래), a circle dance under the full moon. If you are invited into a Korean home over either holiday, bring a modest gift such as fruit, accept the food you are offered, and ask before photographing the ancestral table. It is a family rite, not a display, and asking first is the respectful default.

en.heading: The official 2027 holiday calendar
paragraphs: The Korea AeroSpace Administration (우주항공청, KASA), which publishes the country's official calendar almanac each year, released the 2027 edition on June 29, 2026. It places Seollal on Sunday, February 7, with the holiday from Saturday, February 6 to Tuesday, February 9, the last day being a substitute. Chuseok falls on Wednesday, September 15, with the holiday from September 14 to 16. The almanac also reflects a 2026 change: Labor Day (May 1) and Constitution Day (July 17) became public holidays in April 2026, and because both fall on Saturdays in 2027, each gets a Monday substitute.

For travelers the important pattern is the run of long weekends. The almanac counts ten breaks of three days or more in 2027, six of them Saturday-to-Monday weekends created by substitute holidays. Each one fills domestic trains and popular day-trip destinations, and Seoul's palaces see more local families than usual. None disrupts the city the way Seollal and Chuseok do, but if you plan a trip out of Seoul, check the table before you pick your travel days.
