en.heading: Palaces stay open, and lately they have been free
paragraphs: The royal palaces do not close for the holidays. In 2026 the Korea Heritage Service's palace offices opened them free of charge over both breaks: Gyeongbokgung, the Chilgung shrine, Changdeokgung and Changgyeonggung from February 14 to 18 for Seollal, and those four plus Deoksugung and Jongmyo from September 24 to 27 for Chuseok. Each free window covered the holiday plus the weekend days running into it. Hours followed the season, so Gyeongbokgung closed at 5 p.m., with last entry at 4 p.m., in February and at 6 p.m. in September.

Free does not mean everything runs as usual. Gyeongbokgung's regular guided tours were suspended over both holidays. Changdeokgung's free admission covered the palace buildings but not the Secret Garden (후원, Huwon), which kept its own ticket and its own tours. Jongmyo, normally entered on timed tours, switched to free self-guided visits, with tours offered only in Korean from September 24 to 26. Deoksugung ran its commentary on a holiday schedule, including English sessions at 11:50 and 14:50 at the Daehan Empire History Museum in Seokjojeon.

Watch the closing days. Gyeongbokgung normally closes on Tuesdays, and when Seollal 2026 fell on a Tuesday the palace opened and moved its closure to Thursday, February 19, the first day after the break. Changdeokgung and Deoksugung close on Mondays and also shift closure when a Monday is a holiday. In 2027 both the Seollal substitute holiday (February 9) and the first day of Chuseok (September 14) are Tuesdays, so expect Gyeongbokgung to open on those days and close afterward. The 2026 notices appeared on royal.khs.go.kr between three days and four weeks ahead, so check again the week before.

Free entry plus quiet streets is a strong combination, but Korean families staying in Seoul have the same idea, and afternoons on the main holiday days can be busy at Gyeongbokgung in particular. Arrive at 9 a.m., see the main throne-hall axis first and leave the outer pavilions for later. If you want space for photographs, Jongmyo is a good alternative: public holidays are self-guided days there, so you can linger instead of following a guide on a fixed schedule.

en.heading: What closes: museums on the day itself, and many kitchens
paragraphs: Museums are less generous than palaces. The National Folk Museum of Korea (국립민속박물관, Gungnip Minsok Bangmulgwan), inside the Gyeongbokgung grounds, closes on Seollal and Chuseok days themselves, as both of its 2026 holiday event notices stated, and holds its holiday programs on the days around them. Other museums set their own rules, so read each one's notice board before building a day around it.

Food takes more planning than sightseeing. Banks and government offices close for the holiday, and many family-run restaurants and market stalls shut for at least the main day while their owners travel or host relatives. Chain cafés, convenience stores, hotel restaurants and places in heavily visited districts are the likeliest to stay open. Book a table for the main holiday day if a particular meal matters to you, check opening status in your map app the evening before, and keep breakfast supplies from a convenience store in your room.

en.heading: Getting around when the whole country goes home
paragraphs: The crunch is intercity, not inside Seoul. Trains, express buses and expressways are busiest on the first day out and the last day back. Seoul's own transit gets easier in the middle of the break, and the city sometimes extends service for returning travelers: for Seollal 2026 it ran subway Lines 1 to 9 and buses serving its main rail and bus terminals until 1 a.m. on February 17 and 18, while all 14 overnight Owl bus routes kept their normal schedule throughout the holiday.

The simplest strategy is to stay in Seoul and let the country empty around you. If your itinerary needs an intercity leg, avoid the first and last days of the break, book as soon as your rail or bus operator opens holiday sales, and keep a refundable backup. Expect queues at Seoul Station and the express bus terminals on peak days, and leave extra time for airport trips that pass through them.

en.heading: Where to see the holiday in public
paragraphs: Because the real rituals happen in private homes, museums and heritage villages stage public versions, and these are the best way for a visitor to take part. The National Folk Museum has run both Seollal and Chuseok programs in recent years. Its 2026 Seollal day, on February 16, included a booth for recording New Year's blessings, sebaetdon envelope making, fortune-telling with yut sticks and a family musical. Its Chuseok event on September 26 and 27 offered a ssireum class and children's tournament, a folk-game relay with jegichagi (제기차기, shuttlecock kicking), tuho (투호, arrow throwing) and top spinning, group ganggangsullae and farmers' band performances.

Namsangol Hanok Village (남산골한옥마을, Namsangol Hanok Maeul) is the other dependable stage. Its 2026 Chuseok festival, Namsan Dalbit Madang, ran from September 24 to 27 with a talk on how the charye table is laid out, pansori and traditional tightrope-walking performances, free hanbok and traditional makeup sessions, and craft workshops; on Seollal 2026 itself, February 17, it held a talk on the holiday ancestral table. The hanbok sessions and performances were walk-in, while the craft workshops took advance bookings.

Both venues publish details only a few weeks ahead; the Folk Museum posted its 2026 Chuseok program on September 14, twelve days before the event. Treat 2027 programs as likely rather than certain, and check the museum's seasonal events board (세시풍속행사, sesi pungsok haengsa) and Namsangol's program page in late January and early September. When a program is confirmed, go early: activities with daily limits, such as the craft tables, are first come, first served.

en.heading: Worked example: three days of Chuseok 2027 in Seoul
paragraphs: This plan assumes the 2026 patterns repeat, so confirm each notice before you go. Tuesday, September 14, the day before Chuseok: start at Gyeongbokgung at 9 a.m., ahead of the holiday crowds, and walk to the National Folk Museum inside the grounds before lunch, since it should be open that day. Eat a proper lunch while neighborhood restaurants are still running, and buy songpyeon from a rice-cake shop (떡집, tteokjip) for the next morning's breakfast.

Wednesday, September 15, Chuseok itself, brings the most closures. Spend the morning at Changdeokgung, whose palace buildings were free over Chuseok 2026; if you want the Secret Garden, its tickets still need booking. In the afternoon, head to Namsangol Hanok Village if its festival returns, then eat at a hotel restaurant or a chain in a central district. If the sky is clear, look for the full moon in the evening; it is the reason the holiday exists.

Thursday, September 16, the last holiday day: check whether the Folk Museum's holiday program runs today, since its events have recently fallen on the days around Chuseok. Finish at Jongmyo, which on a public holiday is a self-guided day rather than a timed-tour day; over Chuseok 2026 entry was also free. Do not book an intercity train for this evening, when the return rush peaks; leave Seoul on Friday instead.

faq.q: Is it a bad idea to visit Seoul during Seollal or Chuseok?
faq.a: No, as long as you plan around closures. Seoul is quieter than usual, the palaces opened free over both 2026 holidays, and museums and heritage villages run holiday programs. The costs are closed family restaurants on the main day and crowded intercity transport at the start and end of the break.

faq.q: Are the palaces free during Seollal and Chuseok?
faq.a: They were in 2026: Gyeongbokgung, Changdeokgung and Changgyeonggung over Seollal, and those three plus Deoksugung and Jongmyo over Chuseok. Changdeokgung's Secret Garden was excluded, and regular guided tours were reduced. Check the holiday notice on royal.khs.go.kr before you go.

faq.q: What should I say to Koreans during the holidays?
faq.a: For Seollal, 새해 복 많이 받으세요 (saehae bok mani badeuseyo), 'receive many New Year blessings.' For Chuseok, 즐거운 한가위 보내세요 (jeulgeoun hangawi bonaeseyo), 'have a joyful Chuseok.' Either one, said with a slight bow, will be warmly received.

faq.q: Will restaurants be open on Chuseok day?
faq.a: Many family-run restaurants and market stalls close on the main day, and some close for the whole break. Hotel restaurants, chains, convenience stores and places in tourist districts are your safest options. Check opening status in Naver Map or Kakao Map the evening before.

faq.q: Do the subway and buses run normally over the holidays?
faq.a: Yes, with holiday timetables. Seoul has extended late service on some holiday days, as it did until 1 a.m. on February 17 and 18, 2026, and the overnight Owl buses ran as usual. Intercity trains and express buses are the bottleneck, not city transit.

title.en: Korean Phrases for Palaces, Restaurants, Markets and Temples

summary.en: A practical Korean phrasebook for culture trips: polite endings, pronunciation tips, and phrases for tickets, ordering, markets, temples, taxis and emergencies.

audience: Visitors with no Korean who want enough polite, correctly pronounced phrases to handle palaces, museums, restaurants, markets, temples and taxis on their own.
method: Researched from the official sources listed below, checked on October 20, 2026. Romanization follows Korea's official Revised Romanization; hotline numbers and services can change, and the linked official pages are the final word.
quickAnswer: Learn the polite -yo ending, 주세요 (juseyo, 'please give me'), 저기요 (jeogiyo, 'excuse me' to call staff) and the two different goodbyes, and you can handle most culture-trip exchanges. Save 112 (police), 119 (fire and ambulance) and 1330 (the 24-hour Korea Travel Hotline) in your phone before you land.

en.heading: Two polite styles cover nearly everything
paragraphs: Korean grammar marks the relationship between speaker and listener at the end of almost every sentence, which is why a few endings matter more than a big vocabulary. As a visitor you need two of the language's several speech levels. The everyday polite style ends in -요 (-yo) and is called haeyo-che (해요체): 고마워요 (gomawoyo, 'thanks'), 괜찮아요 (gwaenchanayo, 'it's fine'). The formal style ends in -ㅂ니다 (-mnida) or -습니다 (-seumnida) and is often called hapsyo-che (합쇼체): 감사합니다 (gamsahamnida). You will hear the formal style in subway announcements, from palace staff and at shop counters.

Use the -yo style for your own sentences and the formal version of a few set phrases, such as thanks and apologies, where it sounds naturally respectful. Avoid banmal (반말), the casual speech friends use with each other; dropping the -yo when speaking to a stranger or a server sounds abrupt, whatever your accent. The single most useful word is 주세요 (juseyo), 'please give me.' Attach it to any noun, point if needed, and you have a complete, polite request, as in 물 주세요 (mul juseyo), 'water, please.'

Two short answers round out the basics. 네 (ne) means yes, and you will hear it constantly, often as 'I'm listening' rather than agreement. 아니요 (aniyo) means no. When you do not understand, 다시 한번 말해 주세요 (dasi hanbeon malhae juseyo) asks someone to say it again, and 천천히 (cheoncheonhi), 'slowly,' added before 말해 주세요, asks them to slow down. Both are better than nodding along and hoping.

en.heading: Reading the romanization without sounding robotic
paragraphs: The romanization in this guide follows Korea's official Revised Romanization, which the National Institute of Korean Language bases on standard pronunciation rather than on spelling. That helps, but several letter pairs do not match English habits. Eo is a short, open 'uh' with relaxed lips, so 어디 (eodi, 'where') sounds closer to 'uh-dee' than 'ee-oh-dee.' Eu is said with the lips spread, like the vowel in 'took' pronounced with a smile. Ae and e have merged for most Seoul speakers, and both sound like the e in 'bed.'

Consonants come in sets of three: plain, aspirated with a puff of air, and tense with no puff at all. ㄱ, ㅋ and ㄲ are romanized g, k and kk. Getting them exactly right matters less than keeping the vowels clear. At the end of a syllable, consonants are not released: 밥 (bap, 'rice') ends with closed lips and no burst. Sounds also change where syllables meet. 감사합니다 is written with a b sound before ni but is pronounced, and romanized, gamsahamnida, and 국립 (gungnip, 'national') turns its k and l into ng and n.

Korean has little word stress, so give every syllable roughly equal weight at an even pace rather than punching one. If a listener looks puzzled after two tries, show the Hangul on your screen. Koreans read it instantly, it ends the guessing for both of you, and it is the reason every phrase in this guide is printed in Hangul first.

en.heading: Greetings, thanks and the two goodbyes
paragraphs: 안녕하세요 (annyeonghaseyo) works as hello at any hour, and a slight nod with it is polite in itself. For thanks, 감사합니다 (gamsahamnida) and 고맙습니다 (gomapseumnida) are both correct; the first, built on a Sino-Korean root, sounds a shade more formal. Say 실례합니다 (sillyehamnida) for 'excuse me' when passing someone or interrupting, and 죄송합니다 (joesonghamnida) for a genuine apology, such as stepping on a foot in a crowded train.

Goodbyes depend on who is leaving. If you leave and the other person stays, as when you walk out of a shop, say 안녕히 계세요 (annyeonghi gyeseyo), 'stay in peace.' If they are leaving, or you part on the street, say 안녕히 가세요 (annyeonghi gaseyo), 'go in peace.' The shopkeeper will say 가세요 to you as you go. Getting this right is a small thing that Koreans notice, because it shows you understood the situation instead of reciting a single memorized word.

en.heading: Palaces, museums and temples: tickets, lockers and the camera question
paragraphs: At a ticket window, name the ticket, the number and 주세요: 입장권 두 장 주세요 (ipjanggwon du jang juseyo), 'two admission tickets, please.' Counting tickets uses native Korean numbers (one is 한, han, before a counter word; two 두, du; three 세, se), while prices use the Sino-Korean set, a split that trips up every learner. Ask about lockers with 사물함 어디 있어요? (samulham eodi isseoyo?) and about English tours with 영어 해설 있어요? (yeongeo haeseol isseoyo?). 해설 (haeseol) is the word palace offices use for their guided commentary.

Photography rules differ by venue and even by room, so ask rather than assume: 사진 찍어도 돼요? (sajin jjigeodo dwaeyo?), 'may I take photos?' The -어도 돼요 pattern, 'is it okay if I...', is worth memorizing because it turns any verb into a polite request for permission. In museums the usual follow-up concerns flash, and 플래시 없이요? (peullaesi eopsiyo?), 'without flash?', covers it. Before committing to a long exhibition, 몇 시에 닫아요? (myeot sie dadayo?) asks what time the place closes.

Temples call for quieter manners. Take off your shoes before stepping into a worship hall (법당, beopdang) and keep your voice low. When a monk greets you with palms pressed together (합장, hapjang), return the gesture with a small bow. Before entering any space that looks private, ask 들어가도 돼요? (deureogado dwaeyo?), 'may I go in?', and at traditional houses 신발 벗어야 돼요? (sinbal beoseoya dwaeyo?), 'should I take off my shoes?' A quiet 감사합니다 on the way out completes the exchange.

en.heading: Restaurants: jeogiyo, the table bell and ordering by the portion
paragraphs: Korean restaurants rarely send a server to check on you, so you call one. 저기요 (jeogiyo), literally 'over there,' is the standard polite way to get attention: say it clearly with a raised hand. Many tables have a call button instead, and pressing it is entirely normal. You will hear Korean customers call middle-aged women staff 이모 (imo, 'aunt'), an affectionate habit at casual places, but as a visitor you are on safer ground with jeogiyo.

Grilled meat and many stews are ordered by the portion, 인분 (inbun): 2인분 주세요 (iinbun juseyo) means 'two portions, please,' and some barbecue restaurants will not cook a single portion, so a solo diner may need to order two. For heat, 안 맵게 해 주세요 (an maepge hae juseyo) asks for no spice and 덜 맵게 (deol maepge) for less. Kitchens cannot always remove chili from a dish built on it, so ask 이거 매워요? (igeo maewoyo?), 'is this spicy?', before you order rather than after.

Side dishes (반찬, banchan) come with the meal, and refills are usually free; ask with 반찬 더 주세요 (banchan deo juseyo) or look for a self-service bar marked 셀프 (selpeu). Water is often self-service too. You normally pay at the counter by the door rather than at the table, and 계산해 주세요 (gyesanhae juseyo) works in either place. On the way out, 잘 먹었습니다 (jal meogeotseumnida), 'I ate well,' is the thanks Koreans give the cook and staff. It lands better than a tip, which is not part of Korean restaurant custom.

en.heading: Markets and taxis: the numbers you will actually hear
paragraphs: Prices use Sino-Korean numbers, and Korean counts large sums in units of ten thousand, 만 (man), rather than thousands. 천 원 (cheon won) is 1,000 won, 오천 원 (ocheon won) 5,000, 만 원 (man won) 10,000 and 삼만 원 (samman won) 30,000. Listening for 천 and 만 tells you the scale before you catch the rest, and most vendors will show the total on a calculator or phone if you look unsure. Ask 이거 얼마예요? (igeo eolmayeyo?) and point at the item.

Payment varies from stall to stall, so ask 카드 돼요? (kadeu dwaeyo?) before ordering and carry some cash for the smallest vendors. Haggling is not expected at food stalls; at clothing and souvenir stalls a polite 조금만 깎아 주세요 (jogeumman kkakka juseyo), 'a little discount, please,' may earn a small reduction, but do not push. In taxis, skip pronunciation entirely: show the Hangul address and say 여기로 가 주세요 (yeogiro ga juseyo). When you are close, 여기서 세워 주세요 (yeogiseo sewo juseyo) stops the car.

en.heading: When something goes wrong: 112, 119 and 1330
paragraphs: Save three numbers before you land. Dial 112 for police and 119 for fire and ambulance. The third, 1330, is the Korea Travel Hotline, which the Seoul city government lists as running 24 hours a day; from a foreign phone, dial +82-2-1330. It handles tourist information, interpretation and complaints, and Visit Korea also offers it as a free online call over Wi-Fi and through chat apps including KakaoTalk, LINE and WhatsApp. In Seoul, the city's Dasan call center is 02-120, and immigration questions go to 1345.

In an emergency, short phrases beat sentences. 도와주세요 (dowajuseyo) means 'help me' and carries well when called out. Follow it with what you need: 경찰 (gyeongchal, police), 구급차 (gugeupcha, ambulance), 병원 (byeongwon, hospital) or 약국 (yakguk, pharmacy). 아파요 (apayo) means 'it hurts' or 'I'm ill'; point to where. 지갑을 잃어버렸어요 (jigabeul ireobeoryeosseoyo) is 'I lost my wallet.' If you cannot make yourself understood, call 1330 and pass the phone to the person helping you, so the hotline's interpreter can bridge the gap.

en.heading: Worked example: lunch at a small restaurant, start to finish
paragraphs: Here is a typical exchange at a neighborhood restaurant serving stews and rice dishes, with what you say and why. Step inside, catch someone's eye and say 안녕하세요. Staff will often ask 몇 분이세요? (myeot buniseyo?), 'how many people?' Hold up fingers or answer 두 명이요 (du myeongiyo), 'two people,' and sit where they point. If no menu arrives, look at the wall: many small places post their menu there, sometimes with photos you can point at.

When you are ready, call 저기요, point and say 이거 두 개 주세요 (igeo du gae juseyo), 'two of these, please,' adding 안 맵게 해 주세요 if you want it mild. Side dishes arrive first, and when a dish you like runs out, 이거 더 주세요 (igeo deo juseyo), 'more of this, please,' is all you need. If someone at the next table fetches water from a cooler by the wall, that is your cue that water is self-service.

To finish, walk to the counter by the door and say 계산해 주세요. At very small places, ask 카드 돼요? before handing over a card. On the way out say 잘 먹었습니다 and then 안녕히 계세요, because you are the one leaving and the staff are staying. Total Korean used: about a dozen words, every one of them polite, and every one of them chosen for the situation rather than translated from English.

faq.q: Is it rude to start speaking English to someone in Korea?
faq.a: Not if you open politely. Say 안녕하세요 first, then ask 영어 하세요? (yeongeo haseyo?), 'do you speak English?', in a normal voice. Staff at major sights often have some English, and a Korean greeting first sets a friendly tone either way.

faq.q: What is the difference between 감사합니다 and 고맙습니다?
faq.a: Both mean thank you and both are polite. 감사합니다 (gamsahamnida) comes from a Sino-Korean root and sounds slightly more formal; 고맙습니다 (gomapseumnida) is native Korean and a touch warmer. Either is correct with strangers, staff and elders.

faq.q: Should I bow?
faq.a: A small nod or slight bow with 안녕하세요 or 감사합니다 is polite and enough for visitors. Deep bows belong to family rites, such as the New Year's bow to elders, and to formal occasions. At temples, returning a monk's palms-together greeting with a small bow is appropriate.

faq.q: Do I need to tip in restaurants or taxis?
faq.a: No. Tipping is not part of Korean restaurant or taxi custom. Say 잘 먹었습니다 (jal meogeotseumnida) when you leave a restaurant and 감사합니다 to a taxi driver; that is the expected thanks.

faq.q: Which number should I call if I am lost and cannot explain where I am?
faq.a: Call 1330, the Korea Travel Hotline, which runs 24 hours a day and offers interpretation; from a foreign phone dial +82-2-1330. Give the nearest station name and exit number or read out a shop sign. For crimes or emergencies, call 112 (police) or 119 (fire and ambulance).

title.en: Three Days of Korean Culture in Seoul, Ordered Around Closing Days

summary.en: A day-by-day Seoul culture plan: Gyeongbokgung and Bukchon, the Secret Garden, Jongmyo and Gwangjang, then the National Museum, ordered for every arrival weekday.

audience: First-time independent visitors with one to three days in Seoul who want palaces, hanok lanes, a market and a museum in an order that avoids closed gates.
method: Researched from the official sources listed below, checked on October 20, 2026. Hours, fees and booking rules can change; the linked official pages are the final word.
quickAnswer: Give Day 1 to Gyeongbokgung, Bukchon and Insadong, Day 2 to Changdeokgung's Secret Garden, Jongmyo Shrine and Gwangjang Market, and Day 3 to the National Museum of Korea and Namsan. Gyeongbokgung and Jongmyo close on Tuesdays and Changdeokgung on Mondays, so Day 2 must fall between Wednesday and Sunday, and its garden tour goes on sale online at 10:00 Korea time six days ahead.

keyFacts.label: Day 1

en.heading: Why the three days follow the plan of the Joseon capital
paragraphs: Seoul's oldest cultural sites were laid out to one plan, and following it saves both time and confusion. When the Joseon dynasty (조선, 1392–1910) built its capital, it placed the main palace, Gyeongbokgung (경복궁), under the mountain Bugaksan, and set the royal ancestral shrine, Jongmyo (종묘), to the east and the altar to the gods of land and grain to the west, following a classical rule for capitals. The commercial avenue of Jongno ran below that royal quarter, and Namsan (남산), with the city wall along its ridge, closed the city to the south. Each day of this itinerary takes one band of that map, so you walk most of it instead of crossing town.

Day 1 covers the state's public face. Gyeongbokgung's straight line of gates, throne hall, office and residences is the template the other palaces adapt or ignore, which is why it comes first. Bukchon (북촌), on the slope between the two main palaces, is where officials and noble families settled to stay close to the throne. Insadong (인사동), just below it, grew from the old quarter of the royal painting bureau into the city's street of galleries, brush shops and antique dealers.

Day 2 moves from the state to the royal household and its ancestors. Changdeokgung (창덕궁), not Gyeongbokgung, was where Joseon kings actually lived for about 270 years after the 1592 Japanese invasion, and its rear garden was their private retreat. Jongmyo holds the spirit tablets on which the dynasty's legitimacy rested, and Gwangjang Market (광장시장), founded by Korean merchants in 1905, is the trading city that grew up beside them. Day 3 steps back for the long view: the National Museum of Korea (국립중앙박물관) puts objects to the stories you have walked through, and Namsan shows the wall that once enclosed them.

en.heading: The closing-day grid that sets your order
paragraphs: Three rules decide which day goes where. Gyeongbokgung and Jongmyo close on Tuesdays; Changdeokgung, Changgyeonggung and Deoksugung close on Mondays. Namsangol Hanok Village's houses also close on Mondays unless the Monday is a public holiday, and the National Museum of Korea, otherwise open daily, shuts its exhibition halls on the first Monday of March, June, September and December, next on December 7, 2026. Day 2 is the demanding one, because it needs Changdeokgung and Jongmyo open together, which happens only from Wednesday to Sunday. Day 1 works on any day but Tuesday, and Day 3 is happiest from Tuesday to Sunday.

Two refinements. When a regular closing day falls on a public holiday, the palaces and Jongmyo open that day and close on the next non-holiday instead, so in a week with a Monday holiday the following Tuesday can shut Gyeongbokgung, Jongmyo and the Monday palaces all at once; check the notice board on royal.khs.go.kr before you fix a holiday week. The national museum also closes on January 1 and on the Seollal and Chuseok days themselves, so over the lunar holidays put Day 3 on one of the days around them.

en.heading: Day 1: from the throne hall to a teahouse in Insadong
paragraphs: Be at Gyeongbokgung soon after its 09:00 opening; Exit 5 of Gyeongbokgung Station, on Line 3, is about two minutes from the gate. Buy your ticket, then watch the 10:00 guard-changing ceremony in the forecourt in front of Heungnyemun gate, which takes about 20 minutes. Afterward walk the central axis: the throne hall Geunjeongjeon (근정전) with its rank stones, the king's office Sajeongjeon, the royal residences and the terraced Amisan garden, then cut west to Gyeonghoeru (경회루), the banquet pavilion standing in its square pond. Allow two and a half hours in all.

Leave by the east side around 12:30, eat in Samcheong-dong (삼청동), and climb into Bukchon. Its most photographed lane, Bukchon-ro 11-gil (북촌로11길), lies in a red zone where tourists may walk only from 10:00 to 17:00, and an officer can fine you 100,000 won if you stay after being asked to leave, so an early-afternoon visit fits the rule with time to spare. These are family homes: keep voices low, do not sit on doorsteps, and do not photograph into houses. About 90 minutes covers the view over Changdeokgung's roofs and the lane itself.

From the foot of Bukchon, cross toward Anguk Station and walk Insadong-gil (인사동길) south from its northern end. The main street mixes craft with imported souvenir stock, so spend your time upstairs and in the side alleys: galleries you can walk into without a ticket, brush shops marked 필방 (pilbang), and a traditional teahouse for citron or jujube tea with your shoes off. Around 17:30, walk east along Jongno toward Jongno 3-ga and turn north into Ikseon-dong (익선동), where small 1920s hanok now hold restaurants and cafés, for dinner a few minutes from the subway.

Two swaps are worth knowing. If empty lanes matter more to you than an empty palace, do Bukchon first, soon after 10:00 on a weekday, and Gyeongbokgung from 13:30, catching the 14:00 ceremony; from November to February the palace stops admitting visitors at 16:00, so start by 14:00. And if one museum fits your Day 1, the National Palace Museum at the palace's southwest corner shows the court's furnishings, carriages and ritual objects in an hour, while the National Folk Museum on the east side explains how everyone else lived.

en.heading: Day 2: the Secret Garden, the ancestral shrine and a market supper
paragraphs: Book this day first. The Secret Garden, Huwon (후원), behind Changdeokgung can be entered only on a timed guided session. English sessions leave at 10:30, 11:30 and 14:30, with 15:30 added from March to November; half of each session's 100 places go on sale online at 10:00 Korea time six days ahead, and the other half are sold at the ticket office from 09:00 on the day. Choose 10:30 or 11:30. Arrive at Changdeokgung at 09:00 from Anguk Station Exit 3 and spend the time before your slot in the halls: the throne hall Injeongjeon, the blue-roofed office Seonjeongjeon and the unpainted Nakseonjae compound.

The rest of the day depends on the weekday. On Wednesdays, weekends and public holidays, Jongmyo is a self-guided day and the restored link over Yulgok-ro is open. From the palace halls, walk through Hamyangmun gate into Changgyeonggung (창경궁), see its 1616 throne hall and the white-framed glasshouse, then leave by its Yulgok-ro gate into Jongmyo's north side; that gate stops admitting people at 17:00 in winter and 17:30 in spring and autumn. Each site needs its own ticket. Walk past the shrine's two great halls, Jeongjeon and Yeongnyeongjeon, and out of the main gate onto Jongno, allowing about an hour inside.

On Thursdays and Fridays, Jongmyo admits visitors only on timed guided tours of about 50 minutes, with English tours at 10:00, 12:00, 14:00 and 16:00. After the garden, eat near Changdeokgung, walk south to Jongno 3-ga and join the 14:00 tour, buying your ticket at the shrine and reaching the start early. A guided weekday visit is arguably the better way to understand Jongmyo anyway, because a docent explains what each building was for and the stone court is quiet. Saturdays and holidays offer Korean commentary only, so English speakers who want a guide should choose a weekday or a Sunday.

Finish at Gwangjang Market, a short walk east along Jongno from the shrine. VisitKorea lists its food street as open 09:00 to 23:00 all year, while the general market keeps 09:00 to 18:00 and closes on Sundays. Sit at a counter with a posted price board, name the dish and the quantity before anything is served, and start with mayak gimbap while you decide, then bindaetteok (빈대떡, mung-bean pancake) with a bottle of makgeolli. Cards are accepted at many places, but carry small notes. Adult foreign visitors aged 19 to 64 spend 10,000 won on Day 2's four tickets, or 5,000 won on a Wednesday.

en.heading: Day 3: three objects at the national museum, then up Namsan
paragraphs: Take Line 4 or the Gyeongui-Jungang Line to Ichon Station and either use Exit 2, about 150 meters from the museum, or follow the underground Museum Nadeulgil path, open 07:00 to 23:00. The National Museum of Korea opens at 09:30 and its permanent galleries are free; put any backpack in a first-floor locker, as the museum requires. Resist walking every corridor. Three anchors carry the visit: the marble Gyeongcheonsa pagoda of 1348 in the central hall, the Silla gold crown in the ancient galleries, and the two pensive bodhisattvas in the second-floor Room of Quiet Contemplation, with the celadon and buncheong rooms, 303 and 304, as an optional fourth stop.

Check the museum's notice board for gallery closures before you set out, since older highlight routes can lead to closed doors. Two and a half hours covers the three anchors and the ceramics. Eat lunch at the museum before you move on, so that the afternoon starts on time.

In the afternoon, ride Line 4 from Ichon to Chungmuro and walk up to Namsangol Hanok Village (남산골한옥마을), where late-Joseon houses gathered from around the city, one of them a faithful replica, stand open to walk into, free. Commentary tours in English leave at 14:00 and 15:30 from Tuesday to Friday and at 10:30 and 12:00 at weekends; individuals simply join at the guide office by the main gate. From the top of the village garden, footpaths climb Namsan toward N Seoul Tower in roughly 40 minutes to an hour. See the Joseon beacon mound at the summit, then ride the cable car or a Namsan bus down toward Myeong-dong for dinner.

Seochon (서촌), on Gyeongbokgung's west side, is the alternative for readers who would rather have literature and a market lunch than views: Tongin Market's covered lane, a painter's house turned museum and a poet's hill under Inwangsan. It fits best when Day 3 falls on a Wednesday or Saturday, when the national museum stays open until 21:00 with last entry at 20:30. Then flip the day: Seochon from late morning, and the museum from about 17:30, when the galleries thin out. Our Seochon walk gives the hours and closing days of its small museums.

en.heading: Cutting to two days, or to one
paragraphs: With two days, keep Day 1 and Day 2 and drop Day 3. The palaces, Bukchon and Jongmyo cannot be replaced, while the museum can be squeezed into an evening: if either day is a Wednesday or Saturday, go after dinner for the pagoda and the bodhisattvas, about 90 minutes before the 21:00 close. Inside those two days, cut Changgyeonggung, Ikseon-dong and any second museum before anything else. Keep the Secret Garden; nothing else in Seoul shows so clearly how a Joseon king wanted to spend his time away from the throne.

With one day, let the weekday choose. On most days, shorten Day 1: Gyeongbokgung's central axis and Gyeonghoeru in about 90 minutes, Bukchon-ro 11-gil before 17:00, and tea in Insadong. On a Tuesday, when Gyeongbokgung and Jongmyo are both closed, take Changdeokgung's halls and a garden session, then Changgyeonggung. On a Monday, when the other palaces are closed, pair Gyeongbokgung in the morning with Jongmyo's 14:00 English tour, since Monday is a guided-tour day there, and end in Insadong. One palace and one neighborhood seen properly beat three palaces seen at a run.

en.heading: Meals that fit the route instead of interrupting it
paragraphs: Plan meals by area, not by the clock. Day 1's lunch belongs in Samcheong-dong between the palace and Bukchon, and its dinner in Ikseon-dong or the lanes around Insadong, where many restaurants occupy converted hanok. A traditional teahouse in mid-afternoon doubles as a rest stop: order one leaf tea and one fruit tea and share them. If you want Korean barbecue on one of the evenings, read our ordering guide first, because grill restaurants have their own rules on portions and pricing that regularly confuse first-time visitors.

Day 2 has the itinerary's best built-in meal. On Jongmyo's self-guided days you reach Gwangjang from the shrine in time for an early dinner, and on Thursdays and Fridays you arrive after the 14:00 tour for a late lunch that can run into the evening. Bindaetteok with makgeolli is the pairing Koreans reach for, and yukhoe, seasoned raw beef, is the splurge, usually ordered at sit-down specialists rather than counters. Day 3's lunch is easiest inside the museum, and its dinner in Myeong-dong at the foot of Namsan, where the cable car and buses come down.

en.heading: After the palaces close: evening options for each day
paragraphs: Most palaces close between 17:00 and 18:30 depending on the month, but Deoksugung (덕수궁) opposite Seoul City Hall and Changgyeonggung beside Changdeokgung stay open until 21:00, with last entry at 20:00, every day except Monday. On Day 1, Deoksugung shows a different chapter after dinner: the short-lived Korean Empire and its Western stone halls. On Day 2, Changgyeonggung's grounds and lit glasshouse make a calm return trip from Gwangjang. Separately ticketed night programs occasionally shorten Changgyeonggung's ordinary evening hours, so glance at its notice board first.

Day 3 has the most choice. Namsangol's houses stay open until 21:00 from April to November and until 20:00 from December to March, and Seoul Namsan Gugakdang, an underground hall for traditional music at the edge of the village, lists its evening performances on sgtt.kr. The summit terraces on Namsan cost nothing after dark. In the Seochon version of the day, the national museum's late opening on Wednesday or Saturday is the evening. Whatever you choose, check the last subway train from your stop in Naver Map before a late dinner.

en.heading: Getting around: one transit card and four stations
paragraphs: Almost every connection in this plan is a walk, so a pay-as-you-go T-money card loaded with cash covers the subway rides; unlimited passes pay off only when you make several separate journeys a day, and our subway guide does that arithmetic. Four stations do most of the work: Gyeongbokgung (Exit 5) for Day 1, Anguk (Exit 3) for Changdeokgung and the north end of Insadong, Jongno 3-ga (Exits 11 and 8) for Jongmyo, and Ichon (Exit 2) for the museum. The first three are on Line 3. In Naver Map or Kakao Map, search the Korean names in this guide rather than English spellings.
checklist: Six days before Day 2, at 10:00 Korea time: book an English Secret Garden session through royal.khs.go.kr, or plan to queue at the Changdeokgung ticket office from 09:00 on the day.
In the week of travel, check the palace notice boards for holiday closures and special programs.
Check the National Museum of Korea's notice board for gallery closures before Day 3.
Carry your passport: foreign visitors aged 18 and under or 65 and over enter the palaces and Jongmyo free.
Bring small won notes for Gwangjang's counters and a T-money card for the subway.
Leave Bukchon-ro 11-gil by 17:00.

faq.q: Can I see Gyeongbokgung and Changdeokgung on the same day?
faq.a: Yes, but you will rush both. If you must, walk Gyeongbokgung's central axis in the morning, cross Bukchon on foot, and take a 14:30 English Secret Garden session booked six days ahead. It works only from Wednesday to Sunday, since Gyeongbokgung closes on Tuesdays and Changdeokgung on Mondays, and Jongmyo then has to wait for another day.

faq.q: Do I need to book anything in advance?
faq.a: Only the Secret Garden: online from 10:00 Korea time six days before your visit, or on the day from 09:00 at the Changdeokgung ticket office, where half of each session's places are held back. Palace and Jongmyo tickets are bought at the gate, the national museum's permanent galleries need no ticket, and Namsangol's English tours take walk-ins.

faq.q: Is the integrated palace pass worth it for this plan?
faq.a: Usually, by a small margin. The 6,000-won pass, valid for six months, covers one entry each to Gyeongbokgung, Changdeokgung, Changgyeonggung, Deoksugung and Jongmyo, and this itinerary's tickets for four of them cost adult foreign visitors 8,000 won bought separately. It excludes the 5,000-won Secret Garden ticket, and if Day 2 falls on a Wednesday its sites are free anyway, which makes the pass pointless.

faq.q: What should I change if it rains?
faq.a: Move Day 3 forward: the national museum is reached by an underground path from Ichon Station, and the Namsan walk can become a performance at Namsan Gugakdang. Palace days survive light rain, but the Secret Garden's earth paths turn slippery, so wear shoes with grip, and leave Bukchon's lanes and Jongmyo's open stone courts for a dry afternoon if you can.

faq.q: Which day suits hanbok rental?
faq.a: Day 1. Rental shops cluster around Gyeongbokgung Station, a qualifying hanbok gets you into the palace free, and Bukchon makes a classic backdrop if you keep to its 10:00 to 17:00 window. Avoid it on Day 2 if you hold a garden ticket, because long skirts and the Secret Garden's hillside paths are a poor match.

title.en: Seoul's Palaces, Temples and Markets by Season: What Changes When

summary.en: How spring, summer, autumn and winter change Seoul's palace hours, night openings, Secret Garden tours, lanterns, rites, kimjang, holiday closures and monsoon plans.

audience: Visitors choosing when to come to Seoul, or already booked, who want to know how the season changes palace hours, gardens, temple festivals and day plans.
method: Researched from the official sources listed below, checked on October 20, 2026. Hours, fees and booking rules can change; the linked official pages are the final word.
quickAnswer: Late April to May and the second half of October are the best seasons for Seoul's palace gardens, but they bring sell-out Secret Garden sessions and the short seasonal night openings at Gyeongbokgung. Summer brings the monsoon, normally from about June 25 to July 26 in central Korea, plus heat; winter brings a 17:00 close at Gyeongbokgung but the quietest courtyards. Over Seollal and Chuseok the palaces stay open while the national museum closes on the holiday itself.

en.heading: A year once organized around rites and harvests
paragraphs: Seoul's heritage sites were built for a society that ran on the seasons, and many still keep its calendar. Seollal and Chuseok, the two great family holidays, follow the lunar calendar, so their dates in the solar calendar move every year. Jongmyo's royal ancestral rite was once performed at the main hall five times a year and now survives twice, in early May and early November. Temples hang lanterns for the Buddha's birthday on the eighth day of the fourth lunar month. And kimjang, the late-autumn making of winter kimchi, is the end of a cycle that begins in spring, when households buy seafood for salting.

Knowing that cycle changes what you notice. The same palace that hosts a festival and evening openings in May is nearly empty and shut by five in January. Treat the season as part of the plan rather than the weather around it. The sections below set out what each season adds, what it takes away and which official notice boards announce the changes, because many seasonal programs are confirmed only a few weeks ahead and should not be planned from a previous year's dates.

en.heading: Four timetables a year at the palace gates
paragraphs: Palace hours follow daylight, but the palaces do not change on the same dates. Gyeongbokgung (경복궁) switches on the first of March, June, September and November. Changdeokgung (창덕궁) and Jongmyo (종묘) share their own schedule, closing at 17:30 in the darkest months and moving to longer hours a month earlier, in February. Deoksugung and Changgyeonggung ignore the seasons and stay open until 21:00, with last entry at 20:00, every day except Monday. Elsewhere, last entry is an hour before closing, and the Secret Garden's English sessions change with the months as the table shows.

Two months catch people out. In February, Changdeokgung has already moved to its spring hours while Gyeongbokgung still closes at 17:00, so on a winter afternoon see Gyeongbokgung first. In November the garden still runs its 15:30 English session, but Changdeokgung's last entry is 16:30, so see the palace halls before the walk rather than after it. Closing days, by contrast, never change with the season: Gyeongbokgung and Jongmyo close on Tuesdays, and the other palaces on Mondays.

en.heading: Spring: lanterns, the May rite and the first night openings
paragraphs: From April, the Buddhist calendar takes over central Seoul. Buddha's Birthday falls on Thursday, May 13, in 2027, and for weeks beforehand temples hang lotus lanterns. The Lotus Lantern Festival, Yeondeunghoe (연등회), peaks on a weekend shortly before the holiday: in 2026 lantern displays filled Gwanghwamun Square, Jogyesa and Bongeunsa from April into May, and the main parade ran along Jongno to Jogyesa on a Saturday evening. The 2027 schedule had not been posted on the festival site, llf.or.kr, by October 20, 2026, so treat 2026 as a pattern rather than a promise.

Late April and early May are also festival weeks at the palaces. In 2026 the spring palace festival ran from April 25 to May 3 and ended with Jongmyo Jerye (종묘제례), the royal ancestral rite held on the first Sunday of May, whose ritual and music UNESCO recognized in 2001. That day the rite ran at Yeongnyeongjeon from 10:00 to 12:00 and at the main hall, Jeongjeon, from 14:00 to 16:30; entry to the shrine was free and regular commentary was suspended. The notice went up in early April. If you go, the afternoon rite at the main hall is the one to see.

Spring also brings Gyeongbokgung's first night opening. The 2026 run lasted from May 13 to June 14, from 19:00 to 21:30 with last entry at 20:30, with no night viewing on Mondays or Tuesdays, and it covered the front courts, Gyeonghoeru and the royal residences. Tickets were sold online from early May until the day before each visit, and 300 more a night were sold at Gwanghwamun to foreign visitors only, two per person; the run went ahead in rain. Its notice appeared on April 29, so watch the Gyeongbokgung notice board from late April.

Spring is the Secret Garden's high season, together with autumn: flowering trees and fresh leaves around its ponds, and online sessions that go fast at every release. Gyeongbokgung's special Gyeonghoeru and Hyangwonjeong tour, which in 2026 ran on Wednesdays and Fridays from April to October, takes small groups inside the banquet pavilion, but it is conducted in Korean only. Treat it as a bonus for Korean speakers rather than a reason to choose spring.

en.heading: Summer: monsoon weeks, heat and the evening shift
paragraphs: Summer in Seoul is two seasons in one. The monsoon, jangma (장마), normally covers central Korea from about June 25 to July 26, roughly 32 days, and the Korea Meteorological Administration's normals put average rainfall in that window at about 378 millimeters, though the actual start and end move from year to year. Heat is the other summer factor, and the agency's heat-wave advisories (폭염특보) are worth checking each morning. Neither closes the palaces, whose summer hours are their longest, but both change what is sensible to attempt in the middle of the day.

The heritage authorities adjust as well. Gyeongbokgung's Gyeonghoeru tour pauses from June to August, and in July and August 2026 Jongmyo set aside its timed-tour system for the heat and let visitors walk in on every open day. The practical answer is to split the day: be at a palace gate at 09:00, move indoors from late morning, and come back out after 17:00 to Deoksugung or Changgyeonggung, both open until 21:00, when the stone courtyards have given up some of the day's heat.

Rain is less of a problem than heat for most cultural sights, provided you choose the right ones. Tiled roofs show what they were designed for in a downpour, with water running down the tile channels and dripping clear of the broad eaves, and Seochon's Suseongdong valley only really flows after rain. What rain spoils is anything on earth or stone: the Secret Garden's slopes turn slippery, and long rental-hanbok hems soak up water from palace courtyards. On the wettest days, the National Museum of Korea, open until 21:00 on Wednesdays and Saturdays, is the natural refuge.

en.heading: Autumn: maples, Chuseok and the palace festival season
paragraphs: Autumn color reaches its peak across Korea in late October. The Korea Forest Service's 2026 forecast put the national peak, defined as half of a tree's leaves turned, at October 31 for maples and oaks and October 30 for ginkgo, about a day later than the five-year average, with color starting on Seoraksan, forecast to peak on October 20, and spreading into the central and southern regions. The forecast is published each September; check the new one rather than relying on this year's numbers.

Inside the palaces, put the gardens first. The Secret Garden's valleys of maples are the best-known autumn walk in Seoul, and its October and November sessions fill as quickly as spring's. Changgyeonggung next door has more open ground around its pond, needs no booking and stays open until 21:00, which makes it the fallback if the garden is full; at Gyeongbokgung, aim for the island pavilion Hyangwonjeong in the north of the grounds. Gyeongbokgung's second night run also falls in early autumn: in 2026 it lasted from September 2 to October 2 and was announced in mid-August.

Chuseok, the harvest holiday on the fifteenth day of the eighth lunar month, falls on Wednesday, September 15, in 2027, with the holiday running from September 14 to 16. Early November closes the ritual year at Jongmyo with the second ancestral rite, on the first Saturday of the month; its notice tends to appear in late October, as it did on October 27 in 2025. Palace festival programs run through the season too, and in October 2026 the shrine posted special visiting and commentary hours for an autumn palace festival. Expect similar programs in other years, but take the dates only from the notice boards.

en.heading: Kimjang: the late-autumn ritual you will mostly meet in museums
paragraphs: Kimjang (김장), the shared making of a winter's supply of kimchi, is the season's great domestic ritual, and UNESCO added it to the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2013. Its description follows the whole year: households buy shrimp, anchovies and other seafood for salting in spring, sea salt in summer, and red chilies in late summer to dry and grind, then gather in late autumn to make kimchi together, choosing the day by watching the forecast. Batches are shared between households, and methods pass down within families, often from a mother-in-law to a new daughter-in-law.

You are unlikely to be invited into a family kimjang, and the point is that it is not staged for outsiders. A visitor can still read it. The National Folk Museum's hall on the Korean year places kimjang beside the other winter tasks, making fermented soybean blocks called meju (메주) and cooking red-bean porridge at the winter solstice, and Museum Kimchikan in Insadong is devoted to kimchi itself. Both are indoor stops that suit November, when Gyeongbokgung is back to closing at 17:00 and the afternoons shorten fast.

en.heading: Winter: short days, icy paths and the quietest palaces
paragraphs: Winter is the season most visitors avoid and the one that rewards planning most. With Gyeongbokgung's last entry at 16:00 from November to February, a palace afternoon has to begin by about 14:00. The Secret Garden drops to three English sessions a day from December to February; bare branches open up views of pavilions that summer leaves hide, but paths can be icy, so take the 11:30 slot for the warmest part of the day and wear shoes with grip. After a night of snow, go early, before the courtyards are swept and trodden.

Cold weather also makes sense of Korea's most characteristic indoor culture. Ondol (온돌), the underfloor heating that warms a hanok from below, explains why people traditionally sat and slept on the floor. A teahouse's ginger tea or ssanghwa-cha, a bitter-sweet herbal blend, is a winter order, and a jjimjilbang (찜질방), a bathhouse with heated rooms and a shared floor where everyone wears the T-shirt and shorts provided, is where many Koreans sit out a freezing afternoon. Hanbok rental still works in winter, with thermal layers underneath and a coat on top.

Plan outdoor walks for the middle of the day and keep an indoor fallback in the same district: the national museum in Yongsan, the two museums on Gyeongbokgung's grounds, or Insadong's galleries and teahouses near the palaces. Steep routes such as the Inwangsan wall trail above Seochon need real care in ice, and Bukchon's lanes are steeper than they look when they freeze. Pack shoes with grip, gloves and a layer you can take off indoors, because museums and teahouses are kept warm.

en.heading: Seollal, Chuseok and the Tuesday that can close everything
paragraphs: The two lunar holidays shape a trip more than any weather. In 2027 Seollal falls on Sunday, February 7, with the public holiday running from Saturday, February 6, to Tuesday, February 9, and Chuseok falls on Wednesday, September 15, with the holiday from September 14 to 16. Many Seoul residents travel to family homes, so the city's sights grow quieter while intercity trains and buses fill, and many family-run restaurants close on the main day. Check opening status in your map app the evening before.

Palaces stay open and museums do not. When a palace's regular closing day falls on a public holiday, the palaces and Jongmyo open that day and close on the next non-holiday instead. In 2027 both Seollal's substitute holiday, February 9, and the first day of Chuseok, September 14, are Tuesdays, so expect Gyeongbokgung to open on those days and close later in the week. The National Museum of Korea, by contrast, closes on January 1 and on the Seollal and Chuseok days themselves; in 2026 those were February 17 and September 25.

The same rule hides a trap. Changdeokgung, Changgyeonggung and Deoksugung normally close on Mondays; when a Monday is a holiday they open and close on the next non-holiday, usually Tuesday, which is already Gyeongbokgung's and Jongmyo's closing day. In 2027 that applies after March 1, May 3, July 19, August 16, October 4, October 11 and December 27, all Monday holidays or substitute holidays. Seollal adds a twist, since February 8 and 9 are both holidays, which pushes several closures onto Wednesday, February 10. Expect such days to close most palaces at once, confirm on the notice boards, and give them to a museum.

en.heading: Picking your season, and the notice boards to watch
paragraphs: If you can choose, come from late April to May or in the second half of October, and accept that you will be booking the Secret Garden at the release minute and sharing the courtyards. Early June and September give long opening hours with fewer festival crowds, though September can overlap Chuseok. Winter suits travelers who prefer quiet palaces and indoor culture to gardens, and midsummer suits only those willing to split each day around the heat. Whatever the season, the notices below confirm the details that change every year.
checklist: Gyeongbokgung notice board (royal.khs.go.kr): from late April for a spring night run, from mid-August for an autumn one.
Jongmyo notice board: from early April for the May rite, from late October for the November rite.
llf.or.kr: in spring, for the Lotus Lantern Festival's exhibitions and parade.
Korea Forest Service: from late September, for the year's foliage peak forecast.
Korea Meteorological Administration (weather.go.kr): in the week of travel, for monsoon rain and heat-wave or cold-wave advisories.
National Museum of Korea: in the week before Seollal or Chuseok, for holiday closures.

faq.q: What is the best time of year to see Seoul's palaces?
faq.a: Late April to May and the second half of October, when the gardens are at their best and the weather suits long walks. Both bring crowds and fast-selling Secret Garden sessions. For long hours with fewer festival crowds, try early June or September; for the emptiest courtyards, come in winter and accept a 17:00 close at Gyeongbokgung.

faq.q: Are Seoul's palaces open at night?
faq.a: Deoksugung and Changgyeonggung are open until 21:00 all year, except on Mondays. Gyeongbokgung opens at night only in short seasonal runs with separate tickets: in 2026, from May 13 to June 14 and from September 2 to October 2, announced on its notice board in late April and mid-August. No 2027 runs had been announced by October 20, 2026.

faq.q: Do palace visits stop during the monsoon?
faq.a: No. The palaces keep their longest hours in summer and stay open in rain, though some programs change: Gyeongbokgung's Gyeonghoeru tour pauses from June to August, and Jongmyo switched to walk-in visits in July and August 2026. The monsoon normally covers central Korea from about June 25 to July 26, so carry an umbrella and keep an indoor alternative in the same district.

faq.q: When do autumn leaves peak in Seoul's palaces?
faq.a: Around the end of October in recent years. The Korea Forest Service's 2026 forecast put the national peak at October 30 for ginkgo and October 31 for maples and oaks. In central Seoul, aim for the Secret Garden at Changdeokgung, the pond at Changgyeonggung and Hyangwonjeong at Gyeongbokgung, and check the new forecast each September.

faq.q: Can visitors take part in kimjang?
faq.a: Rarely. Kimjang is a family and community practice of making a winter's kimchi together in late autumn, recognized by UNESCO in 2013, and it is not normally staged for outsiders. To understand it, visit the National Folk Museum's hall on the Korean year or Museum Kimchikan in Insadong, both indoors and easy to fit into a short November day.

title.en: Rain, Freeze or Heat Wave in Seoul: Indoor Culture That Is Worth It

summary.en: When rain, cold or heat breaks a palace day in Seoul: the indoor museums, performances, teahouses, bathhouses and covered markets to choose, by area and weekday.

audience: Visitors whose Seoul plans meet a downpour, a cold snap or a heat wave and who want indoor cultural experiences worth the trip, not just shelter.
method: Researched from the official sources listed below, checked on October 20, 2026. Hours, fees and booking rules can change; the linked official pages are the final word.
quickAnswer: Go to the National Museum of Korea, reached by an underground path from Ichon Station, or pair a short walk through Gyeongbokgung with the National Palace Museum and National Folk Museum on its grounds. Add a traditional teahouse, Gwangjang Market's covered food street or the Saturday Gugak Concert, and save palace gardens and Namsan for a clear day. Monday is the hardest day to rearrange, because several indoor sights close.

en.heading: Why Joseon measured its rain
paragraphs: Weather mattered enough to the Joseon state that King Sejong's government made instruments to measure it. A replica of the supyo (수표), the stone gauge set in a stream to warn of drought and flood, stands in the National Folk Museum's open-air area, and the palace buildings around it are weather engineering too. Their deep eaves shade rooms from the high summer sun, let the low winter sun reach inside and keep rain off timber posts, while ondol (온돌), the underfloor heating of traditional houses, holds warmth through the freezing months.

Koreans keep their own habits for bad weather. Ask what to eat on a rainy evening and the likely answer is jeon, savory pan-fried pancakes, with makgeolli; on a hot afternoon, something cold and sour such as iced omija-cha; on a freezing one, a heated floor at the bathhouse. This guide follows the same logic. Rather than looking for any shelter, it swaps each outdoor plan for an indoor one that still teaches you something about the same culture, in the same part of the city.

en.heading: First decide what the weather has actually broken
paragraphs: Not every forecast should cancel a palace. Light rain thins the crowds at Gyeongbokgung (경복궁) and shows Bukchon's roof drainage at work; what it spoils are earth paths, long hanbok hems and outdoor ceremonies. Heat is the bigger threat, because the palaces' stone and gravel courtyards offer little shade. Freezing days are manageable in the morning and miserable by late afternoon, and from November to February Gyeongbokgung stops admitting visitors at 16:00 in any case.

Use the Korea Meteorological Administration's own thresholds as switch points. It issues a heat-wave advisory (폭염주의보) when the daily maximum feels-like temperature is expected to reach 33°C or more for at least two days, and a warning at 35°C. Between October and April it issues a cold-wave advisory (한파주의보) when morning lows are expected to stay at −12°C or below for two days, or to fall 10°C or more from the day before to 3°C or lower. On those days, keep outdoor sights to the first hour after opening and plan indoors from late morning.

Heat calls for a change of clock as much as a change of place. Be at a palace gate at 09:00, go indoors from late morning to late afternoon, and come back out after 17:00, when Deoksugung and Changgyeonggung stay open until 21:00 with last entry at 20:00. The National Museum of Korea's Wednesday and Saturday evenings, and the Seoul Museum of History's Friday evenings, give you cool galleries while the streets are at their hottest.

Some plans are simply not worth saving. The views from the Namsan summit and N Seoul Tower disappear in low cloud and rain, so swap them rather than ride up hoping for a gap. Steep stone routes, such as the Inwangsan wall trail above Seochon, turn slick in rain and dangerous in ice. And Jongmyo (종묘), a place of open stone courts with nothing to enter, is best moved to a dry day. Keep these for the clearest day of your trip and give the bad one to the indoor sights below.

en.heading: The National Museum of Korea: a whole day without surfacing
paragraphs: If you can choose only one indoor experience, choose this. From Ichon Station, on Line 4 and the Gyeongui-Jungang Line, the Museum Nadeulgil underground path runs to the National Museum of Korea (국립중앙박물관) between 07:00 and 23:00, so you need not surface in rain or heat. The permanent galleries are free and open 9:30 to 17:30, until 21:00 on Wednesdays and Saturdays, with last entry 30 minutes before closing. Leave backpacks in the first-floor lockers. Focus on the Gyeongcheonsa pagoda, the Silla gold crown and the two pensive bodhisattvas, then the celadon and buncheong rooms.

Plan around two caveats. Several upper-floor galleries are closed for renovation, so check the museum's notice board, or our museum guide, for the rooms that are open before you build a route. And on the first Monday of March, June, September and December the exhibition halls close for maintenance, next on December 7, 2026, though the outdoor area stays open. The museum also closes on January 1 and on the Seollal and Chuseok days themselves.

Give it the whole bad-weather day if you like. The building has a restaurant and cafés for a long visit, and the outdoor garden, open 07:00 to 22:00, is worth a walk once the weather turns. On a Wednesday or Saturday, arrive after lunch and stay until closing, when the galleries are at their quietest and the late hours spare you the evening heat or the worst of the rush-hour rain outside.

en.heading: Gyeongbokgung in the rain: the axis, then two museums on its grounds
paragraphs: A wet day does not have to cost you the palace. Gyeongbokgung's central axis, from the main gate through the throne hall to the king's office and residences, takes about an hour and stays worth seeing under an umbrella, and its courtyards are quieter than on any sunny weekend. Then move indoors. The National Palace Museum of Korea (국립고궁박물관), at the palace's southwest corner, is free and shows the court's own objects, from royal carriages and court painting to ritual vessels and scientific instruments. It opens 09:30 to 17:30, until 21:00 on Saturdays and the last Wednesday of the month, and closes on the last Monday of each month.

On the palace's east side, the National Folk Museum of Korea (국립민속박물관) is free and explains how ordinary Koreans lived: the farming year, first birthdays, weddings and ancestral rites. It opens 9:00 to 18:00 from March to October, until 20:00 on Wednesdays, and 9:00 to 17:00 from November to February, and unlike the palace it stays open on Tuesdays. Its open-air street of 1970s and 1980s shops is less fun in the rain, and the shop interiors are closed to visitors on weekends and holidays anyway, so spend a wet visit in the indoor halls.

Together the palace axis and the two museums make a four-hour wet-weather plan that costs no more than one palace ticket. On a Tuesday, when Gyeongbokgung closes, the folk museum on its own still justifies the trip, and in a downpour the walk between its gate and Anguk or Gyeongbokgung station is the only stretch outdoors.

Other palace days rearrange less neatly. Changdeokgung's halls are seen from their courtyards, and the Secret Garden's earth slopes turn slippery after rain, so if you already hold a garden ticket, keep your slot, wear shoes with grip and shelter afterward in Insadong's teahouses rather than adding Changgyeonggung. Deoksugung, open until 21:00, is the palace to save for the evening of a hot day, when its compact grounds have cooled; its Western-style stone hall, Seokjojeon, can be seen indoors on a guided session booked online in advance.

en.heading: Indoor performances: the Saturday concert and smaller stages
paragraphs: A traditional performance is one of the best uses of a wet afternoon, because music needs no translation. The National Gugak Center (국립국악원) in Seocho-gu runs its Saturday Gugak Concert (토요명품) every Saturday from 15:00 to 16:20, a sampler of court music, folk music and dance; the 2026 season runs to December 26, with A seats at 30,000 won and B seats at 20,000 won. Online booking closes at 18:00 the day before, so a rainy Saturday needs a decision on Friday, though leftover seats go on sale at the box office an hour before the show.

Closer to the palaces, Seoul's two municipal gugak halls share one website, sgtt.kr, which has an English option: Seoul Namsan Gugakdang, an underground hall beside Namsangol Hanok Village, and the smaller Seoul Donhwamun Gugakdang near Changdeokgung. Programs change week by week, so check each listing for running time, language and whether it is a rental production sold through another company. Our performance guide explains which forms, from court music to samulnori drumming, work best without any Korean.

en.heading: Teahouses and heated floors: staying warm, or cool, the Korean way
paragraphs: A traditional teahouse (전통찻집, jeontong chatjip) is the low-cost answer to a cold or wet afternoon in Insadong or Bukchon. Many seat you on floor cushions in hanok rooms, take an order of one drink per person and leave you alone for as long as you like. Order by the weather: yuja-cha, citron preserve stirred into hot water, or ginger tea when it is freezing; iced omija-cha, the sour-sweet 'five flavors' berry drink, when it is hot; and a pot of green tea in any season, brewed more than once. Search 전통찻집 in Naver Map or Kakao Map and check each listing's hours.

A jjimjilbang (찜질방) is the other Korean way through a freezing day. Beyond the single-sex baths, where everyone bathes nude, lies a shared floor where men and women in the provided T-shirt and shorts move between heated rooms, a snack bar and mats on a warm floor. Start in the gentler rooms before trying the hottest kiln room, drink water between rounds, and pair roasted eggs with sikhye, a sweet rice drink. On a heat-wave day the same place works in reverse, with the ice room and cold plunge as the attraction. Our jjimjilbang guide walks through the entry routine.

en.heading: Swaps by area, so every dash outside is short
paragraphs: The trick on a bad-weather day is to stay in one district. In Jongno, Gwangjang Market (광장시장) is a covered grid of arcades whose food street VisitKorea lists as open 09:00 to 23:00 all year, even on Sundays when the market's shops close; mung-bean bindaetteok with makgeolli under the arcade roof is the classic rainy-evening order. Nearby Insadong adds teahouses, galleries, the main hall of Jogyesa temple and Museum Kimchikan, a museum of kimchi culture open Tuesday to Sunday from 10:00 to 18:00, with last entry at 17:30.

Around Gwanghwamun, Gyeongbokgung and its two museums anchor the day, and the Seoul Museum of History, beside Gyeonghuigung palace to the west, is free and open 09:00 to 18:00, with Friday hours extended to 22:00. In Seochon, Tongin Market's covered lane fills a wet lunchtime. On the Namsan side, swap the summit walk for Namsangol's houses and a show at the underground Gugakdang, and in Yongsan the national museum covers the day on its own.

en.heading: Mondays and holidays: when the indoor plan fails
paragraphs: Monday is when a bad-weather plan most often breaks. Changdeokgung, Changgyeonggung and Deoksugung are closed, and so are several indoor sights: Museum Kimchikan and the Seoul Museum of History close every Monday, the National Palace Museum on the last Monday of the month, and the national museum's halls on the first Monday of March, June, September and December. What reliably opens on an ordinary Monday in the rain: the National Museum of Korea, Gyeongbokgung with its folk museum, Gwangjang's food street and a jjimjilbang.

Tuesday has its own trap, since Gyeongbokgung and Jongmyo close; put the folk museum, which opens on Tuesdays, or the national museum first. Holidays add more. The national museum closes on the Seollal and Chuseok days, and Museum Kimchikan for the whole of both holiday breaks, while the palaces stay open, opening even on their usual closing day when it falls on a holiday. A wet holiday is therefore best spent at a palace and its covered corners, then a bathhouse. The worked example below shows a wet Monday in October.
checklist: 09:30 Walk from Ichon Station through the underground path into the National Museum of Korea (not on the first Monday of March, June, September or December).
09:45 The Gyeongcheonsa pagoda in the central hall, then the Silla gold crown in the ancient galleries.
11:00 The Room of Quiet Contemplation, then the celadon and buncheong rooms if energy remains.
12:30 Lunch inside the museum.
14:00 The National Folk Museum's indoor halls on the Gyeongbokgung grounds; walk the palace axis only if the rain eases.
16:30 A traditional teahouse in Samcheong-dong or Insadong for ginger or citron tea.
18:30 Gwangjang Market's food street for bindaetteok and makgeolli under the arcade roof.

faq.q: Is the National Museum of Korea a good rainy-day choice?
faq.a: It is the best one in Seoul. An underground path links Ichon Station to the museum from 07:00 to 23:00, the permanent galleries are free, and the collection can fill a whole day. It opens 9:30 to 17:30, and until 21:00 on Wednesdays and Saturdays. Avoid the first Monday of March, June, September and December, when the halls close for maintenance.

faq.q: Do Seoul's palaces close when it rains?
faq.a: No. Palaces keep their normal hours in rain, and their courtyards are quieter under umbrellas. Outdoor programs such as guard ceremonies may be cancelled, and Jongmyo, which has nothing to go inside, is best left for a dry day. Pair a wet palace visit with an indoor museum nearby, such as the National Palace Museum at Gyeongbokgung's southwest corner.

faq.q: What is open on a rainy Monday?
faq.a: The National Museum of Korea (except on the first Monday of March, June, September and December), Gyeongbokgung with the National Folk Museum, the National Palace Museum except on the last Monday of the month, Gwangjang's food street and jjimjilbang bathhouses. Changdeokgung, Deoksugung, Museum Kimchikan and the Seoul Museum of History are closed on Mondays.

faq.q: Where can I see traditional music indoors at short notice?
faq.a: The National Gugak Center's Saturday Gugak Concert runs every Saturday at 15:00, but online booking closes at 18:00 the day before; leftover seats are sold at the box office from an hour before the show. On other days, check the listings for Seoul Namsan Gugakdang and Seoul Donhwamun Gugakdang on sgtt.kr, which has an English option.

faq.q: Is a jjimjilbang a good idea on a very hot day?
faq.a: Yes, if you use its cool side as much as its heat. In summer the ice room and the cold plunge are the attraction, and the shared floor is a calm place to sit out the hottest hours. Drink water between rounds, skip the hottest kiln rooms, and avoid alcohol beforehand, since heat and drinking are a bad mix.
