title.en: Free Korean Culture in Seoul: Palaces, Museums, Ceremonies and Walks

summary.en: Which Seoul palaces are free on Wednesdays, three free national museums, guard ceremonies, temples, Bukchon's 10-to-5 rule and a sample free culture day.

audience: Independent first-time visitors who want a full day of Korean culture in Seoul without entry fees, and want to know where each free rule has a catch.
method: Researched from the official sources listed below, checked on October 20, 2026. Hours, fees and booking rules can change; the linked official pages are the final word.
quickAnswer: Go on a Wednesday. Culture Day makes Changdeokgung's palace halls, Changgyeonggung, Deoksugung and Jongmyo free, though not Gyeongbokgung or the Secret Garden. Add a free national museum, the Gyeongbokgung guard ceremony, Jogyesa and a stretch of Cheonggyecheon or the city wall, and a full culture day costs you only lunch.

keyFacts.label: Free palace day
keyFacts.value: Every Wednesday (Culture Day); Gyeongbokgung and the Secret Garden excluded

keyFacts.label: Free at palaces any open day
keyFacts.value: Foreign visitors 18 and under or 65+ (show a passport) and hanbok wearers

keyFacts.label: Free-for-all windows
keyFacts.value: Announced on palace notice boards; in 2026 Seollal, Chuseok and Oct 29–Nov 15

keyFacts.label: Free national museums
keyFacts.value: National Museum of Korea (permanent galleries), National Palace Museum, National Folk Museum

keyFacts.label: Gyeongbokgung guard ceremony
keyFacts.value: 10:00 and 14:00, about 20 minutes; the palace closes on Tuesdays

keyFacts.label: Deoksugung guard ceremony
keyFacts.value: 11:00 and 14:00 at Daehanmun gate; none on Mondays

keyFacts.label: Bukchon red zone
keyFacts.value: Tourists 10:00–17:00 only; KRW 100,000 fine

keyFacts.label: Where free windows are posted
keyFacts.value: royal.khs.go.kr notice board, 공지사항 (search 무료)

en.heading: Wednesday opens the palaces, except Gyeongbokgung
paragraphs: Seoul's royal sites are inexpensive even at full price. An adult foreign visitor, which the fee table defines as ages 19 to 64, pays 3,000 won at Gyeongbokgung (경복궁) and Changdeokgung (창덕궁) and 1,000 won at Changgyeonggung (창경궁), Deoksugung (덕수궁) and Jongmyo Shrine (종묘). The free rules therefore matter less for the money than for the planning, because they decide which day suits which site. Three apply all year: a weekday rule, an age rule and a dress rule.

The weekday rule is Culture Day, 문화가 있는 날 (munhwaga inneun nal). The palace fee page now lists every Wednesday as free, so a blog that says only the last Wednesday of the month counts is out of date. Two exclusions catch people. Gyeongbokgung charges its normal fee on Wednesdays, and Changdeokgung's Secret Garden (후원, Huwon) keeps its paid, timed tours. Everything else in the system is free that day, including Changdeokgung's palace halls, and Wednesday is also one of Jongmyo's self-guided days rather than a timed-tour day.

The age rule covers foreign visitors aged 18 and under or 65 and over, and the dress rule covers anyone in hanbok (한복), Korean or foreign. Both work at Gyeongbokgung on any open day, Wednesdays included. The fee page states that visitors claiming free entry must show proof, so carry your passport if age is your reason. What counts as hanbok depends on the outfit's structure, not its style; our hanbok rental guide walks through what passes at the gate. The Secret Garden ignores both rules: its own free list covers children six and under and a few categories of Korean nationals.

One royal landmark is free on every open day without conditions. Sungnyemun (숭례문), the old south gate of the walled city, opens from 09:00 to 18:00 and closes on Mondays. Treat it as a fifteen-minute stop rather than a destination, but it is the simplest way to walk through one of the city's great gates without a ticket, and it sits on the way between Seoul Station and the City Hall area if you are heading to Deoksugung.

en.heading: Free-for-all windows, and how to spot the next one
paragraphs: On top of the weekly rules, the Korea Heritage Service's palace offices periodically open everything to everyone at no charge. In 2026 free windows were set for Seollal and Chuseok, covering most or all of the palaces, and for the Korea Grand Festival from October 29 to November 15, covering the four palaces, Jongmyo and the Joseon royal tombs. Regular closing days still apply during these windows, so Gyeongbokgung and Jongmyo close on Tuesdays and the others on Mondays, and the Secret Garden's tours stay paid.

The notice for that window, posted on September 22, shows how to read these announcements. One table listed three different things: an opening on the October 5 substitute holiday, openings on normal closing days during the palace culture festival from October 7 to 11, and the free period itself. Being open on a closing day is not the same as being free, so look for the word 무료 (muryo, free) in the row that covers your dates, not just in the headline.

To check for yourself, open the Royal Palaces and Tombs site (royal.khs.go.kr), go to the notice board, 공지사항 (gongjisahang), and filter by palace. The search terms that find these notices are 무료개방 (muryo gaebang, free opening) and 휴궁일 개방 (hyugungil gaebang, opening on a closing day). Holiday periods deserve a look too; our Seollal and Chuseok guide covers what opened over the 2026 holidays. If your trip overlaps a free window, spend the saving on the one thing that stays paid, a Secret Garden ticket, and expect more company everywhere else.

en.heading: Three national museums with free permanent galleries
paragraphs: The National Museum of Korea (국립중앙박물관, Gungnip Jungang Bangmulgwan) in Yongsan charges nothing for its permanent galleries; only special exhibitions have tickets. It opens from 09:30 to 17:30, until 21:00 on Wednesdays and Saturdays, and admission closes 30 minutes before closing time. Check the museum's notice board for gallery closures before you plan a route. Our National Museum guide builds a visit around what is open.

The National Palace Museum of Korea (국립고궁박물관, Gungnip Gogung Bangmulgwan), at the southwest corner of the Gyeongbokgung grounds, holds the court's own objects and is free. It opens from 09:30 to 17:30, until 21:00 on Saturdays and the last Wednesday of each month, and closes on January 1, Seollal, Chuseok and the last Monday of each month. On weekdays a free English tour starts at 14:00 at the Kings of the Joseon Dynasty gallery on the second floor and lasts about an hour. It is the natural follow-up to a palace visit, because it shows the furnishings the empty halls lack.

The National Folk Museum of Korea (국립민속박물관, Gungnip Minsok Bangmulgwan), on the palace's northeast side, covers how ordinary Koreans lived and marked the year, and all of its exhibitions are free. From March to October it opens from 09:00 to 18:00, until 20:00 on Wednesdays; from November to February it closes at 17:00, and entry always ends an hour before closing. The outdoor buildings' interiors close to visitors on weekends and public holidays.

Do not try all three in one day. Choose by the question you have: the palace museum if you want to know what the king's rooms held, the folk museum if you want the customs behind weddings, holidays and ancestral rites, and the National Museum if you have a rainy half day and want the long arc from prehistory to Joseon. The National Museum sits in Yongsan, away from the palace district, so give it its own morning or a late Wednesday or Saturday.

en.heading: Guard ceremonies, drills and a Sunday patrol to Insadong
paragraphs: The Korea Heritage Agency stages the changing of the royal gate guard, 수문장 교대의식 (sumunjang gyodae uisik), at Gyeongbokgung at 10:00 and 14:00, about 20 minutes each time. It also runs a shorter Gwanghwamun watch ceremony, 광화문 파수의식 (Gwanghwamun pasu uisik), at 11:00 and 13:00, and a 15-minute public drill at 09:35 and 13:35. All of it happens in the squares in front of Gwanghwamun and Heungnyemun gates, before the ticket barrier, so it costs nothing to watch. The palace itself closes on Tuesdays, so plan the ceremony for another day.

In spring and autumn the guards also leave their posts. From March to May and from September to November, on Saturdays, Sundays and public holidays between 15:00 and 16:00, a patrol procession, 순라의식 (sulla uisik), sets out with its musicians. On Saturdays it stays inside Gyeongbokgung; on Sundays and holidays it starts at the stone platform in front of Gwanghwamun and walks to Insadong's culture street, and you can photograph it along the way. Protests or road conditions can move the street route back inside the palace, so treat it as a likely bonus rather than a fixed appointment.

Deoksugung has its own ceremony, run by the Seoul Metropolitan Government in front of Daehanmun (대한문) gate opposite City Hall, at 11:00 and 14:00 every day except Monday. It is free and takes place outside the palace's ticket gate. The Gyeongbokgung organizers ask spectators not to walk between the ranks, not to touch the guards' ceremonial gear or talk to them while posing for photos, and to keep the noise down; the same courtesy suits Daehanmun. One ceremony is enough for most visitors, so watch whichever stands at the palace you are visiting anyway.

en.heading: Temples and a hanok village that charge nothing at the gate
paragraphs: Jogyesa (조계사), the chief temple of the Jogye Order, which represents mainstream Korean Seon (Zen) Buddhism, stands in central Jongno a short walk from Insadong. Entry is free, and its main hall is open 24 hours a day to locals and foreigners alike. The courtyard asks nothing of you; inside a hall, take your shoes off, use a side door, keep your voice low and never photograph people at prayer. Our guide to Seoul's Buddhist temples explains the bows and why the center door is reserved for monks.

Bongeunsa (봉은사), just north of the COEX complex in Gangnam, is the counterpart south of the river. VisitKorea dates its founding to 794, and its halls climb a wooded slope with office towers behind them. The grounds are open from 05:00 to 22:00 every day and admission is free. Choose Jogyesa if your free day is in the palace district, Bongeunsa if you are staying in Gangnam or want the contrast of temple eaves against glass.

Namsangol Hanok Village (남산골한옥마을, Namsangol Hanok Maeul), below Namsan, is the free place to walk into the hanok courtyards that Bukchon's private homes keep closed. Entry costs nothing. The houses open Tuesday to Sunday, from 09:00 to 21:00 between April and November and to 20:00 from December to March, and stay shut on Mondays unless the Monday is a public or substitute holiday; the traditional garden is open around the clock. Commentary tours of 40 to 60 minutes need no booking for individuals, who join at the guide office by the main gate. English sessions run at 14:00 and 15:30 from Tuesday to Friday, for ages ten and up.

en.heading: Bukchon, Seochon and the Naksan wall on foot
paragraphs: Bukchon (북촌), the hanok neighborhood between Gyeongbokgung and Changdeokgung, has no ticket, but it does have hours. The red zone around Bukchon-ro 11-gil (북촌로11길), about 34,000 square meters, is closed to tourist visits from 17:00 to 10:00 the next morning, and since March 1, 2025 breaking that rule can bring a fine of 100,000 won. The orange and yellow zones around it carry no hour limit, but they are residential streets too. Walk through between 10:00 and noon on a weekday, quietly, and you will see it at its best.

West of the palace, Seochon (서촌) is the quieter counterpart: public lanes of urban hanok and small studios, Tongin Market, and Suseongdong Valley (수성동계곡) at the foot of Inwangsan, all of it free to walk. It makes a good second neighborhood when Bukchon's main lanes feel crowded, though the same courtesy applies, since these are homes as well. Our Seochon guide sequences the stops and notes which of its small museums close on Mondays.

For a walk with history underfoot, take the Naksan (낙산) section of the Seoul City Wall, 서울 한양도성 (Seoul Hanyangdoseong). The official trail runs 3.2 kilometers from Hyehwamun gate to Heunginjimun, the great east gate, in about an hour on a gentle slope, and it is open 24 hours. Start five minutes from Hyehwa Station Exit 1 and finish near Dongdaemun Station, where stones along the wall at Dongdaemun Seonggwak Park carry inscriptions naming the counties that built each stretch or, in later repairs, the supervisors and master builders. Parts of the route pass through residential villages, so keep your voice down after dark.

en.heading: Cheonggyecheon: a free corridor through the old city
paragraphs: Cheonggyecheon (청계천) is the stream that once ran through the walled city and was later covered over, with a highway overpass built on top. Seoul demolished the covering structures and the overpass and restored a 5.84-kilometer stretch, from the Taepyeong-ro end at Cheonggye Plaza to the Sindap railway bridge, in works that ran from July 2003 to September 2005. Today it is a sunken path with water at your feet and the city's traffic one level up, free and open to anyone.

Use it as a connector rather than a destination. From Cheonggye Plaza the path runs east toward Jongno 5-ga, where Gwangjang Market's food alley makes a natural lunch stop; our Gwangjang guide covers how its counter stalls work. You can climb out at most bridges to reach Jogyesa, Insadong or Jongmyo to the north. In the evening, walk the first stretch and come back west: Cheonggye Plaza is a short walk from City Hall and Deoksugung, which stays open until 21:00.

en.heading: Every free option, and the catch that comes with it
paragraphs: The table pulls the options together. Closing days cause more wasted trips than fees do, so read the last column before you fix a day, and check the linked official pages for anything that falls on or near a public holiday, when palaces and museums often change their normal schedules.

en.heading: A free culture Wednesday, hour by hour
paragraphs: Wednesday is the strongest day for a free itinerary: Culture Day covers most of the palace system, the National Museum stays open until 21:00, and from March to October the Folk Museum stays open until 20:00. This plan suits spring or autumn. From November to January, Changdeokgung's last entry is at 16:30 and daylight goes early, so do not let lunch run long. The only thing you pay for is lunch.

Two swaps cover most situations. On a rainy Wednesday, replace the stream and Deoksugung with the National Museum of Korea, open late. If you are under 19, over 64 or in hanbok, the same day works at Gyeongbokgung itself on any day except Tuesday: go inside after the ceremony, then take the National Folk Museum in place of Changdeokgung after lunch.
checklist: 09:35 Gyeongbokgung forecourt: the public drill, then the 10:00 guard-changing ceremony (about 20 minutes).
10:30 National Palace Museum at the southwest corner of the grounds: an hour in the royal galleries.
11:45 Walk east through Bukchon, inside the red zone's 10:00–17:00 window, keeping your voice down.
12:45 Lunch near Anguk Station, the day's one expense.
13:45 Changdeokgung's palace halls, free on Wednesdays (the Secret Garden is not).
15:30 Walk south to Jogyesa; look into the main hall from the doorway or sit quietly at the side.
16:30 Cheonggye Plaza, then the stream path east for half an hour and back.
18:00 Deoksugung, free on Wednesdays and open until 21:00 (last entry 20:00), as the light fades.

en.heading: Where free ends up costing you
paragraphs: The common mistakes are about days rather than money. Visitors arrive at Gyeongbokgung on a Wednesday expecting Culture Day, plan a palace Monday when Changdeokgung, Changgyeonggung and Deoksugung are all shut, or assume a Secret Garden slot is included on a free day. Others leave the passport at the hotel and pay the adult fee at a gate where their age would have got them in. Read the closing days first, then the free rules.

The other cost is time. Seoul's free sites fall into separate clusters, the palace district, Yongsan and Gangnam, and crossing between them eats more of a day than any ticket saves. Build the day around one cluster, take free entry where it falls, and pay the 1,000 or 3,000 won when a paid site is the better choice. Do not rent hanbok just to save a palace fee either: the rental costs many times more. A 5,000-won Secret Garden ticket on a free Wednesday is still money well spent.

faq.q: Is Gyeongbokgung free on Wednesdays?
faq.a: No. Culture Day makes the other palaces and Jongmyo free every Wednesday, but Gyeongbokgung is specifically excluded, as is the Secret Garden at Changdeokgung. You still enter Gyeongbokgung free if you are a foreign visitor aged 18 or under or 65 or over, if you wear hanbok, or during a free-for-all window announced on the palace notice boards.

faq.q: Do I need ID for free palace entry by age?
faq.a: Yes. The palace fee page says visitors claiming free entry must show proof, and for a foreign visitor that means a passport showing you are 18 or under or 65 or over. Without it, expect to pay the adult fee of 1,000 or 3,000 won, depending on the palace.

faq.q: Are Seoul's national museums really free?
faq.a: Their permanent galleries are. The National Museum of Korea charges only for special exhibitions, and the National Palace Museum and National Folk Museum charge for nothing. Each has its own closing days and current renovation closures, so check its official site for the week you visit.

faq.q: When are the palaces free for everyone?
faq.a: Only during windows the heritage service announces on each palace's notice board at royal.khs.go.kr. In 2026 they were set for Seollal, Chuseok and October 29 to November 15, with regular closing days and the Secret Garden excepted, and the autumn window was posted five weeks before it began.

faq.q: Can I watch a royal guard ceremony without buying a ticket?
faq.a: Yes. At Gyeongbokgung the ceremony takes place in front of Gwanghwamun and Heungnyemun, before the ticket barrier, at 10:00 and 14:00. At Deoksugung it runs in front of Daehanmun gate at 11:00 and 14:00 every day except Monday. Both are free.

faq.q: Can I walk around Bukchon in the evening?
faq.a: Not in the red zone around Bukchon-ro 11-gil, which is closed to tourist visits from 17:00 to 10:00, with a 100,000-won fine for breaking the rule. Plan Bukchon for late morning and spend the evening at Deoksugung or Changgyeonggung, which stay open until 21:00.

title.en: How to Read a Korean Menu: Dish Names, Portions, Spice and Allergens

summary.en: Read a Hangul menu: the cooking-method endings in dish names, portion words like 인분 and 공기밥, spice cues, set meals, restaurant types and how to ask about fish broth.

audience: Visitors who cannot read Korean yet and want to order confidently in ordinary Seoul restaurants, including travelers with allergies or vegetarian diets.
method: Researched from the official sources listed below, checked on October 20, 2026. Hours, fees and booking rules can change; the linked official pages are the final word.
quickAnswer: Most Korean dish names are an ingredient followed by a cooking method, so about fifteen endings, such as 찌개 (stew), 구이 (grilled), 볶음 (stir-fried) and 전 (pancake), let you read most of a menu. Check the portion words 인분 and 2인분 이상, ask 이거 매워요? before ordering, and assume kimchi and clear broths may contain seafood until someone tells you otherwise.

keyFacts.label: How dish names work
keyFacts.value: Ingredient + cooking method: 고등어 + 구이 = grilled mackerel

keyFacts.label: Soup words
keyFacts.value: 국/탕 = more broth; 찌개 = less broth, thicker; 전골 = shared hot pot

keyFacts.label: Portion word

en.heading: Most dish names are an ingredient plus a cooking method
paragraphs: A Korean menu looks impenetrable until you notice that most dish names are built the same way: what goes in, then how it is cooked. 고등어구이 (godeungeo gui) is mackerel plus grilled. 오징어볶음 (ojingeo bokkeum) is squid, stir-fried. 김치찌개 (gimchi jjigae) is kimchi stew, and 갈비찜 (galbijjim) is braised short ribs. Read the last syllable or two first, because the ending tells you the format of the dish: how much liquid it has, whether it is grilled, fried or simmered, and roughly how it will arrive at the table.

Modifiers go in front. 매운 (maeun) means spicy, 해물 (haemul) seafood, 돼지 (dwaeji) pork, 소고기 (sogogi) beef, 닭 (dak) chicken, 버섯 (beoseot) mushroom and 두부 (dubu) tofu. So 해물파전 (haemul pajeon) is a seafood and green-onion pancake, and 버섯전골 (beoseot jeongol) a mushroom hot pot. Some names are fixed phrases that ignore the pattern, and the standard dictionary admits as much: 매운탕 (maeuntang) ends in tang, a word for soup, yet the dictionary defines it as a spicy stew with chili paste stirred in, the category Koreans call jjigae.

Menus are usually grouped by purpose. 식사 (siksa) means meals, the rice and noodle dishes that make a lunch or dinner; 안주 (anju), which the dictionary defines as food eaten with alcohol, means plates meant to go with drinks, usually shared. 주류 (juryu) is alcohol and 음료 (eumnyo) soft drinks. Small restaurants often post the whole menu on the wall, with 추천 (chucheon, recommended) or 대표 메뉴 (daepyo menyu, signature dish) marking what the kitchen is proud of. A short menu is usually a sign of focus, not a lack of choice.

en.heading: Fifteen endings that tell you how a dish is cooked
paragraphs: These endings cover most of what appears on an ordinary menu, and the soup family needs the most care. The Encyclopedia of Korean Culture separates boiled dishes by how much liquid they hold: 국 (guk) and 탕 (tang) have plenty of broth, while 찌개 (jjigae) has less and is seasoned with soybean paste or chili paste, so it is thicker, more strongly seasoned and meant to be eaten with rice. The standard dictionary lists tang as the honorific form of guk, and in practice tang tends to name heartier soups such as 갈비탕 (galbitang) and 삼계탕 (samgyetang).

Two other pairs confuse newcomers. 찜 (jjim) covers both steaming and cooking in very little liquid, so 갈비찜 is a glossy braise rather than a steamed dish. 조림 (jorim) means simmering something down until almost no liquid remains, which gives the sweet, salty glaze of 감자조림 (gamja jorim), braised potatoes. 전골 (jeongol) differs from 찌개 mainly in how it is served: ingredients arranged in a wide pot with a little broth, often finished on a burner at your table, and meant for sharing.

en.heading: Ingredient words, including the ones that surprise people
paragraphs: A handful of nouns covers most proteins: 돼지고기 (dwaejigogi, pork), 소고기 (sogogi, beef), 한우 (hanu, Korean native beef), 닭 (dak, chicken), 오리 (ori, duck), 생선 (saengseon, fish), 오징어 (ojingeo, squid), 낙지 (nakji, small octopus), 새우 (saeu, shrimp), 조개 (jogae, clams) and 굴 (gul, oysters). For vegetables and staples, learn 두부 (dubu, tofu), 버섯 (beoseot, mushroom), 감자 (gamja, potato), 콩나물 (kongnamul, soybean sprouts), 나물 (namul, seasoned greens) and 계란 (gyeran, egg).

Then there is a short list of words for cuts and dishes that many visitors would rather know about in advance: 순대 (sundae, blood sausage), 곱창 (gopchang, small intestines), 선지 (seonji, congealed blood), 내장 (naejang, offal), 족발 (jokbal, braised pig's trotters) and 홍어 (hongeo, skate, often fermented). These are prized dishes, not traps, and several are worth trying. If you would rather not, these are the words to scan for.

Many menus also carry a small origin panel, 원산지 (wonsanji), listing where the main ingredients come from; our barbecue guide explains how to read it for beef and pork. Do not assume a familiar word settles the dish, either: 갈비 (galbi) simply means ribs, so look for 소 (so, beef) or 돼지 (dwaeji, pork) in front of it before you order.

en.heading: Reading the heat before it reaches the table
paragraphs: Spice is usually announced in the name or the ingredients. Look for 매운 (maeun, spicy), 얼큰한 (eolkeunhan, hot in a warming, hearty way) and 칼칼한 (kalkalhan, sharply hot), and for the ingredients that carry the heat: 고추장 (gochujang, chili paste), 고춧가루 (gochutgaru, chili flakes) and 청양고추 (Cheongyang gochu, a small, very hot green chili). Mild cues are 순한맛 (sunhanmat, mild flavor), 맑은 (malgeun, clear, meaning a broth without chili) and 백김치 (baekgimchi, white kimchi made without chili flakes).

Some places print heat levels, often under 맵기 조절 (maepgi jojeol, adjustable heat), with steps such as 순한맛, 보통 (botong, regular) and 매운맛 (maeunmat, spicy). If chili heat is new to you, order one step milder than you think you need, because the regular level is set for local tastes. Red color is not a perfect guide either: chili flakes can be mild, and a pale broth can hide sliced green chilies.

To ask, say 이거 매워요? (igeo maewoyo?, is this spicy?) before you order, not after it arrives. Then 덜 맵게 해 주세요 (deol maepge hae juseyo) asks for less heat and 안 맵게 해 주세요 (an maepge hae juseyo) for none. A kitchen cannot take the chili out of a dish whose sauce is built on it, such as tteokbokki or jeyuk bokkeum, so for those the honest answer may be no. Choose a clear soup instead: 설렁탕 (seolleongtang), 갈비탕 and 삼계탕 all arrive without chili.

en.heading: Portions, rice and the small print around the price
paragraphs: Grilled meat and many stews are sold by the portion, 인분 (inbun). A sign reading 2인분 이상 (iinbun isang) means the kitchen will not cook fewer than two portions per order. The Korea JoongAng Daily found diners turned away when eating alone at barbecue and kimchi-stew restaurants, and the Fair Trade Commission told the paper this is the owner's decision. Look for 1인분 가능 (irinbun ganeung) or 1인 가능 (irin ganeung), which welcome solo orders. Shared dishes often come in 소, 중 and 대 (so, jung, dae: small, medium, large); ask 몇 인분이에요? (myeot inbunieyo?) to learn how many each size feeds.

Rice is a separate line more often than visitors expect. 공기밥 (gonggibap) is a bowl of steamed rice, ordered when a dish does not include it, typically with grilled meat or a shared stew. The standard dictionary spells it 공깃밥, with an extra ㅅ, but nearly every menu writes 공기밥, and both mean the same bowl. 사리 (sari), which the dictionary defines as a coiled bundle of noodles, is the add-in you drop into a stew or hot pot: 라면사리 (ramyeon sari) for instant noodles, 우동사리 (udong sari) for thick wheat noodles. 추가 (chuga) means extra, as in 치즈 추가 (chijeu chuga), add cheese.

Two price rules work in your favor. Seoul's food safety office requires restaurants to show the final price, with VAT and any service charge included, so the menu price is what you pay and no tip is expected. Meat for the grill must be priced per 100 grams, with any per-portion price shown beside its weight. Watch for 시가 (siga), which the dictionary defines as market price: on a seafood menu it means the price moves with the day's catch, so ask before ordering. 곱빼기 (gopppaegi) at a noodle shop is a double portion in one bowl.

en.heading: Which kind of restaurant you have walked into
paragraphs: The sign outside tells you how to order before you see a menu. A 분식집 (bunsikjip) is a snack shop; the dictionary defines 분식 as food made from flour, and the menu runs to gimbap, tteokbokki, ramyeon and dumplings, ordered by the item and eaten fast. A 국밥집 (gukbapjip) serves soup with rice, one bowl per person, which makes it the simplest solo meal in Seoul. A 고깃집 (gogitjip) is a barbecue house with grills at the table and, often, portion minimums.

At the formal end, 한정식 (hanjeongsik), which the dictionary describes as a set meal of many dishes based on the traditional Korean table, arrives as a full spread; check whether the listed price is per person or per table before you sit. The everyday cousin is 정식 (jeongsik), a main dish with a fixed set of side dishes. The dictionary notes that its price depends on how many side dishes come with it, which is why one menu can list two or three grades of the same 정식.

포장마차 (pojangmacha) shows how a word drifts: its first dictionary sense is a canvas-covered wagon, but on the street it means a tented stall or small bar where the menu is mostly 안주 to share over soju. Order one or two plates for the table rather than one dish each. The same rule suits most places with an anju section: dishes there are sized for the group.

en.heading: Allergies, vegetarian diets and the seafood you cannot see
paragraphs: Labeling will not do the work for you. Under the enforcement decree of Korea's special act on children's dietary safety, the duty to display allergen information falls on franchise chains with 50 or more outlets, for the children's foods the law covers. A neighborhood stew house or market stall is not required to post anything. Plan to ask, and carry your allergen written in Korean: 땅콩 (ttangkong, peanut), 호두 (hodu, walnut), 잣 (jat, pine nut), 밀 (mil, wheat), 메밀 (memil, buckwheat), 대두 (daedu, soybean), 우유 (uyu, milk), 계란 (gyeran, egg), 새우 (saeu, shrimp), 게 (ge, crab), 조개 (jogae, shellfish) or 참깨 (chamkkae, sesame).

Some risks are built into the cuisine. UNESCO's description of kimjang, the kimchi-making tradition, describes kimchi as vegetables seasoned with spices and fermented seafood, so ordinary kimchi is rarely vegetarian. The words to know are 젓갈 (jeotgal, salted fermented seafood), 액젓 (aekjeot, the fish sauce strained from it) and 새우젓 (saeujeot, salted shrimp). Clear soups are not safe by default either: VisitKorea describes Gwangjang Market's knife-cut noodles as served in clear anchovy broth, and 멸치 (myeolchi) means anchovy. 메밀 in a name, as in 메밀국수 (memil guksu), signals buckwheat, and the encyclopedia lists barley among the grains used to make gochujang.

A few sentences cover most situations: 저는 고기를 안 먹어요 (jeoneun gogireul an meogeoyo, I don't eat meat), 이거 고기 들어가요? (igeo gogi deureogayo?, is there meat in this?), 육수는 뭘로 만들어요? (yuksuneun mwollo mandeureoyo?, what is the stock made from?) and, after your allergen, 알레르기가 있어요 (allereugiga isseoyo, I have an allergy). Ask about fish and anchovy separately, because a dish can be free of meat and still use a seafood stock or fish sauce.

For strict vegetarians, the most reliable option is temple cuisine: search 사찰음식 (sachal eumsik) on a map app for restaurants specializing in it, a tradition the Korea Herald describes as plant-based and rooted in respect for all life. Otherwise, choose dishes you can strip down, such as bibimbap with 고기하고 계란 빼 주세요 (gogihago gyeran ppae juseyo, without meat and egg), and leave the kimchi aside. Our Buddhist temples guide explains where temple food comes from.

en.heading: Why the English spelling on a menu rarely matches
paragraphs: English menus in Seoul mix several spelling systems, which is why one dish can appear as kimchi, gimchi or kimchee. This guide uses the Revised Romanization of Korean, the official system published by the National Institute of Korean Language. It spells by pronunciation rather than letter by letter. An initial ㄱ is written g, so 김치 becomes gimchi, though kimchi is the established English word and you will see both. A final ㄱ, ㄷ or ㅂ becomes k, t or p, and sounds that change where syllables meet are written as heard, so 국물 (broth) is gungmul.

Two more rules explain the oddities. Tense sounds that arise inside compound words are not marked, so 공기밥 is gonggibap even though it sounds closer to gonggi-ppap, and 떡볶이 is tteokbokki. A hyphen may be added where syllables could split two ways, which is why some guides, ours included, write 두 명이요 as du myeong-iyo. If the romanization on a sign does not match this guide letter for letter, sound it out, since pronunciation is what staff recognize. Better still, point at the Hangul.

en.heading: Ordering at a stew restaurant, start to finish
paragraphs: Here is how a weeknight dinner for two runs at a neighborhood restaurant serving stews and pancakes. Staff ask 몇 분이세요? (myeot buniseyo?, how many?); you answer 두 명이요 and sit where they point. Read the wall: 식사 on one side, 안주 on the other. You want kimchi stew and a pancake, so you call 저기요 (jeogiyo) and point: 김치찌개 2인분하고 해물파전 하나 주세요 (gimchi jjigae iinbunhago haemul pajeon hana juseyo), two portions of kimchi stew and one seafood pancake.

Before the order goes in, ask 이거 많이 매워요? (igeo mani maewoyo?, is this very spicy?) and add 덜 맵게 해 주세요 if needed. If the stew arrives with rice in steel bowls, you are set; if not, order 공기밥 두 개 (gonggibap du gae), two bowls of rice. Halfway through, 라면사리 추가해 주세요 (ramyeon sari chugahae juseyo) adds noodles to the pot. Finish with 계산해 주세요 (gyesanhae juseyo) at the counter and 잘 먹었습니다 (jal meogeotseumnida) on the way out. Our table manners guide covers the courtesies in between.

faq.q: What is the difference between jjigae, guk and tang?
faq.a: In the Encyclopedia of Korean Culture's account, guk and tang are boiled dishes with plenty of broth, while jjigae has less broth and is seasoned with soybean paste or chili paste, so it is thicker and saltier. The standard dictionary treats tang as the honorific word for guk. Names are not always consistent: maeuntang is defined as a jjigae despite its name.

faq.q: How do I ask for food that is not spicy?
faq.a: Ask 이거 매워요? (igeo maewoyo?, is this spicy?) before ordering, then 덜 맵게 해 주세요 (deol maepge hae juseyo) for less heat or 안 맵게 해 주세요 (an maepge hae juseyo) for none. If the sauce is built on chili paste, the kitchen may not be able to change it, so pick a clear soup such as galbitang or seolleongtang.

faq.q: Is kimchi vegetarian?
faq.a: Usually not. UNESCO's description of the kimjang tradition presents kimchi as vegetables seasoned with spices and fermented seafood, such as salted shrimp or anchovies. Temple-cuisine restaurants, which cook plant-based food, are the likeliest places to find kimchi without seafood. To check, ask 젓갈 들어가요? (jeotgal deureogayo?), meaning 'does it contain salted seafood?'

faq.q: Do Korean restaurants list allergens on the menu?
faq.a: Only some are required to. The legal duty to display allergen information applies to franchise chains with 50 or more outlets, for the children's foods covered by the law. Independent restaurants and market stalls have no such duty, so ask directly and show your allergen written in Korean.

faq.q: What does 공기밥 mean on a menu?
faq.a: A bowl of steamed rice, ordered separately when a dish does not come with rice, as at barbecue houses or with a shared stew. The standard dictionary spells it 공깃밥, but menus nearly always write 공기밥, romanized gonggibap. Say 공기밥 하나 주세요 (gonggibap hana juseyo) for one bowl.

faq.q: Why does a menu say 2인분 이상?
faq.a: It means the minimum order is two portions, which is common at barbecue and stew restaurants. Turning away solo diners is the owner's call under Korean fair-trade rules. Look for 1인분 가능 or 1인 가능 if you are eating alone, choose a soup-and-rice or snack shop, or simply order two portions.

title.en: K-Drama Filming Locations in Seoul: Verified Spots Grouped Into Walks

summary.en: Seoul drama and film locations checked against city and tourism-board sources, grouped into six walks with Hangul map searches, Bukchon hours and palace photo rules.

audience: Drama and film fans on a first or second Seoul trip who want to stand where scenes were shot without trespassing, disturbing residents or chasing unconfirmed fan lists.
method: Researched from the official sources listed below, checked on October 20, 2026. Hours, fees and booking rules can change; the linked official pages are the final word.
quickAnswer: The most rewarding drama locations in Seoul are free public places: the Deoksugung stone-wall road (My Love from the Star, Reborn Rich), Gamgodang-gil in Bukchon (Our Beloved Summer), the city wall at Naksan Park (KPop Demon Hunters, Doona!) and the Noksapyeong overpass and Baekbeom Square (Itaewon Class). Group them by neighborhood, type the Hangul names into Naver Map, and treat schools and homes as views from the street.

en.heading: What a filming location can give you, and what it cannot
paragraphs: Seoul is the backdrop for a large share of Korean television, and the same palaces, stone walls and footbridges reappear across decades of series. That makes the city rewarding for fans, and it also makes it a place where fan-made lists repeat each other's mistakes. Every drama and location pairing in this guide comes from Seoul Metropolitan Government, the Korea Tourism Organization's VisitKorea, the Seoul Tourism Organization's Visit Seoul or the city's own news service. When official pages disagree about a spot, as they do about which Itaewon building played the pub Danbam in Itaewon Class, we leave it out.

The best locations share three traits: they are public, they still look like the screen, and they sit near other things worth your time. A city-wall rampart, a stone-walled street or a pedestrian overpass passes all three tests. Restaurants and cafés from older series often fail the second, because businesses change hands and interiors are sometimes built in a studio. Schools and private homes fail the first. Photograph those from the street, briefly, and move on.

Seoul's own answer to scattered fan lists is SOUL SPOT (소울스팟), a map of drama, film and K-pop locations run by the city government's tourism industry division, with spoken commentary you can play on your phone in English, Korean, Japanese or Chinese. In October 2026 its English site featured 20 spots, from Naksan Park for Doona! and Jeongdong-gil for Gyeongseong Creature Season 2 to Hyoja-ro, the road along Gyeongbokgung's west side, for When Life Gives You Tangerines. The city has also put up clapperboard-style plaques at some of them, which make a tidy photo frame of their own.

en.heading: Verified pairs, and the Hangul to type into Naver Map
paragraphs: English place names often fail in Korean map apps, so the middle column gives the search term to paste into Naver Map or Kakao Map. The last column tells you which of the walks below each place belongs to. Scenes are described only where an official source describes them; for the rest, the source confirms the location but not the moment, so you will have to match the frame from memory.

en.heading: Anguk to Samcheong-dong: Goblin's alleys, a 1913 mansion and a school gate
paragraphs: Start at Anguk Station on Line 3. Visit Seoul's Goblin walk begins beside Unhyeongung (운현궁), where an early modern Western-style building served as the Goblin's private house; frame it from the surrounding grounds and street rather than expecting to walk in. The same feature places Eun-tak's first meeting with the Goblin in a stone-walled alley near the station, and their many dates in the café and boutique lanes of Samcheong-dong. Treat those two as atmospheres rather than exact frames: the walls, not one particular stone, are the point.

Cross toward Bukchon for Baek In-je House (백인제가옥) at 16 Bukchon-ro 7-gil, which Visit Seoul lists as a Reborn Rich location. Built in 1913 by Han Sang-ryong of Hanseong Bank and opened as a museum by Seoul in 2015, it is run by the Seoul Museum of History. The courtyard and exteriors are free to see from 9:00 to 18:00 (last entry 17:30), closed Mondays unless a holiday and on January 1. The rooms open only on guided tours booked through Seoul's public reservation site; the English tour runs on Fridays at 16:00. From Anguk Exit 2, walk about 500 meters toward the Constitutional Court.

Choong Ang High School (중앙고등학교), at 164 Changdeokgung-gil, is the school Choi Ung and Kook Yeon-soo attended in Our Beloved Summer, according to VisitKorea, and Seoul's news service lists it among Lovely Runner's locations. It is a working school: photograph the gate from outside and leave. Lovely Runner also used Bokjeong Well (복정우물), where Sol appears in a monk's robes trying to change Sun-jae's fate; the city's report places it in Bukchon beside the old Korea bathhouse building (코리아목욕탕). Search the Hangul names and let the map pick the lane.

Finish downhill on Gamgodang-gil (감고당길) in Anguk-dong, which VisitKorea identifies in Our Beloved Summer's last episode and in a flashback of the pair getting drunk. The narrow alley where Yeon-soo carries Ung on her back is Yunboseon-gil (윤보선길), opening off the middle of Gamgodang-gil. It is a short loop back to Anguk Station, which makes this the most efficient drama walk in the city: six locations and four series in about two hours.

Timing matters because the route crosses Bukchon. Seoul's red zone on Bukchon-ro 11-gil admits tourists only from 10:00 to 17:00, and an officer can fine you KRW 100,000 if you stay after being warned. Start at 10:00 on a Tuesday to Friday: Baek In-je House closes on Mondays, and Seoul asks visitors to give Bukchon's alleys a rest on Sundays. Be out of the red zone well before 17:00. Our Bukchon guide explains the zones in full.

en.heading: Jeong-dong: three series on one curve of the Deoksugung wall
paragraphs: The road that curves along Deoksugung's stone wall (덕수궁 돌담길) is the most dependable drama street in Seoul, because it changes so little from one decade to the next. Visit Seoul identifies it as the place where Do Min-joon walks with his lawyer friend Jang and takes a call from Cheon Song-yi in My Love from the Star. The city's tourism site lists it for Reborn Rich, and Seoul's news service names it among the locations of Chief Detective 1958. Begin at City Hall Station on Lines 1 and 2; Visit Seoul directs walkers to Exits 11 and 12 for the Seoul Museum of Art, which stands beside the road.

Follow the wall west onto Jeongdong-gil (정동길), a SOUL SPOT for Gyeongseong Creature Season 2, and keep going to Gyeonghuigung (경희궁) at 45 Saemunan-ro. In Kingdom, its throne hall Sungjeongjeon stood in for Gangnyeongjeon, the quarters of the zombie-stricken king, and the boulder called Seoam at the back of the palace is where the young Crown Prince Lee Chang hid and was found by Lord Ahn Hyeon. Gyeonghuigung is free, open Tuesday to Sunday from 9:00 to 18:00 and closed on Mondays.

Gyeonghuigung is also the easiest palace in Seoul in which to compose a period-drama shot without a crowd, because few visitors know it. For the stone-wall road, come early on a weekday if you want the curve empty, or late afternoon for warmer light on the wall. Avoid Mondays for this walk, since Gyeonghuigung is closed that day.

en.heading: Kingdom in the royal palaces, and the costume rule
paragraphs: Kingdom is the most useful historical series for a location hunt because it filmed in sites you can enter on an ordinary ticket. Visit Seoul records that Crown Prince Lee Chang's first appearance, kneeling at what the drama calls Gyotaejeon, was shot at Tongmyeongjeon, once the queen's bedchamber, in Changgyeonggung; that the Secret Garden of Changdeokgung appears several times, with its Gwallamji pond as the place where bodies were hidden; and that in season 2 Seo-bi rescues the queen's baby during a zombie attack at Jeongjeon, the main hall of Jongmyo Shrine.

Plan around the calendar. Changdeokgung and Changgyeonggung close on Mondays and Jongmyo on Tuesdays, and the Secret Garden can be seen only on a capped, timed tour with its own ticket. Our guides to Changdeokgung's Secret Garden, Jongmyo and the five grand palaces cover booking, guided-only days and fees, so check them before building a Kingdom day around Gwallamji.

Recreating a scene has limits. Under the visiting rules of the Korea Heritage Service's royal palaces office, ordinary souvenir photos count as already permitted, but shoots using character costumes, mascot suits or similar non-everyday outfits and props need a permit, because they disrupt other visitors and the dignity of the site. Filming for dramas, films or advertising is commercial and needs a paid permit, and drones are limited to approved public-interest work. Hanbok is everyday dress here and fine; a full costume with prop sword or zombie makeup is not.

en.heading: Naksan Park and the city wall: KPop Demon Hunters after dark
paragraphs: Naksan Park (낙산공원) sits on the ridge where the old city wall climbs east of Daehangno. Visit Seoul places the scene in KPop Demon Hunters where Rumi meets Jinu along the city wall here, and SOUL SPOT lists the park for the series Doona! as well. The Seoul City Wall office keeps the trail open 24 hours and calls the hill the Montmartre of Seoul for its sunsets and night views. From Hyehwa Station Exit 2 on Line 4, the top of the park is about 15 minutes' walk uphill.

Below the park lies Ihwa Village (이화마을), which the wall office describes as a long-neglected neighborhood transformed after 2006, when government support helped artists add murals and sculptures. People live behind those painted walls, and the office asks walkers on this stretch of wall to keep quiet for residents. Walk through Ihwa in daylight, in small groups, without speakers or long photo sessions on doorsteps, and save your evening for the park and the ramparts.

For a Lovely Runner stop, add the footbridge over Seongbukcheon (성북천) that SOUL SPOT calls Yeouldari, the bridge where Seoul's news service says the drama's time slip begins. The stream runs through Seongbuk-gu near the northern end of the Naksan wall trail, whose entrance is about three minutes from Hansung University Station Exit 4. A good sequence is the bridge in late afternoon, then the wall south to Naksan Park for sunset, then down through Ihwa to Hyehwa for dinner in the Daehangno theater district.

en.heading: Namsan to Itaewon: My Love from the Star and Itaewon Class
paragraphs: N Seoul Tower is the one location that links generations of fans. Visit Seoul lists it for scenes between Min-joon and Song-yi in My Love from the Star, SOUL SPOT for the film Single in Seoul, and Visit Seoul's KPop Demon Hunters guide notes the tower appears several times in that film. On Namsan's east side, the National Theater of Korea (국립극장) is where My Love from the Star's final-episode kiss was filmed, about 1 kilometer from Dongguk University Station Exit 6 on Line 3. Korea House (한국의집), a SOUL SPOT for The Whirlwind, is on the mountain's north foot.

Baekbeom Square (백범광장) in Namsan Park, five minutes from Hoehyeon Station Exit 4 on Line 4, is where Park Sae-ro-yi and Jo Yi-seo share the final-episode kiss in Itaewon Class, with the tower and the city wall behind them. The series' other signature, the Noksapyeong overpass at 195 Noksapyeong-daero, is just across the crosswalk from Noksapyeong Station Exit 3 on Line 6. Visit Seoul points out that the wide road beneath it runs toward Namsan and the tower, which is why the shot works. It is a working footbridge, so shoot from the side and keep the walkway clear.

If you walk on from the overpass into Itaewon, remember that a narrow sloping alley there is where 159 people died in the crowd crush of October 29, 2022. In October 2023 it was marked as the Path of Memory and Safety, with boards explaining what happened and messages of mourning in 14 languages. It is a place to pause quietly, not a photo backdrop. For the cable car, buses and tower tickets, use our Namsangol and Namsan guide.

en.heading: Cheonggyecheon to Sewoon: Marry My Husband, Queen of Tears and Vincenzo
paragraphs: Cheonggye Plaza (청계광장), where the restored stream begins, is the location Visit Seoul pairs with Marry My Husband, and the city's news service adds Gwangtonggyo (광통교), the stone bridge a few minutes downstream, as a location for both Marry My Husband and Queen of Tears. Jonggak Station, one block north of the stream, is SOUL SPOT's stop for Squid Game Season 2. Walk down to the water level, where the noise of the city drops away and the bridges frame each other.

Continue east along the stream to the bridge in front of the Sewoon arcade (세운상가), which Visit Seoul's SOUL SPOT course lists for Vincenzo, whose fictional Geumga Plaza tenants gave the series its warmth. Sewoon is still a working shopping center, so come on a weekday daytime if you want to see it open rather than shuttered. Gwangjang Market is a further walk east along the stream, and our market guide makes it the natural end of this route, with mung bean pancakes and makgeolli.

en.heading: Yeonnam and the riverside: lighter scenes for a second visit
paragraphs: Some locations reward a relaxed afternoon more than a pilgrimage. Gyeongui Line Forest Park (경의선숲길), the linear park laid over the old Gyeongui rail line, is the SOUL SPOT for Daily Dose of Sunshine; its Yeonnam-dong stretch near Hongik University Station is the liveliest part. Visit Seoul notes that Twenty Again also filmed in Yeonnam-dong and nearby Mangwon-dong. These are residential neighborhoods with cafés, not sets, so the right way to see them is with a coffee on a bench rather than a tripod in a doorway.

Along the Han River, SOUL SPOT pairs Yeouido Park with Melo Movie, Yeouido Hangang Park with A Time Called You and Jamsugyo Bridge with the film Single in Seoul. None of these needs a ticket, and all are better at dusk, when office workers and families come out and the bridges light up. If you have only one evening for drama sites, though, choose Naksan Park or the Namsan route over the riverside: the frames there are far more recognizable.

en.heading: Photo timing, and the courtesy that keeps these places open
paragraphs: Most of these locations are quiet streets, schools and homes that never asked to be famous, and Seoul has already restricted visiting hours in Bukchon because of tourist pressure. Fans who keep the habits below make it easier for the next fan to be welcome. They also make for better photos, since a calm weekday morning beats a crowded weekend afternoon at almost every spot in this guide.
checklist: Walk Bukchon's red zone only between 10:00 and 17:00, and keep your voice low in every residential lane.
Avoid Mondays for the Anguk and Jeong-dong walks: Baek In-je House, Gyeonghuigung, Changdeokgung and Changgyeonggung are closed. Jongmyo closes on Tuesdays.
Photograph schools from the gate only, and never during arrival or dismissal times.
Leave character costumes, prop weapons and mascot suits at home for palace visits unless you hold a filming permit.
On overpasses, bridges and stairways, shoot from the side and keep moving so others can pass.
In cafés and shops that appeared on screen, ask before photographing inside, and buy something if you stay.
Treat the Itaewon memorial alley as a place of mourning: no posing and no filming of people paying respects.

faq.q: Is there an official map of K-drama filming locations in Seoul?
faq.a: Yes. Seoul Metropolitan Government runs SOUL SPOT at soulspot.co.kr, with English, Japanese and Chinese pages for each location and recorded commentary you can play on your phone. In October 2026 it featured 20 drama, film and K-pop music video locations, including Naksan Park, the Noksapyeong overpass, N Seoul Tower and Jeongdong-gil. Some spots also carry a clapperboard-style plaque.

faq.q: Which single walk covers the most drama locations in the least time?
faq.a: The Anguk to Samcheong-dong loop: the Goblin house beside Unhyeongung, Baek In-je House from Reborn Rich, the Choong Ang High School gate, Bokjeong Well from Lovely Runner and Gamgodang-gil from Our Beloved Summer, in about two hours. Do it from 10:00 on a Tuesday to Friday, when Bukchon's red zone is open to visitors, Baek In-je House is open and the lanes are calmer than at weekends.

faq.q: Can I recreate a scene from Kingdom or another period drama at a palace?
faq.a: In ordinary clothes or hanbok, yes; souvenir photography is treated as already permitted. Character costumes, mascot suits and similar non-everyday outfits or props need a filming permit from the palace administration, and anything for commercial use needs a paid permit. Gyeonghuigung, where Kingdom used the throne hall, is free and quiet enough to compose a shot without crowds.

faq.q: Can I go inside the school from Our Beloved Summer and Lovely Runner?
faq.a: Plan not to. Choong Ang High School at 164 Changdeokgung-gil is an operating school, and its students have lessons, exams and breaks like any other. Photograph the gate from the street, outside arrival and dismissal times, and then move on to Gamgodang-gil, the other Our Beloved Summer location, which is a public street a short walk away.

faq.q: When is the best time to visit Naksan Park for KPop Demon Hunters photos?
faq.a: Late afternoon into evening. The Seoul City Wall office keeps the trail open around the clock and highlights the park's sunsets and night views, which match the film's night-time scene on the ramparts. Walk up from Hyehwa Station Exit 2 in about 15 minutes, and go through Ihwa Village before dark rather than after, out of courtesy to residents.

title.en: Korean Street Food in Seoul: What Each Snack Is, Where to Eat, How to Pay

summary.en: Tteokbokki, eomuk, sundae, hotteok and bungeoppang explained, with Seoul's street-food clusters, winter snacks, dated prices, ordering phrases and stall etiquette.

audience: First- and second-time visitors to Seoul who want to eat from stalls, carts and market counters with confidence: what to order, where, how to pay and what is in it.
method: Researched from the official sources listed below, checked on October 20, 2026. Hours, fees and booking rules can change; the linked official pages are the final word.
quickAnswer: Start with the classic trio of tteokbokki, twigim and sundae at a market counter, add a fish-cake skewer with its cup of broth, and in winter look for bungeoppang, hotteok and gyeranppang carts. Gwangjang Market's food alley (09:00–23:00 daily) is the most reliable cluster; Myeong-dong's evening stalls are a spectacle at higher prices. Carry small notes, check the price board and ask before you order if you avoid fish, pork or heat.

en.heading: Counters, carts and tents: three ways Seoul eats on the street
paragraphs: Street food in Seoul is less a cuisine than a habit: something hot, quick and cheap, eaten standing up between other plans. It comes in three settings that work differently. A bunsik (분식) counter, named for flour-based food, sells tteokbokki, gimbap, fried snacks and dumplings by the plate, and you usually sit on a stool or bench. A street stall or cart (노점, nojeom) does one or two things well, such as a fish-shaped pastry or a skewer, and you eat on the spot. A pojangmacha (포장마차), literally a covered wagon, is a tented stall that becomes a small bar after dark, where the food is anju, plates to share over soju.

Choose the setting before you choose the snack. For a first taste, a market counter with a posted price board is the easiest: you can see everything, point and sit. Carts are best for a single item on a cold afternoon. A pojangmacha is an evening out with drinks, better for two or more people than for a solo snack. Tourist streets charge noticeably more than markets for the same food, so decide whether you are paying for the spectacle or for the snack.

en.heading: How a soy-sauce dish became Seoul's red snack
paragraphs: Tteokbokki (떡볶이) was not always red. In a March 2026 column for the Korea JoongAng Daily, agricultural economist Moon Jung-hoon notes that a 1936 newspaper ingredient chart lists rice cakes with beef, mushrooms, egg, soy sauce and sesame oil and no chili, and that recipes of the 1950s and early 1960s still stir-fried the dish in oil with soy sauce. That savory style survives as gungjung tteokbokki (궁중떡볶이), royal-court tteokbokki, which VisitKorea says you will find mainly at traditional Korean restaurants rather than on the street.

The red version spread later. Its commonly cited origin is a Sindang-dong vendor in 1953, often identified as Ma Bok-rim, who mixed black bean paste and gochujang with boiling rice cakes. Moon points out that packaged gochujang only appeared in the mid-1960s, and that red tteokbokki took hold near schools in the late 1960s as an after-school snack. Government policies promoting wheat made wheat-based rice cakes cheaper than rice ones, which is why menus still distinguish 쌀떡 (ssal-tteok, rice) from 밀떡 (mil-tteok, wheat).

Today's street version is rice or wheat cakes and fish cake simmered in sweet-spicy gochujang sauce until it turns sticky, often with boiled eggs, and VisitKorea lists newer jjajang, cream and rosé flavors too. The sauce is cooked in one large pan for the whole day, so the heat is fixed; a vendor cannot make your portion milder. If chili is new to you, try a forkful from a companion's plate before ordering your own.

en.heading: The staples, decoded, and what to check before ordering
paragraphs: Most stalls display their food rather than a written menu, so recognizing the snacks matters more than reading Hangul. The table gives the Korean name you will see on signs, a plain description from VisitKorea and the press sources listed below, and the one thing worth checking. Winter-only items are marked, because many carts appear only when the weather turns cold.

rows: Rice or wheat cakes and fish cake in sweet-spicy gochujang sauce
Heat is fixed; contains fish cake
Fried fish-paste cakes threaded on long skewers and kept hot in broth
Fish; broth is often made with anchovy
Pork intestine filled with glass noodles and vegetables, steamed with pork blood
Pork and blood; served with seasoned salt or red sauce in Seoul

Nuts; the molten sugar is very hot

Muffin-style bread baked with a whole egg (winter)
Charcoal-grilled chicken skewer finished with salt, soy or spicy sauce
Fried rice cakes on a stick glazed with sweet-spicy sauce
Steamed bun, originally red bean or vegetable, kept in shop steamers (winter)
Tornado potato: a whole potato spiral-cut on a skewer, deep-fried and dusted with seasoning
Sweet potatoes or chestnuts roasted in their skins (winter)

en.heading: The tteok-twi-sun plate and the fish-cake pot
paragraphs: At a bunsik counter the classic order is 떡튀순 (tteok-twi-sun): tteokbokki, twigim and sundae on one plate, a trio VisitKorea singles out by that very nickname. The fried pieces are meant to be dragged through the tteokbokki sauce. In Seoul, sundae comes with seasoned salt or the same red sauce, while VisitKorea notes that other regions prefer soybean paste, chili paste with vinegar, salted shrimp or soy sauce. Say so if you want the sauce on the side rather than over everything.

Eomuk (어묵) is the most useful first snack on a cold day: cheap, mild and quick. Stalls keep the long skewers in a simmering pot and pour you a paper cup of the broth to sip, which VisitKorea describes as made with anchovy and radish. Many Koreans still say odeng (오뎅), a word the Korea Times traces to the Japanese oden, while eomuk is the Korean term. The same paper notes that Japanese colonial-era factories in Busan helped establish the industry, and that fish cakes became an affordable protein after the Korean War.

At stands where you pick skewers straight from the pot yourself, keep your empty sticks in your hand or in the cup the vendor provides. They are how the vendor counts what you owe, so do not drop them in a bin until you have paid. The trio plus one fish cake makes a full, filling meal for one person, and it is the best order for anyone who wants to understand why Koreans call these snacks comfort food.

en.heading: Winter snacks, and why Koreans now need a bungeoppang map
paragraphs: Cold weather brings out the carts. Bungeoppang (붕어빵), a fish-shaped pastry usually filled with red bean, descends from Japan's taiyaki, which reached Korea during the 1910–45 occupation, according to a December 2024 Korea Times guide. Cheap wheat flour after the Korean War made it a working-class snack through the 1960s and 1970s, and it came back during the late-1990s financial crisis. Its cousin ingeoppang (잉어빵), made with glutinous rice flour, has a chewier, thinner shell and more filling.

Prices tell the story of a shrinking trade. The Korea Times recalls bungeoppang selling at three for KRW 2,000 and reported in December 2024 that some downtown Seoul vendors were charging KRW 1,000 each. Rising costs have thinned out the carts so much that Koreans joke about living in a bungsegwon (붕세권), a neighborhood within reach of one, and Korean map services and the secondhand marketplace Karrot have built maps of where they are still sold. Searching 붕어빵 in Naver Map is a reasonable start.

Hotteok (호떡) is a chewy dough pancake folded around brown sugar, cinnamon and nuts and pressed flat in oil until the filling melts. The Korea Times cites the Korea Heritage Service's estimate that it arrived in the late 19th century with Qing merchants, and adds that Busan's seed-filled version dates from the Korean War, when refugees added seeds. Namdaemun Market's yachae hotteok swaps in glass noodles and vegetables; the Korea Times put it at KRW 2,500 in December 2024. Bite carefully, because the sugar inside is far hotter than the crust.

Gyeranppang (계란빵), a muffin-style bread with a whole egg baked into it, began in 1984 at a shop near Inha University in Incheon for customers who did not eat red bean, the Korea Times reports. Hoppang (호빵), the steamed bun, is a packaged-food story: Samlip launched it in October 1971 in red bean and vegetable versions and began supplying steamers to shops the following year, according to the Korea JoongAng Daily. VisitKorea notes that roasted sweet potatoes and chestnuts are now sold in convenience stores and subway stations as well as on the street.

en.heading: Myeong-dong at dusk: spectacle, price boards and the card question
paragraphs: Myeong-dong is the street-food scene most visitors picture: rows of stalls down the main shopping streets, with vendors setting up one by one in the late afternoon and crowds swelling toward dusk, as Financial News described in March 2026. The menu has drifted toward showpieces for tourists. In that report, chicken skewers and a single roll of gimbap cost KRW 5,000, fruit juices KRW 5,000 to 10,000, and steak or grilled lobster around KRW 20,000, prices the paper called relatively high.

Jung District, which manages the area, supplies the price boards that many stalls now use under a fixed-price policy. The same 2026 report found QR payments such as Alipay widely accepted, but some vendors discreetly covering their card-payment signs and reacting reluctantly when customers offered a card. Read the board before you order, ask 카드 돼요? if you need to pay by card, and keep a few small notes as a fallback.

Our judgment: go to Myeong-dong for the atmosphere and one or two novelty snacks, not for value or tradition. Early evening, before the densest crowds, is the most comfortable time to walk the stalls. If you want classic bunsik at ordinary prices, or a seat while you eat, the markets below serve the same staples to a largely local clientele.

en.heading: Market counters by daylight: Gwangjang, Namdaemun and Tongin
paragraphs: Gwangjang Market (광장시장) is the most dependable cluster. VisitKorea lists its food street at 09:00 to 23:00 and open all year, even though the market's other shops close on Sundays, and the counters there serve mung bean pancakes, mayak gimbap, sundae and tteokbokki. VisitKorea lists cards as accepted, but individual counters vary, so carry cash too. Our Gwangjang guide covers ordering, the market's price disputes and the measures Seoul has taken since.

Namdaemun Market (남대문시장), with over 10,000 stores and roots that Visit Seoul traces to King Taejong's reign, closes on Sundays; use Hoehyeon Station on Line 4. Its kalguksu alley is easy to miss: VisitKorea directs you from Exit 5 to a small transparent plastic door beside an eyeglasses shop, behind which diners sit shoulder to shoulder over knife-cut noodles and barley rice, often with cold buckwheat noodles on the side. Go on a weekday or Saturday, and combine it with a yachae hotteok.

Tongin Market (통인시장), about 515 meters from Gyeongbokgung Station Exit 2 on Line 3, is the gentlest introduction. Visit Seoul lists the market at 07:00 to 21:00, varying by shop, and points visitors to its gireum tteokbokki, rice cakes stir-fried in oil and chili rather than simmered in sauce. Its lunchbox café sells tokens you spend at stalls along the lane, and Visit Seoul gives the café's hours as 11:00 to 15:00, to 16:00 at weekends, closed on Mondays and the third Sunday of each month. Our Seochon guide explains the token system.

en.heading: Jongno 3-ga's tents, and a winter evening for two
paragraphs: The strip of pojangmacha near Jongno 3-ga Station, on the edge of the Ikseon-dong hanok lanes, is the easiest place to try a tented stall-bar. Visit Seoul, in a page edited in June 2026, says the tents start going up around 17:00 and serve chicken feet, rolled omelet, chewy udon and seafood pancakes with cold beer and soju. Sit down, order one or two plates for the table plus drinks, and expect to stay a while: these are bars, not snack counters, and a single skewer is the wrong order.

A worked example for a winter weekday. Arrive at Gwangjang's food alley around 16:00 and share a plate of mayak gimbap and one mung bean pancake. At about 16:45, walk west along Jong-ro, buying a bungeoppang or a hotteok if you pass a cart. Reach Jongno 3-ga around 17:30 as the tents fill, and order fish-cake soup and a rolled omelet with a bottle of soju or beer between two. Finish with a walk through Ikseon-dong's lanes, having eaten from a market counter, a cart and a tent in one evening.

en.heading: Ordering, paying and the words that do the work
paragraphs: Most exchanges at a stall take four steps: point at the food, say how many, confirm the price, pay. At counters and tent bars you usually pay when you finish; at carts you pay as you are served. Bring small notes, ask before ordering if you need to pay by card, and if a vendor asks for a bank transfer, offer cash or a card instead, since a transfer needs a Korean bank account. These phrases cover nearly every situation, and pointing does the rest.

en.heading: Heat, fish, pork and the empty-skewer problem
paragraphs: Spice and diet need planning, because labels are rare on the street. The mildest staples are eomuk, gyeranppang, hotteok, roasted sweet potatoes and sundae with salt. For vegetarians, the honest picture is that fish runs through the core menu: tteokbokki contains fish cake, eomuk is fish and its broth is commonly anchovy-based, and sundae is filled pork intestine steamed with blood. Roasted sweet potatoes and chestnuts are the safest choices; hotteok and bungeoppang usually are, but ask about the batter. Anyone with a nut allergy should treat hotteok as off limits.

Eat at the stall rather than walking off with a dripping cup of broth, and hand your cup and skewers back to the vendor when you finish. Public bins are scarce: the Korea Times reported in 2023 that Seoul had 4,956 street bins, down from 7,607 in 1995, after a volume-based waste fee led people to dump household rubbish in them and the city removed many. The city has said it will add bins back, but carry a small bag for wrappers, and never leave skewers on walls, steps or shop windowsills.

faq.q: Can I pay by card at Seoul street food stalls?
faq.a: Often, but not everywhere. Gwangjang Market's listing says cards are accepted, and many Myeong-dong stalls display card signs, yet a March 2026 report found some Myeong-dong vendors hiding them and reluctant to take cards. Market counters and carts vary. Ask 카드 돼요? before ordering, carry 1,000- and 5,000-won notes as a fallback, and decline any request to pay by bank transfer.

faq.q: Where should I go for street food on a first trip to Seoul?
faq.a: Gwangjang Market's food alley if you want classic dishes at counters where you can sit and see prices; it runs 09:00 to 23:00 every day. Myeong-dong in the early evening if you want the stall-lined spectacle and novelty snacks, at noticeably higher prices. Tongin Market near Gyeongbokgung is the calmest option, with its token lunchbox and oil-fried tteokbokki.

faq.q: What can vegetarians eat from Korean street stalls?
faq.a: Roasted sweet potatoes and chestnuts are the safest choices, and sweet hotteok and red-bean bungeoppang usually work, though batters vary. Avoid assuming that anything red or fried is meat-free: tteokbokki contains fish cake, eomuk broth is commonly anchovy-based, and sundae is pork intestine steamed with blood. Ask 고기 들어가요? and name fish separately.

faq.q: When is street food season in Seoul?
faq.a: Staples such as tteokbokki, gimbap and fish cakes are sold all year at markets and bunsik counters. The carts selling bungeoppang, hotteok, gyeranppang, roasted sweet potatoes and chestnuts are a cold-weather tradition, and convenience stores bring out steamed hoppang buns in winter. In summer, markets and Myeong-dong's evening stalls are the dependable options.

faq.q: Is it rude to eat while walking in Seoul?
faq.a: It is not forbidden, but stall food is designed to be eaten where you buy it: broth comes in a cup, sauces drip and vendors take back cups and skewers. Eating at the stall also solves the problem of Seoul's scarce public bins. On crowded shopping streets, step to the side rather than eating in the middle of the flow.

title.en: DMZ Tour from Seoul: What's Open in Paju and Where the JSA Stands

summary.en: Visiting the DMZ from Seoul in 2026: Paju's tour to the Third Tunnel and Dora Observatory, fees, passport and photo rules, and why the JSA is still closed.

audience: Independent visitors in Seoul deciding whether, how and on which day to see the DMZ, and whether the Joint Security Area at Panmunjom is possible.
method: Researched from the official sources listed below, checked on October 20, 2026. Hours, fees and booking rules can change; the linked official pages are the final word.
quickAnswer: You can see the DMZ from Seoul in a day, but not the Joint Security Area: the Ministry of Unification's Panmunjom tour site still lists public tours as suspended since July 18, 2023, with no reopening date. What is open is Paju City's DMZ Peace Tour from Imjingak, a roughly three-hour shuttle loop to the Third Tunnel, Dora Observatory and Unification Village, Tuesday to Sunday, with your original passport.
